questions.question: The origin of social and preventive medicine dates back to the:
questions.explanation: The origin of social and preventive medicine dates back to the 18th century. It began even before the germ theory had been proposed.

questions.question: Which medicine claims to be the world’s first organized body of medical knowledge?
questions.explanation:
Chinese medicine claims to be the world's first organized body of medical knowledge. It dates back to 2700 B.C. They are also considered to be the pioneers of immunization (used variolation against smallpox).

Modern Chinese medicine includes barefoot doctors and acupuncture.

questions.question: All of the following are true about the ministry of AYUSH except:
options: It was formed in 2014 in India for education and research on AYUSH
It aims to mainstream AYUSH as part of the National Rural Health Mission
It was previously known as department of Indian system of medicine and homeopathy
It regulates the fields of Ayurveda, Yoga, Homeopathy and Siddha only
questions.answer: D. It regulates the fields of Ayurveda, Yoga, Homeopathy and Siddha only
questions.explanation:
The Ministry of AYUSH was established to regulate the fields of Ayurveda, Yoga, and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, and Homeopathy.

It was formed in 2014 in India for the development of education and research in AYUSH. It was previously known as the Department of Indian System of Medicine and Homeopathy (ISM&H). It aims to mainstream AYUSH as part of the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM).

The Ayurveda, Siddha, and Yoga systems of medicine are of Indian origin. Ayurveda means knowledge of life. Its origin can be traced back to 5000 B.C (Vedic times). The medical knowledge in the Atharvaveda eventually developed into Ayurveda.

The Unani system is of Greek origin.

questions.question: Samuel Hahnemann is referred to as the founding father of:
questions.explanation:
Samuel Hahnemann is the founding father of homeopathy. He was German.

There are 3 principles in homeopathy:

1. Similia similibus curentur or human drug pathogenicity study: Treatment of disease using small amounts of drug that, in healthy people, would produce similar symptoms of the disease itself.

2. A single medicine is used for the treatment.

3. The minimum dose of the drug should be used.

questions.question: The Tridosha theory of disease explains disease as a disturbance in the equilibrium of the three humors. To which system of medicine does this theory belong to?
questions.explanation:
Tridosha theory of disease belongs to Ayurveda. It explains disease as a disturbance in the equilibrium of the three humors, namely:

• Vata (wind)

• Pitta (gall)

• Kapha (mucus).

A healthy person has a perfect balance of these humors.

This theory is similar to the Unani-tibb system of medicine which is based on four humors.

questions.question: Which system of medicine originated in Tamil–speaking areas in south India?
questions.explanation:
The Siddha system of medicine originated from Tamil culture. It means achievement.

This system believes that sociodemographic, psychological, and physiological factors related to a person must be taken into account while deciding the medical treatment. They believe that disease is a disturbance in the equilibrium of three humors called vaadham, pittam, and kapham.

questions.explanation:
The Unani-Tibb system of medicine originated in ancient Greece.

The Greeks believed that matter was made up of four elements. These elements had certain qualities that were represented in the body by the 4 humors and also determined the person's temperament.

questions.explanation:

He introduced the concept of the relationship between the environment and human health. He was the author of Airs, Water, and Places, a treatise on social medicine and hygiene as well as the Corpus Hippocraticum, a collection of 72 volumes of clinical case histories.

He also developed the Hippocratic Oath, which is considered the keystone of medical ethics.

Note: Tuberculosis is called the barometer of social welfare.

Match the following scientists with their discoveries:

1. John Snow
a. Germ theory of disease

2. Edward Jenner
b. Prevention of scurvy by citrus fruits

3. Louis Pasteur
c. Association of cholera with polluted water

4. James Lind
d. Smallpox vaccination
questions.explanation:
The discoveries of the given scientists are as follows:

• John Snow - association of cholera with polluted water

• Edward Jenner - smallpox vaccination

• Louis Pasteur - the germ theory of disease

• James Lind - prevention of scurvy by intake of citrus fruits

Louis Pasteur was the first to advance the germ theory of disease, which stated that most diseases were caused by microorganisms. This theory was later expanded by Robert Koch, who put forth Koch's postulates.

Pasteur is also known for the following contributions:

• Disproved the theory of spontaneous generation

• Developed vaccines for rabies and fowl cholera

• Pioneer of techniques of pasteurization and sterilization

questions.question: Who was the architect of the Public Health Act of 1848?
questions.explanation:
Edwin Chadwick was the architect of the Public Health Act of 1848.

He was an English lawyer during the 1832 cholera epidemic. He compiled a report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population in Great Britain that eventually led to the passing of this act. It is considered a landmark act in the history of public health.

questions.question: Identify the scientist who showed that anthrax was caused by a bacteria.
questions.explanation:
Robert Koch discovered that anthrax was caused by bacteria.

He also discovered the causative agents of tuberculosis and cholera. He won the Nobel prize in Physiology in 1905.

He also proposed Koch's postulates linking specific microorganisms to specific diseases. They state that the microorganism must be:

1. Found in abundance in diseased organisms, but not in healthy organisms.

2. Isolated from a diseased organism and grown in pure culture

3. Able to cause disease when inoculated into a healthy organism

4. Re-isolated from the diseased experimental host and identical to the original specific causative agent

The following images show Robert Koch and his drawing of the anthrax bacillus:

questions.question: In 1902, it was discovered that malaria was transmitted by the Anopheles mosquito. Who was behind this discovery?
questions.explanation:
Ronald Ross showed that malaria was transmitted by Anopheles mosquito.

Option B: Charles Alphonse Laveran discovered the malarial parasite.

Option C: Walter Reed showed that yellow fever transmitted by Aedes mosquito.

Option D: David Bruce showed that African sleeping sickness/trypanosomiasis transmitted by the tsetse fly.

questions.question: The first bacterium discovered as a cause of the disease was:
questions.explanation:
The first bacterium discovered as a cause of the disease is leprosy bacillus.

In 1873, Armauer Hansen demonstrated Mycobacterium leprae (rod-like bodies) from a leprosy nodule. This is the first time that chronic infectious disease in humans was shown to be related to a bacillus.

In 1876, Robert Koch validated the germ theory of disease after discovering the anthrax bacillus as the cause of anthrax.

questions.question: Max Joseph von Pettenkofer described the concept of:
questions.explanation:
Pettenkofer of Munich put forth the theory of multifactorial causation of disease.

Other theories of causation of disease include:

• Spontaneous generation theory - given by Aristotle

• Web of causation theory - given by MacMahon and Pugh

• Supernatural theory of disease

questions.question: In which country was the last case of naturally occurring smallpox in the world recorded?
questions.explanation:
The last case of naturally occurring smallpox was in Somalia in 1977.

The last case of smallpox occurred in 1978 when a medical photographer was accidentally exposed to the smallpox virus in a research laboratory in Birmingham.

India was declared smallpox-free on 24th May 1975. WHO declared smallpox as eradicated globally on 8th May 1980.

questions.question: Who first coined the term social medicine?
questions.explanation:
Jules Guérin coined this term as editor of the Gazette médicale de Paris. He was a French orthopaedist in the mid-1800s.

Option A: John Ryle promoted social medicine in England in the early 1900s.

Option C: Alfred Grotjahn described social pathology, the social factors influencing diseases.

Option D: Francis Albert Eley Crew stated that social medicine stood on the pillars of medicine and sociology.

questions.question: How would you define socialized medicine?
options: Subsidized medical care at government's expense
Free medical care provided and regulated by government alone
Free medical care at government expense, regulated by professional groups
Integration of social medicine with health care
questions.answer: C. Free medical care at government expense, regulated by professional groups
questions.explanation:
Socialized medicine is the provision of medical service at the government's expense but is operated and regulated by professional groups, and not the government. Russia was the first country to completely socialize medicine.

Free medical care by a government alone is called state medicine.

questions.question: All of the following are true about socialized medicine except:
options: Ensures social equity and universal coverage
Use state funds for free medicine
questions.answer: D. Promotes utilization of health facilities
questions.explanation:
Increasing the utilization of health services is not a component of socialized medicine.

It refers to the provision of medical service through the state funds; however, it is operated and regulated by professional groups. Russia was the first to completely socialize medicine.

It eliminates competition among physicians as well as ensures social equity and universal health coverage.

questions.question: Who said that the secret of national health lies in the homes of people?
questions.explanation: Florence Nightingale said that the secret of national health lies in the homes of people. She is considered the the founder of modern nursing.

questions.question: Which of the following is not included in the WHO definition of health?
questions.explanation:
According to the WHO, health is “a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity”.

In recent years, the definition has been modified to also include the ability to lead a “socially and economically productive life.”

questions.question: Which of the following is the biomedical concept of disease based upon?
options: Combination of social, economic and political influences
questions.explanation:
The biomedical concept of disease is based on the germ theory of disease, which was postulated by Louis Pasteur.

The germ theory of disease states that microorganisms known as pathogens or germs can lead to disease. It was criticized that it did not include environmental, social, psychological, and cultural determinants of health.

The ecological concept of disease states that disease is the maladjustment of the human organism to the environment.

The psychosocial concept of disease hypothesised that health is also influenced by social, psychological, cultural and economic factors as well.

The holistic concept of disease includes all the above concepts to describe health.

questions.question: Which of the following is a mortality indicator?
questions.explanation:
Life expectancy is a positive mortality indicator.

A set of values that measure the rate of mortality or death is known as mortality indicators.

Disability-adjusted life years (DALY), health adjusted life expectancy (HALE), and Sullivan’s Index are disability rates.

questions.question: An epidemiologist is tasked with measuring the overall health status of a community using a morbidity indicator. Which of the following indicators will she not use?
options: Number of days of restricted activity
questions.answer: C. Number of days of restricted activity
questions.explanation:
Number of days of restricted activity is a disability indicator.

Morbidity is defined as public health outcomes focusing on diseases, traumas, or injury. Morbidity indicators can be used to measure the overall health and extent of healthcare utilisation in a given population.

Disability is defined as public health outcomes related to health conditions that include limitations in personal activities and societal participation. There are two types of disability indicators as follows:

• Event type indicators-

• Number of days of restricted activity

• Bed disability days

• Work loss days (or school loss days) within a specified period

• Person type indicators-

• Limitation of mobility: e.g confined to bed

• Limitation of activity: e.g limitation to perform the basic activities of daily living such as eating and going to the toilet

questions.question: Which of the following indicators can be used to estimate the number of years a newborn would be expected to live in full health based on the current rates of ill health and mortality?
questions.explanation:
HALE (Health Adjusted Life Expectancy) is an indicator that can be used to estimate the number of years a newborn is expected to live in full health based on the current rates of ill health and mortality.

HALE is calculated using the life expectancy at birth with an adjustment for time spent in poor health. It captures both fatal and non-fatal health outcomes of average levels of population health. It is also sensitive to changes over time or differences between countries in the distribution of health states.

Sullivan's index is also known as disability-free life expectancy (DFLE) or active life expectancy. It is the average number of years an individual is expected to live free of disability if the current patterns of mortality and disability continue to apply. It doesn’t take into account premature death. As HALE includes not just disability but the larger definition of poor health, it is a better option with respect to the question.

questions.question: While assessing the health needs of a community, an epidemiologist is tasked with estimating the burden of cholera in the area. Which of the following is the simplest measure he can use?
questions.explanation:
The proportional mortality rate is the simplest measure of estimating the burden of disease in the community. It signifies the proportion of all deaths that can be attributed to the disease.

It is calculated as follows:

Proportional mortality rate of a disease = (No. of deaths due to that disease in the year/ Total no. of deaths in the year) *100.

Option A: Case fatality rate measures the risk of persons dying from a certain disease within a given time period. It measures the killing power of a disease. It is used to link mortality to morbidity.

Option B: Incidence measures the rate at which new cases are occurring in a population. It is not influenced by the duration of the disease. The use of incidence is generally restricted to acute diseases.

Option C: Crude death rate is considered a fair indicator of the comparative health of the people. It is the rate of total deaths in a year compared to the mid-year population.

questions.question: You are researching the overall burden of COVID on a given population. Which of the following disability indicators is the best measure of this?
questions.explanation:
Disability adjusted life years (DALY) is the best measure of the overall burden of a disease in a defined population. It is also the best measure of the effectiveness of interventions.

DALY is calculated as - Years of lost life prematurely (YLL) + Years lost to disability (YLD). It can measure both mortality and disability together.

As DALY is affected by premature loss of life, conditions that affect younger individuals like road traffic accidents have a high DALY. In comparison to this, Alzheimer's disease has a lower DALY as it is a disease that mostly develops during old age and so has a lower YLL.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a health utilisation rate?
options: Average length of stay in hospital
questions.explanation:
Bed disability days is not a utilisation rate. It is an event-type disability indicator. It is defined as the number of days a person spent in a hospital bed due to illness or injury.

Health utilisation rate is defined as the number of people making use of the available health services to the total number of individuals in that population.

Health utilisation rates include:

• Proportion of infants immunized against 9 diseases in the expanded program on immunization (EPI)

• Proportion of women receiving antenatal care and supervised delivery

• Percentage of population using family planning methods

• Bed occupancy rate

• Average length of stay in the hospital

• Bed turnover ratio

questions.question: As the medical superintendent of a hospital, you wish to optimise the utilization of health services. What bed turnover interval should you aim for?
questions.explanation:
For optimum utilization of health services in a hospital, bed turnover interval must always be slightly positive.

Bed turnover interval is defined as the time interval where a hospital bed is left unoccupied following a patient’s discharge till the next patient occupies it after admission.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best indicator of availability, utilization, and effectiveness of health services?
questions.explanation:
Infant mortality rate (IMR) is the best indicator of the availability, utilization, and effectiveness of health care. It is a very sensitive indicator.

Infant mortality rate (IMR)= Number of deaths in the first year of life/Number of live births x 1000

It is also one of the best indicators of state failure. It is the most universally accepted health status indicator of the whole population and of the socio-economic status in which they live.

Note: The best indicator of socio-economic development is the under-5 mortality rate.

questions.question: While reviewing a national health programme, you are asked to assess the cost-effectiveness of the interventions provided under it. Which indicator will you use to measure this?
questions.explanation: QALY(Quality Adjusted Life Years) is used in assessing the cost-effectiveness (value of money) of a medical intervention. It is a measure of both the quality and quantity of life lived. It indicates the number of years of life that would be added by the intervention.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a socio-economic determinant of health?
questions.explanation:
Lifestyle is a behavioural and socio-cultural determinant of health. It is not a socio-economic determinant.

Socio-economic determinants of health are the following:

• Economic status (per capita GNP)

• Education

• Occupation

• Political system

Lifestyle is simply the way people live. It reflects our social values, attitudes, and activities. It is composed of:

• Cultural patterns (daily nutrition, superstitions)

• Behavioral patterns (personal hygiene, sedentary life)

• Lifelong personal habits (e.g. smoking, alcoholism)

Lifestyle is learned by social interaction with parents, siblings, friends, school, and mass media.

Our political system determines our health. It can help shape community health services with regards to resource allocation, manpower policy, choice of technology, and the degree to which these services are made available & accessible to all segments of the society.

The percentage of GDP spent on health is an indicator of political commitment. WHO recommends at least 5% of GDP to be spent on health care. India spends about 2.1 % of its GDP on health(budget 2022-23).

questions.question: Which of the following is not a socio-economic indicator of health?
questions.explanation:
Annual family income is not a socioeconomic indicator of health.

Socio-economic indicators of health (mnemonic: H – FLAGGED):

• Housing (number of persons per room)

• Family size

• Literacy rate (especially female literacy rate)

• Availability of per capita calorie

• GNP per capita

• Growth rate of population

• UnEmployment level

• Dependency ratio

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding positive health in today’s world?
options: It is dependent on social, economic, and cultural determinants
It is a mirage because of changing environment
It means that the body and mind are at peace
It includes provision of free health camps by the government
questions.answer: D. It includes provision of free health camps by the government
questions.explanation:
The provision of free health camps by the government is a concept of state medicine.

Health does not merely mean the absence of disease or provision of diagnostic, curative, and preventive services. It is a state of physical, mental, and social well-being.

The state of positive health is based on the idea of perfect functioning of the body and mind. According to this concept, health is:

• Biologically a state in which every cell and organ in the body is functioning at optimum capacity

• Psychologically a state in which the individual feels a sense of perfect well-being and mastery over his environment

• Socially a state in which the individual's capacities for participation in the social system are optimal

This concept is too idealistic and can never become a reality. Humans can never be so perfectly adapted to the environment because everything in our life is subject to change.

As the goal of positive health is unattainable, a broader concept of improving the quality of life has emerged. This highlights that positive health depends on medical action and also on economic, cultural, and social factors in the community.

questions.question: As per the WHO, which of the following is not included in the standard of living?
questions.explanation:
Social security is a component of the level of living as per the United Nations and not standard of living.

According to the WHO, the standard of living includes:

• Income and occupation

• Standards of housing, sanitation, and nutrition

• Level of provision of health, educational, and recreational services

It depends on per capita GNP.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best measure of the standard of living?
questions.explanation:
Human development index (HDI) is the best measure of the standard of living of a population.

Physical quality of life index (PQLI) measures the quality of life.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a component of the human development index (HDI)?
questions.explanation:
Infant mortality rate (IMR) is not a component of HDI. It is a component of the physical quality of life index (PQLI).

The human development index (HDI) is used to compare living standards in different countries. It includes the following dimensions or components:

Component
Indicator
Index

Longevity
Life expectancy at birth
Life expectancy index

Knowledge
Literacy and enrolment
Education index

Income
GNI per capita US$ (purchasing power parity-PPP)
GNI index (income index)

Each dimension index is calculated using the formula: Dimension Index = (Actual Value - Minimum Value)/(Maximum Value - Minimum Value)

HDI is the geometric mean of the three indices: ILife1/3 x IEducation1/3 x IIncome1/3.

As per the Human Development Report 2023-2024, India's Human Development Index (HDI) value is 0.644. This places India at 134th out of 193 countries.

questions.question: What are the minimum and maximum values established for the calculation of the life expectancy index in HDI?
questions.explanation:
The minimum value established for the calculation of the life expectancy index in HDI is 20 years and the maximum is 85 years.

These minimum and maximum values are used to calculate the dimension indices in HDI and are called goalposts.

Each dimension index is calculated using the formula:

Dimension Index = (Actual Value - Minimum Value)/(Maximum Value - Minimum Value).

questions.question: Which of the following is not true regarding the education index used for calculating the HDI?
options: It includes expected years of schooling
Adult literacy rate is not considered
Minimum and maximum values are based on global data
questions.answer: B. Gross enrollment ratio is considered
questions.explanation:
The gross enrollment ratio is no longer used in obtaining the education index in HDI. It was used as an indicator earlier.

The education index is calculated by taking into account the mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling. Maximum and minimum values are based on global data.

Adult literacy rate and gross enrollment ratio were used as indicators before 2009.

questions.question: Which of the following indices measures the deprivation in basic dimensions of the country in human development?
questions.explanation:
Human poverty index (HPI) measures deprivation in basic dimensions of human development.

HPI-1 is used for developing countries and HPI-2 is used for developed countries. It is based upon the following indicators:

Human Poverty Index (HPI-1) for developing countries

Human Poverty Index (HPI-2) for selected OECD countries

A long and healthy life

Probability at birth of not surviving to age 40

Probability at birth of not surviving to age 60

Knowledge
Adult illiteracy rate
Percentage of adults lacking functional literacy skills

A decent standard of living

Percentage of the population not using an improved water source

Percentage of children underweight for age

Deprivation of a decent standard of living

Percentage of people living below the poverty line

Social exclusion
Not included as a dimension
Long term unemployment rate

The range of HPI is from 0 to 100. The term HPI has now been replaced with multidimensional poverty index (MPI).

questions.question: Which of the following is not included in the Ottawa charter for health promotion?
questions.explanation:
Building social security is not included in the Ottawa charter for health promotion.

The first international conference for health promotion was held in Ottawa on 21st Nov 1986. It produced a charter known as the Ottawa charter.

The charter identified five key action areas as given below:

• Build healthy public policy

• Create supportive environment for health

• Strengthen community action for health

• Develop personal skills

• Reorient health services

questions.question: Which of the following is not a component of the epidemiological triad for tuberculosis?
questions.explanation:
Duration of illness is not a part of the epidemiological triad for tuberculosis.

The epidemiological triad includes host, agent and environment:

• Host factors: Age, sex, religion, race, genetic profile, immune system

• Agent factors:

• Biological - bacteria, viruses

• Chemical - poisons, alcohol, smoke

• Physical - trauma, fire, radiation

• Nutrition - lack/excess

• Environmental factors:

• Temperature, humidity, altitude

• Water, milk, food

• Radiation, pollution, noise

• Crowding, housing, neighborhood

Hence, a malnourished child (host), Mycobacterium tuberculosis (agent) and overcrowding (environment) form the epidemiological triad for tuberculosis.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most logical sequence?
questions.explanation:
Disease → Impairment → Disability → Handicap is the most logical sequence among the given options.

Disease is a state of physiological/psychological dysfunction.

Impairment is any loss or abnormality in normal structure or function.

Disability is the inability to carry out normal actions due to impairment.

Handicap is the disadvantage due to disability that limits fulfilment of a role that is normal.

questions.question:
A salesman met with an unfortunate accident that led to him eventually losing his left foot. He has been unable to walk after this incident and so been rendered unemployed. Match the following examples with the corresponding events explaining the concept of disability.

Event
Example

1.Disability
A. Loss of foot

2. Disease/Disorder
B. Cannot Walk

3. Handicap
C. Accident

4. Impairment
D. Unemployed
questions.explanation:
The correctly matched events relating to the given example are as follows:

Event
Example

Disease/Disorder
Accident

Impairment
Loss of foot

Disability
Cannot Walk

Handicap
Unemployed

The WHO definition of impairment is "any loss or abnormality of psychological, physiological or anatomical structure or function". E.g., loss of a foot. An initial impairment may cause a secondary impairment as well.

The WHO defines disability as ''any restriction or lack of ability to perform an activity in the manner or within the range considered normal for a human being". Because of impairment, the affected person may be unable to carry out certain activities and hence the person is considered disabled.

According to the WHO, a handicap is "a disadvantage for a given individual, resulting from an impairment or a disability, that limits or prevents the fulfilment of a role that is normal (depending on age, sex, and social and cultural factors) for that individual". The disadvantages experienced by a person as a result of disability makes them handicapped.

questions.question: Which of the following is most appropriate about the web of disease causation?
options: It implies that individual factors in the web have equal weightage
It implies that all the chains of causation must be controlled to prevent disease
It is mostly applicable for acute and rare diseases
It suggests ways of interrupting the disease occurrence
questions.answer: D. It suggests ways of interrupting the disease occurrence
questions.explanation:
The web of causation for a disease suggests a number of ways to interrupt the disease occurrence/progression.

This model was suggested by MacMahon and Pugh in their book ‘Epidemiologic Principles and Methods’.

Web of causation considers all the predisposing factors and their complex interrelationship with each other. This model is ideally suited in the study of chronic disease. The web of causation does not imply that the disease is controlled only when all the multiple chains of causation are removed. Sometimes removal of one significant link is sufficient to control the disease.

In a multifactorial event, individual factors are by no means of equal weightage. The importance of each factor is expressed in terms of relative risk.

questions.question: Which of the following is not true regarding the pathogenesis period of a disease?
options: Recovery is seen in this period
Entry of causative agent is seen
questions.explanation:
Primary prevention is not possible in the pathogenesis period of a disease. It can only be done in the period of pre-pathogenesis.

The two phases in the natural history of a disease include:

• Period of pre-pathogenesis: It is before the onset of disease in humans. The disease agent has not entered the host, but the factors favouring the disease already exist. Primary prevention (health promotion and specific protection) is applicable in this period.

• Period of pathogenesis: It begins with the entry of the organism till recovery, death or disability. Secondary (halting of the disease process) and tertiary prevention (measures to limit disability) are applicable in this period. It isn't always characterised by the presence of disease symptoms as it also includes subclinical cases.

questions.question: In the iceberg phenomenon of disease, which of the following does not represent the submerged portion of the iceberg?
questions.explanation:
Epidemiologically, the iceberg phenomenon of disease, diagnosed cases are represented by the floating tip of the iceberg.

The iceberg phenomenon of disease is related to the spectrum of disease. The water surface is the line of demarcation between the apparent and inapparent infections.

The submerged portion of the iceberg represents the hidden mass of diseases like asymptomatic, latent, and undiagnosed cases. Screening is done to identify these cases.

The iceberg phenomenon of disease is depicted in the image below.

questions.question: Which of the following diseases shows the iceberg phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
Rubella shows the iceberg phenomenon of disease.

The iceberg phenomenon of diseases is not shown by diseases such as tetanus, rabies, and measles.

Iceberg phenomenon is shown by:

• Polio

• Influenza

• Rubella

• Mumps

• Japanese Encephalitis

• Diphtheria

• Hepatitis A and B

• Tuberculosis

• Diabetes

• Malnutrition

• Hypertension

Note: If a disease has more number of subclinical infections, it shows the iceberg phenomenon of disease depicted in the image below.

questions.question: What is the term used to describe the interruption in the transmission of a disease?
questions.explanation:
Interruption in the transmission of a disease is called elimination. It is a step towards eradication.

Elimination is a reduction in the number of new cases of an infectious disease to zero (or a very low defined target rate) in a defined geographical area as a result of deliberate efforts. Continued measures to prevent re-establishment of transmission are required.

Eradication is a complete and permanent worldwide reduction to zero new cases of an infectious disease through deliberate efforts. No further control measures are required.

Surveillance is the continuous scrutiny of factors that determine the occurrence and distribution of disease and ill health.

Control aims at decreasing the incidence, duration and transmission of the disease. It also aims at decreasing the physical and psychological complications of a disease.

questions.question: Among the following options, which aids the most in disease elimination?
questions.explanation:
Herd immunity aids the most in disease elimination.

Herd immunity achieved, especially through immunization, goes a long way in helping the elimination of diseases. When a high level of herd immunity is maintained, the susceptible population is reduced to a small proportion, thereby eliminating the disease.

The purpose of isolation is to protect the community by preventing the transfer of infection from the reservoir to the possible susceptible hosts. Quarantine refers to restrictions on the healthy contacts of an infectious disease.

questions.question: While collecting surveillance data for disease X, you find that the incidence of the disease is zero in your region. Which of the following statements best describes this scenario?
options: Disease is eliminated from the region.
Disease is well controlled in the region.
Disease is eradicated from the region.
Disease shows iceberg phenomenon in the region.
questions.answer: A. Disease is eliminated from the region.
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, as the disease has zero incidence, we can say the disease has been eliminated from the region.

Elimination is a reduction in the number of new cases of an infectious disease to zero (or a very low defined target rate) in a defined geographical area as a result of deliberate efforts. Continued measures to prevent re-establishment of transmission are required.

Eradication is a complete and permanent worldwide reduction to zero new cases of an infectious disease through deliberate efforts. No further control measures are required.

Control aims at decreasing the incidence, duration and transmission of the disease. It also aims at decreasing the physical and psychological complications of a disease.

The iceberg phenomenon of disease is related to the spectrum of disease. The submerged portion of the iceberg represents the hidden mass of diseases like asymptomatic, latent, and undiagnosed cases. The clinical or diagnosed cases are represented by the floating tip of the iceberg and not the submerged portion. As disease incidence is zero here, there are no cases to form the iceberg.

questions.question: Which of the following is a silent epidemic?
questions.explanation:
Alzheimer’s disease is referred to as the silent epidemic of the century.

Nearly 50 million people globally are living with this disease. Since it strikes so often, so arbitrarily, and with such little warning, many have dubbed it the silent epidemic.

questions.question: What is the analysis of routine measurements aimed at detecting changes in the health status of a population called?
questions.explanation:
The analysis of routine measurements aimed at detecting changes in the health status or environment of a population is called monitoring.

Surveillance is the continuous scrutiny of factors that determine the occurrence and distribution of disease and ill health.

Sentinel surveillance is a method of identifying the missing cases and thereby supplementing the notified cases.

Systematic reviews involve a detailed plan with the goal of reducing bias by identifying, appraising, and synthesizing all relevant studies on a particular topic.

questions.question: In which of the following does surveillance of disease not have a direct role?
options: Data on new and changing trends
questions.explanation:
Surveillance of a disease does not have a direct role in breaking the chain of transmission.

Surveillance is the continuous scrutiny of factors that determine the occurrence and distribution of disease and ill health.

It helps in health planning and provides information about public health disasters including data on new and changing trends of disease.

Surveillance requires professional analysis and sophisticated judgment of data, leading to recommendations for control activities.

questions.question: Measures in sentinel surveillance do not aim at identifying:
questions.explanation:
Sentinel surveillance does not include identifying cases free of disability.

Sentinel surveillance helps in identifying the missing cases, in addition to the already existing and new cases. It is used for supplementing routine notifications.

questions.question: Which of the following is public health surveillance preferentially aimed at?
questions.explanation:
Public health surveillance is preferentially aimed at health planning.

Public health surveillance provides important feedback on the health status of the population, about planning control and prevention activities, and also for public health disasters.

questions.question: Which of the following is included under primordial prevention of coronary artery disease?
questions.explanation:
Adoption of a healthy lifestyle from childhood would fall under the category of primordial prevention of coronary artery disease.

Primordial prevention is preventing the emergence of risk factors among population groups in which these risk factors have not yet appeared. Most adult health problems (obesity, hypertension) have their early origins in childhood. It is in childhood that lifestyles are formed i.e. eating patterns, physical exercise, smoking, etc.

In primordial prevention, efforts are made to discourage children from adopting harmful lifestyles.

These lifestyle changes when made by adults are known as primary prevention.

questions.question: What type of prevention is the prescriptive screening of a disease?
questions.explanation:
Prescriptive screening of a disease is an example of secondary prevention.

Prescriptive screening of disease can lead to early diagnosis of disease. By early diagnosis, intervention can be made to prevent disability. Hence, it comes under secondary prevention.

questions.question: What form of prevention is prospective screening?
questions.explanation:
Prospective screening is a type of primary prevention.

Prospective screening is done on healthy individuals to screen for disease. It is done prior to the onset of the disease. E.g., screening donated blood for HIV before it is transfused. This type of prevention reduces the incidence of disease.

Note: Prescriptive screening is done for case detection. People are screened for their own benefits. It is an early diagnosis of diseases existing in them. This is a form of secondary prevention. E.g., neonatal screening for hypothyroidism, pap smear for detection of cervical cancer.

questions.question: You advise a reproductive age woman to vaccinate against HPV. What is this type of prevention called?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario of immunisation is an example of primary prevention.

Primary prevention is an action taken before the onset of disease. This reduces the possibility of disease occurrence. Hence, immunization is a form of primary prevention, through specific protection.

Examples of primary prevention include immunization, sanitation, solid and liquid waste management etc.

questions.question: Who among the following is not a target for primary prevention?
questions.explanation:
Asymptomatic patients are the target population for secondary prevention but not for primary prevention.

Primary prevention is implemented before the onset of the disease. Hence, all patients including asymptomatic ones are not included in the target group.

questions.question: As a part of the iodine deficiency control programme, you advocate the usage of iodized salt in hilly areas. What is this type of prevention an example of?
questions.explanation: The usage of iodized salt in iodine-deficient areas like in hilly regions is an example of primary prevention as it provides specific protection.

questions.question: You are performing a routine pap smear on a 30-year-old woman in the gynecology OPD. What level of prevention does this fall under?
questions.explanation:
Pap smear is a screening test for carcinoma cervix and is an example of secondary prevention.

Early diagnosis (including screening) and treatment are the components of secondary prevention. Some of the examples of secondary prevention are as follows:

• Papanicolaou (Pap) smear for early detection of cervical cancer

• Mammography for early detection of breast cancer

• Colonoscopies for early detection of colon cancer

• Blood Pressure Screening

Secondary prevention measures focus on the sub-clinical stage and the early clinical stage, such as dysplasia in this case.

These measures enable early detection and prompt effective intervention to correct departures from a state of health.

questions.question: What mode of prevention is disability prevention by appropriate treatment an example of?
questions.explanation:
Disability prevention by appropriate treatment is an example of secondary prevention. This is because disability has not occurred yet so correct treatment can stop it from developing.

After the disability has set in, prevention of progression of disability from transitioning into a handicap is tertiary prevention. It is also called disability limitation.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of disability limitation?
options: Starting a patient on anti-tuberculous therapy
questions.answer: A. Prescribing spectacles for refractive error
questions.explanation:
Prescribing spectacles for refractive error is an example of disability limitation which is a component of tertiary prevention. This mode of intervention is applicable when the patient presents late in the pathogenesis phase.

The objective of this intervention is to prevent or halt the transition of the disease process from impairment to handicap.

Option B: Starting a patient on anti-tuberculous therapy is secondary prevention as it is a part of treatment.

Option C: Abstinence from smoking is a modification of the risk factor. Hence it is an example of primary prevention.

Option D: Early fixation of fractures will prevent disability. Hence, it is an example of secondary prevention.

questions.question: Which among the following diseases was eliminated in India in 2015?
questions.explanation:
Maternal and neonatal tetanus was eliminated from India in 2015, as certified by the WHO.

Important years for India (declared disease-free):

• Infective trachoma - 2017

• Yaws - 2016

• Maternal & neonatal tetanus - 2015

• Polio - 2014

• Guinea worm disease (dracunculiasis) - 2000

Worldwide eradication:

• Type-2 wild poliovirus - 2015

• Type-3 wild poliovirus- 2019

• Smallpox - 1980

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about ICD- 11?
options: It includes a new chapter on traditional medicine
Gender incongruence is now listed as part of mental health
The codes relating to antimicrobial resistance are more closely in line with the Global Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance System
It has come into full effect from January 2022
questions.answer: B. Gender incongruence is now listed as part of mental health
questions.explanation:
The new ICD-11 has a new chapter on sexual health that contains gender incongruence, which was previously listed under mental health conditions in the ICD-10.

The ICD 11 was released by the WHO in June 2018 and was presented at the World Health Assembly in May 2019 for adoption by the Member States. It has come into effect from 1 January 2022.

Its designations for antibiotic resistance align with the Global Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance System (GLASS). It is given by the WHO and is revised every 10 years.

New chapters added in ICD-11 are:

• Traditional medicine

• Sexual health: Gender incongruence has been moved from mental health to sexual health.

• Gaming disorder has been added under Addictive disorders.

• Immune system disorders, which will enable the better study of allergies.

It has more detail on cancer, specifically different types of skin cancer, as well as on heart health and weight disorders compared to ICD-10.

questions.question: What is meant by the term sociology?
options: Study of developments in the society
Study of formation of social organisations and government
Study of human relationships and behavior
Study of social and cultural history of man
questions.answer: C. Study of human relationships and behavior
questions.explanation: Sociology is considered to be both the study of human relationships and of human behavior.

questions.question: Which of the following social sciences does not deal directly with human behavior?
questions.explanation:
Political science refers to the study of the judicial systems and institutions that constitute the government. It does not deal directly with human behavior.

Anthropology is the study of the physical, social, and cultural history of man. Social anthropology is extensively used in preventive and social medicine.

Social psychology is aimed at understanding the basis of perception, thoughts, ideas, etc., among people in a society or group.

Sociology is the study of human relationships and human behavior.

questions.question:
Match the following:

Social Sciences
Definition

1.
Social pathology
i.
Study of social factors influencing human disease

2.
Social medicine
ii.
The provision of medical service by State, operated and regulated by professional groups

3.
Socialized medicine
iii.
Effect of social environment on people and their attitude

4.
Social psychology
iv.
Promotion of methods for prevention of disease and health measures
questions.explanation:
Social pathology refers to the study of social factors, which influence human disease and incite social disorganization. This includes crime, poverty, delinquency, abuse, etc.

Social medicine is an organized investigation of the social, environmental, and genetic factors affecting disease patterns and disability. It also deals with the promotion of methods for the prevention of disease and health measures.

Socialized medicine is the provision of medical service and education by the State. It is operated and regulated by professional groups, and not the government.

Social psychology is the effect of the social environment on people, their attitudes, and motivation. It deals with the study of human behavior, thoughts, and feelings and how they are influenced by the perception of others in society.

questions.question: 'Putting profit ahead of health' as a cause of disease belongs to which theory of sociology of health?
questions.explanation:
Putting profit ahead of health is termed as the cause of disease in the Marxist theory of sociology of health.

Elias' theory focused on the relationship between power, behavior, emotion, and knowledge over time.

Theory
Marxist
Parsonian
Foucauldian

Description
Emphasized causal role of economics in disease and the role of medical knowledge in sustaining class structure
Emphasized role of medicine in maintaining social harmony
Emphasized the role of ‘helping professions’ in inducing individuals to comply with social roles

Model of Society
Conflictual and exploitative
Harmonious and stable set of interlinked social roles and structures
Net of power relations with no one dominant source

Cause of Disease
Putting profit ahead of health
Social strain caused by meeting the demands of social roles
Diseases are labels used to sort and segregate the population to make it easier to control

Role of Medical Professional

To discipline and control the working class

To provide individualized explanations of the disease

Rehabilitate individuals to carry out their social roles

To enforce compliance with the normal social roles and to ensure internalization of these norms.

questions.question: Which of the following refers to a system of social relationships between individuals?
questions.explanation:
Society is the system of social relationships between people in an area.

A community is a social group determined by geographical boundaries and/or common values and interests.

A family is a group of biologically related individuals living together under the same roof and eating from a common kitchen.

Social Institutions are organized complex patterns of behavior in which a number of people engage to further a common interest.

questions.question: Which of the following options is correctly matched?
options: Social institution- the pattern of inter-relations between persons in a society
Socialism- organised complex patterns of behaviour in people with a common interest
Social structure- system of governance based on social ownership
Socialization- the process by which a person imbibes the social beliefs and customes
questions.answer: D. Socialization- the process by which a person imbibes the social beliefs and customes
questions.explanation:
Socialization is the process by which a person in a society imbibes its beliefs, customs, etc. through daily interaction with its members.

Social institutions are organized complex patterns of behaviour in which a number of people engage to further a common interest. Examples are families, schools, hospitals, etc.

Socialism is a system of governance in which production and distribution is based on social ownership (and not private ownership). It is aimed at improving the living standard.

Social structure is the pattern of inter-relations between persons in a society.

questions.question: Which of the following terms is used to describe the preventive, therapeutic, and rehabilitative services for the protection of society from antisocial, criminal, or deviant conduct of man?
questions.explanation:
Preventive, therapeutic and rehabilitative services for the protection of society from antisocial, criminal or deviant conduct of man is known as social defence.

This is in the form of acts, laws and judicial instructions for elements like juvenile delinquency, begging, prison reforms, gambling, etc.

questions.question:
Match the following.

Terms
Definitions

1. Customs
i. Scale of the expenditure of a society, the goods, and services

2. Standard of living
ii. Duties assumed by a person of a particular society

3. Culture
iii. Learned behavior which is socially acquired

4. Role
iv. Traditionally accepted ways of behaving in a society
questions.explanation:
Culture is the socially acquired learned behaviour. It is passed onto generations through formal and informal learning. It is the representation of customs, beliefs, laws, arts, and moral values of a society. Cultural factors have a large part to play in health.

Customs are the traditionally accepted ways of behaving that is specific to a society. They can be folkways, which are referred to as the right ways of doing things in less vital areas of human conduct. Mores are stringent customs followed by a society.

Standard of living refers to the scale of the expenditure of a society, the goods they consume and the services they enjoy.

Role is the function or duties assumed by a person of a particular society.

questions.question: Which of the following does not bring about acculturation?
questions.explanation:
Acculturation is the process by which there is the diffusion of cultures between two culturally different groups of people. Acculturation does not take place by folklore. Folklore is the passage of customs and beliefs of a community through generations, merely by word of mouth.

Acculturation can happen in the following ways:

• Trade and commerce

• Industrialization

• Religious propagation

• Education

• Conquest

This phenomenon is also known as culture contact.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct ascending order of the Maslow’s hierarchy of needs?
questions.answer: D. Physiological, safety, belonging, esteem, self-actualization
questions.explanation:
Maslow’s hierarchy of needs was suggested by psychologist Abraham Maslow. It is a motivational theory in psychology where human needs are arranged according to hierarchy in a five-level pyramid.

He suggested that the higher needs can be fulfilled only once the lower needs are fulfilled.

The ascending order of the needs is shown in the image below.

questions.question: Which of the following could be classified as an ego-integrative need of man?
questions.explanation:
Ego-integrative needs of man include power, prestige and self-respect.

The needs of man are as follows:

• Biological needs- water, food, warmth, medicines, etc.

• Social needs- love and affection, fellowship, education, etc.

• Economic needs- money and security

• Ego-integrative needs- power, prestige and self-respect.

questions.question: What is the benefit that comes from solving one’s own problems termed?
questions.explanation:
Intrinsic incentives are the benefits that come from solving one’s own problems.

Incentives are entities that motivate or encourage a specific behaviour. They are generally positive motivators. The various types of incentives are:

• Intrinsic incentives are the benefits that come from solving one’s own problems.

• Extrinsic incentives are rewards that do not relate directly to the goal of the desired behaviour like financial compensation for sterilization.

• Psychological incentives include satisfaction, increased self-esteem, etc.

• Material incentives include goods or services or financial compensation.

questions.question: Which of the following is false about attitudes in human behaviour?
options: It is acquired from social interactions
It includes an affective or feeling element
It pre-disposes one to respond in a preferential manner
It is a temporary and fleeting aspect of human behaviour
questions.answer: D. It is a temporary and fleeting aspect of human behaviour
questions.explanation:
Attitude is usually a permanent aspect of a human’s behaviour and is difficult to change.

It is the enduring organization of beliefs around something that pre-disposes one to respond in a preferential manner. It is usually acquired through social interactions.

Attitude includes three components:

• A cognitive or knowledge element

• An affective or feeling element

• A tendency to act

questions.question: Which of the following terms represent the temporary and provisional views held by people at a point of dispute?
questions.explanation:
Opinions are temporary and provisional views held by people at a point of dispute.

Beliefs are permanent and stable inner subjective thoughts of a person towards things that are without proof. These are usually acquired from family and other close contacts.

questions.question:
Match the following types of learning:

1. Cognitive learning
A. Skills

2. Affective learning
B. Knowledge

3. Psychomotor learning
C. Attitudes
questions.explanation:
Learning is any relative or permanent change in behaviour as a result of practice or experience. It includes acquiring knowledge and skills, formation of habits and development of perception.

Types of learning:

• Cognitive learning – knowledge

• Affective learning – attitudes

• Psychomotor learning – skills

The conditions that affect learning are as follows:

• Intelligence

• Age

• Learning situation

• Motivation

• Physical and mental health

Theories of learning:

• Learning by conditioned reflex

• Trial and error

• Learning by observation and imitation

• Learning by doing

• Learning by remembering

• Learning by insight

• Demonstration

• Field experience

• Problem solving

questions.question: A 6-yr-old boy is brought to the clinical psychologist for evaluation of intellectual disability. Which formula will she use to calculate the IQ of the child?
questions.answer: B. Mental age x 100 / Chronological age
questions.explanation:
The intelligence quotient is a score that is obtained from several standardized tests to assess human intelligence.

Intelligence quotient (IQ) = Mental age x 100 / Chronological age

questions.question: Evaluation for mental retardation was done for a Down syndrome patient. His IQ was found to be 56. According to Levine and Mark's classification, you would classify him as?
questions.explanation: According to the Levine and Mark’s classification, a moron would have an IQ of 50–74.

questions.question: A clinical psychologist was asked to ascertain the IQ of a patient. She categorized the patient as having mild mental retardation. Which of the following represent's the patient's IQ range?
questions.explanation: Mild mental retardation based on IQ score would fall in the range of 50–70.

questions.question: According to Wechsler’s scale, which of the following persons would be categorized to have average intelligence?
options: A banker with an IQ of 95
An alcoholic man with an IQ of 85
questions.answer: C. A banker with an IQ of 95
questions.explanation: According to the Wechsler’s Scale, average intelligence would fall in the range of 91–110.

questions.question: Which of the following is an important epidemiological tool to assess disability in children?
options: Wing’s Comprehensive Handicaps, Behaviour and Skills Schedule
questions.answer: B. Wing’s Comprehensive Handicaps, Behaviour and Skills Schedule
questions.explanation:
Wing’s Comprehensive Handicaps, Behaviour and Skills Schedule (HBS) has been used in epidemiological studies to assess the total child population in terms of detailed scales of specific abilities and disabilities.

HBS is not useful for children with mental retardation.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most powerful example of social cohesion in social organisation?
questions.explanation:
The most powerful example of social cohesion in social organization is the family.

It is the most basic and primary unit in all societies.

questions.question: Which of the following is an unstable and emotional temporary social group with a leader?
questions.explanation:
A mob is an unstable and emotional temporary social group with a leader.

Temporary social groups can be classified into:

• Crowd- It is a temporary group motivated by a common interest or curiosity. It lacks an internal organization and has no leader.

• Mob- It is a crowd with a leader, and is more emotional than a crowd. It is unstable and has no internal organization.

• Herd- This social group has a leader and the members have to follow his/her orders without question.

A band is a permanent spatial group that constitutes a few families living together. Other permanent spatial groups are villages, cities, towns and the state.

questions.question: What is the correct order of a family cycle?
options: Formation, extension, complete extension, dissolution, contraction, complete contraction
Formation,contraction,extension, complete extension, dissolution, complete dissolution
Formation, contraction, complete contraction, extension, complete extension, dissolution
Formation, extension, complete extension, contraction, complete contraction, dissolution
questions.answer: D. Formation, extension, complete extension, contraction, complete contraction, dissolution
questions.explanation: The order of the family cycle is formation, extension, complete extension, contraction, complete contraction and dissolution.

questions.question: What are the constituents of a nuclear family?
options: Father, mother, son and his wife
Husband, wife and 4 year old daughter
Husband and wife only, without their children
questions.answer: B. Husband, wife and 4 year old daughter
questions.explanation:
A nuclear family consists of a married couple and their children when they are dependant.

They are also called elementary families.

questions.question:
Match the following:

Term
Definition

A. New family
1. A family which lags behind the rest of the community

B. Problem family
2. A family in which all the members play a part in its management

C. Joint family
3. A family in which the parental system has been disrupted by separation, divorce or death

D. Broken family
4. A nuclear family which is less than 10 years consisting of parents and children

E. Communal family
5. A number of married couples and their children who live together in the same household with usually the men being related by blood
questions.explanation:
The correct match is A-4, B-1, C-5, D-3, E-2.

Term
Definition

Problem family
A family which lags behind the rest of the community

Communal family
A family in which all the members play a part in its management

Broken family
A family in which the parental system has been disrupted by separation, divorce or death

New family
A nuclear family which is less than 10 years consisting of parents and children

Joint family
A number of married couples and their children who live together in the same household with usually the men being related by blood

questions.question: In urbanized and industrialized countries, occupation is a major determinant of all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Occupation is not a determinant of community participation.

Occupation in most urbanized and industrialized communities is a major determinant of:

• Economic rewards

• Extent of authority

• Extent of obligations

• Degree of status

• Values and lifestyles

questions.question: Which of the following is not a limitation of classifying social class according to occupation?
options: Inequality between men and women in same jobs
questions.answer: C. Rarely taking skills into consideration
questions.explanation:
Most classifications of social class based on occupational take skills into consideration.

Occupation is a useful measure of social differentiation particularly in communities highly industrialised and urbanized.

Limitations of cccupational classification of social class:

• Heterogenous grouping- occupations grouped together are not usually related to each other

• Occupational mobility- occupations practiced by the members of a social class as well as the perception of a certain occupation in the hierarchy may change over a period of time

• Gender biases- the same occupation may be considered as belonging to a superior class for men as compared to women

questions.question: You are tasked with conducting a health and wellness survey of the employees of your hospital. Which of the following scales will you not use to classify their socio-economic statuses?
questions.explanation:
Likert scale is not a scale used for socio-economic status (SES). It is a psychometric scale used to understand the attitude of people from their responses. It is a scale widely used in questionnaire-based research.

Scales that have been used for SES are:

• Udai Pareek scale

• Kuppuswamy scale

• Radhukar scale

• Jalota scale

• Shirvastava scale

• Bharadwaj scale

• Kulshestra scale

• Hollingshead scale.

questions.question: As a part of a community health survey team, you interview 50 families from a nearby village in your district. Which of the following scales would you use to classify the socio-economic statuses of these families?
questions.explanation: The Uday Pareek scale is used for the classification of socio-economic status in rural areas.

questions.question:
Which of the following components are included under the modified Kuppuswamy scale for socio-economic status ?

1. Income of family

2. Monetary value of material possessions

3. Education of head of family

4. Occupation of head of family

5. Number of family members
questions.explanation: The modified Kuppuswamy scale uses income of the family, education and occupation of head of family.

questions.question:
Match the following scores in accordance with Modified Kuppuswamy’s scale.

Scores
Socioeconomic class

1. 11-15
a. Upper

2. 16-25
b. Upper middle

3. 26-29
c. Upper lower

4. 05-10
d. Lower middle
questions.explanation:
The correct match is 1-d, 2-b, 3-a, 4-c.

Socioeconomic class according to Modified Kuppuswamy Scale:

Socioeconomic class
Scores

25-29

Upper Middle
16-25

01-04

questions.question: In the doctor-patient relationship, which of the following is not a level of communication?
questions.answer: C. Communication on a psychological plane
questions.explanation:
Communication on a psychological plane is not a level of communication in a doctor-patient relationship.

For a successful doctor-patient relationship, a doctor must have in his/her regard communication on the following levels:

• Communication on an emotional plane: To build rapport, ensure openness and incite trust from the patient.

• Communication on a cultural plane: To understand the community to which the patient belongs, his/her cultural factors that may influence health and disease and also for economic understanding of the patient.

• Communication on an intellectual plane: To give adequate explanation for their conditions and help the patients develop insight into their ailments.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best suited role for a medical social worker?
options: Designing coping strategies, interviewing and case work
questions.answer: B. Designing coping strategies, interviewing and case work
questions.explanation:
A medical social worker is a person who is trained mainly in social work and interviewing.

He/she carries out duties that augment public and community healthcare by way of identifying, understanding and relaying important information about a patient’s determinants of health.

They are not involved in active treatment, prescribing or providing economic support.

questions.question: Which of the following practices is covered under the COPRA act?
questions.explanation:
Consumer Protection Act or COPRA was instituted in 1986 and deals with consumer rights.

It recognizes six rights of the consumers, which are:

• Right to safety

• Right to be informed

• Right to be heard

• Right to choose

• Right to seek redressal

• Right to consumer education

questions.question: Which of the following is used to describe an interview used to note the gradual influence of some social or psychological process?
questions.explanation:
A repetitive interview is used to note the gradual influence of some social or psychological process. A record is maintained to understand the changes.

Interviews are methods used widely in investigations and in research. A proper interview technique must be employed to achieve the objective.

Aims of an interview:

• To secure information usually through face to face association and to understand the individual/group being interviewed.

• To form a hypothesis.

• To collect personal data for quantitative purposes.

• To collect data from secondary sources of information.

Types of interviews:

• A direct or structured interview consists of predetermined questions and sequence.

• A non-directive or unstructured interview doesn’t have any sequence of questions set beforehand. The interviewer listens and allows the speaker to narrate his/her own experiences or opinions.

• A focused interview is usually used to study effects of mass communication like radio broadcasts or film. In this, the interviewer/researcher focuses on a particular aspect on the problem and draws responses from people.

• A repetitive interview is used to note the gradual influence of some social or psychological process. A record is maintained to understand the changes.

questions.question: Arrange the following steps of an interview in the correct order in a sequence.
options: Starting an interview, making a report, establishing contact, securing rapport
Establishing contact, making a report, starting an interview, securing rapport
Establishing contact, starting an interview, securing rapport, making a report
Starting an interview, securing rapport, making a report, establishing contact
questions.answer: C. Establishing contact, starting an interview, securing rapport, making a report
questions.explanation:
The correct sequence of steps of interviewing are establishing contact, starting an interview, securing rapport, making a report.

Technique of interviewing involves:

1. Establishing contact

2. Starting an interview

3. Securing rapport

4. Recall

5. Probe questions

6. Encouragement

7. Guiding the interview

8. Recording

9. Closing the interview

10. Report

questions.question: What is the application of scientific methods to investigate the study of complex human organizations, services and management called?
questions.explanation:
Operational research is the application of scientific methods of investigation to study complex human organizations, services and management.

Pure research is also called fundamental research or basic research. It is aimed at improving scientific theories or understanding of them.

Applied research is a methodology used for a specific, practical problem like diseases or business. It involves the practical application of science.

questions.question: What was the purpose of setting up the Nirbhaya Fund?
options: Providing free medical care for women
questions.explanation: The Nirbhaya Fund was set up by the government of India for promoting the safety of women.

questions.question: Choose the correct match.
options: Gross Domestic Product- gross income generated only from within the country
Gross National Product- gross domestic product minus the depreciation on a country’s capital goods
Net National Product- income generated from within the country and income received from abroad
Net Domestic Product- market value of all final goods and services in a country during a year after allowing for depreciation
questions.answer: A. Gross Domestic Product- gross income generated only from within the country
questions.explanation: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the income generated only from within the country and does not include income received from abroad.

questions.question: What percentage of GDP was spent on public health in 2020?
questions.explanation:
The total public health expenditure is around 1.25% percentage of India's GDP (National Health Profile 2020 report).

The National Health Policy, 2017 states the aim to increase this to around 2.5% by 2025.

questions.question: A mother brings her 4-year-old boy for a well-baby check-up. Upon examination the paediatrician diagnoses her son with hidden hunger. What is meant by the term hidden hunger?
options: Child's diet is deficient in carbohydrates
Child is taking a diet that is deficient in essential amino acids
Child suffers from deficiency of omega 3 fatty acids
questions.answer: B. Child suffers from micronutrient deficiency
questions.explanation:
Hidden hunger refers to micronutrient deficiency. It occurs when there is deficiency in intake or absorption of micronutrients like vitamins, iron, zinc, etc.

The health effects of these deficiencies are less obvious or invisible and thus referred to as hidden hunger. The consequences of hidden hunger are seen in all ages.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct with regards to the estimation of poverty line?
options: Per capita expenditure of Rs. 32 per day in urban areas
Per capita expenditure of Rs. 47 per day in rural areas
Daily calorie intake of 2100 calories in urban areas
Daily calorie intake of 2700 calories in rural areas
questions.answer: C. Daily calorie intake of 2100 calories in urban areas
questions.explanation:
An estimate of the poverty line is the expenditure required for a daily calorie intake of 2100 in urban areas and 2400 in rural areas, per person.

Income-based poverty line in India is per capita expenditure of Rs. 47 in urban areas and Rs. 32 in rural areas per day.

questions.question: Which of the following legislations does not offer social security for industrial workers?
questions.explanation:
The Labour Charter Act does not offer social security for industrial workers.

Social security is the security that society furnishes through appropriate organization, against certain risks to which its members are exposed. These risks include sickness, maternity, old age and death.

Social security for industrial workers is given by:

• Workmen’s Compensation Act

• The Family Pension Scheme

• Central Maternity Benefit Act

• Employees’ State Insurance Act

Social security for civil servants is given by governments in the form of pension, gratuity, provident fund, etc. The Central Government Health Scheme provides security to employees of the Central Government.

Insurance schemes from the likes of Life Insurance Corporation of India, etc. have security schemes for the general public.

questions.question: Which of the following was the world’s first international health agency?
options: Health Organization of the League of Nations
United States Agency for International Development
questions.explanation:
The first international health agency to be established was the Pan American Sanitary Bureau (PASB) in 1902.

This was followed by the establishment of the Health Organization of the League of Nations in 1923.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) was established on 7th April 1948.

questions.question: When is breastfeeding week celebrated?
questions.explanation:
Breastfeeding week is celebrated in the 1st week of August.

questions.question: What was the theme for World Health Day 2023?
questions.explanation:
The theme for World Health Day 2023 was Health for all.

World Health Day is celebrated on 7th April and each year a different theme is adopted such as:

• 2024- My health, my right

• 2022- Our planet, our health

• 2021- Build a fairer, healthier world for everyone, everywhere

questions.question: When is World No Tobacco Day observed?
questions.explanation:
World No Tobacco Day is observed on 31st May.

The theme of World No Tobacco Day 2021 is 'commit to quit'. It conveys that the COVID-19 pandemic has led to millions of tobacco users saying they want to quit.

The theme of World No Tobacco Day 2020 was #TobaccoExposed. It aimed to provide a counter-marketing campaign that shows smokers have a higher risk of getting a severe case of COVID-19 and to empower young people to engage in the fight against tobacco.

questions.question: What was the theme of World TB Day 2023?
options: Invest to End TB. Save Lives
questions.answer: A. Yes! We can end TB!
questions.explanation:
The theme of world TB day 2023 was 'Yes! We can end TB!'.

World Tuberculosis Day is observed on 24th March of every year.

The themes for the other world TB days are:

The theme of 2024 continues to be, 'Yes! We can end TB!'

2022: Invest to End TB. Save Lives

2021: The clock is ticking

2020: It's time to End TB

2019: It’s time for action

2018: Wanted: Leaders for a TB-free world

questions.question: Where is the headquarters of the WHO located?
questions.explanation:
The headquarters of the WHO is in Geneva, Switzerland.

The WHO is a specialized, non-political health agency of the United Nations. It came into force on 7th April 1948.

Its objective is the attainment of the highest level of health by all people. The structure of the WHO includes:

• The World Health Assembly

• The Executive Board

• The Secretariat

Important headquarters of international organisations include:

• The headquarters of UNICEF and UNDP is in New York, USA.

• Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) headquarters is in Rome, Italy.

• Headquarters of the International Labor Organization (ILO) and the International Red Cross are also in Geneva.

The image below shows the WHO emblem.

questions.question: Which of the following is not one of the duties of the WHO?
questions.explanation:
State health is not one of the duties of the WHO. It is the responsibility of the government.

Work and duties of the WHO:

• Prevention and control of specific diseases

• Development of comprehensive health services

• Family health

• Environmental health

• Health statistics

• Biomedical research

• Health literature and information

• Cooperation with other organizations

questions.question: Where is the South East Asian Regional Office of the WHO located?
questions.explanation:
The South-East Asian Regional Office (SEARO) of the WHO is located in New Delhi. Duties of the SEARO include planning for malaria eradication, tuberculosis control, and rural health services.

Members of SEARO are:

• Bangladesh

• India

• Bhutan

• Indonesia

• Democratic People’s Republic of Korea

• The Republic of Maldives

• Myanmar

• Nepal

• Sri Lanka

• Thailand

• Timor-Leste

The regional offices of the WHO are listed below.

Regional office
Location

South-East Asian office
New Delhi, India

Brazzaville, Republic of Congo

American regional office
Washington D. C., USA

European regional head office
Copenhagen, Denmark

Eastern Mediterranean office
Alexandria, Egypt

Western Pacific regional office
Manila, Philippines

questions.question: What is the surveillance reporting system used by the WHO?
questions.explanation:
The surveillance reporting system used by the WHO is the Weekly Epidemiological Record (WER).

The WHO collects and disseminates epidemiological information on diseases subject to International Health Regulations. It is done through an Automatic Telex Reply Service (ATRS) and the Weekly Epidemiological Record (WER).

questions.question: As a part of the ‘Clean care is safer care’ campaign, you have been asked to give a presentation to the nurses in the obstetrics and gynecology department. Which of the following areas is targeted in this campaign?
questions.explanation:
‘Clean care is safer care’ campaign was started by the WHO to improve hand hygiene practices.

In 2005, WHO developed this campaign aimed at the reduction of healthcare-associated infections (HCAI) through the worldwide promotion of appropriate hand hygiene practices.

questions.question: Which agency of the United Nations has the given logo?
questions.explanation:
The given logo is that of the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF). It works closely with the WHO on health matters.

UNICEF’s content of services include:

• Child health

• Child nutrition

• Family and child welfare

• Formal and informal education

UNICEF participates in urban basic services (UBS) with the aim to promote access to basic services like nutrition, water supply, and sanitation.
