UNICEF started the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI) to promote breastfeeding and improve maternal and child care. In 2016, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare launched the Mothers Absolute Affection (MAA) programme to revitalize efforts towards protection, promotion and support of breastfeeding practices.

questions.question:
Which of the following are components of UNICEF’s GOBI FFF strategy?

1. Growth monitoring with growth charts

2. Oral hygiene

3. Family planning and birth spacing

4. Food fortification

5. Female literacy promotion
questions.explanation:
The components of the GOBI FFF strategy by the UNICEF are:

• Growth monitoring with growth charts

• Oral rehydration therapy for diarrhoea and dehydration

• Breastfeeding

• Immunization of children

• Family planning and birth spacing

• Food supplementation

• Female literacy promotion

The GOBI FFF strategy is aimed at revolutionising child health and survival. Initially, it was called GOBI strategy and later the FFF aspect was added to it.

questions.question: Which agency of the UN gives funds for technical assistance and has the following as part of its logo?
questions.explanation:
United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) is an agency of the UN that gives funds for technical assistance. It has the following logo.

Its main objective is to help poorer nations develop their human and natural resources to their potential.

Some other agencies of the UN include:

• UNESCO - United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization

• UNEP - United Nations Environment Programme

• UNHCR - United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees

Their logos are given below.

questions.question: Which organisation gives the highest funding for reproductive health?
questions.explanation:
United Nations Fund for Population Activities (UNFPA) gives the highest funding for reproductive health. It works in the area of health and family welfare.

It mainly works by:

• Developing the national capability in manufacturing contraceptives,

• Promoting population education programmes

• Introducing innovative approaches to family planning and MCH care.

Sexual and Reproductive Health Awareness Day is organized on February 12th every year to raise awareness about sexual and reproductive health.

The logo of the UNFPA is given below.

questions.question: Which of the following is not an objective of the FAO?
options: To better the condition of rural people
Improve nutrition of people of all countries
questions.answer: D. Improve access to nutritious foods
questions.explanation:
Improving access to nutritious foods is not one of the objectives of the FAO.

Aims of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO):

• To help nations raise living standards

• To improve the nutrition of people of all countries

• To increase the efficiency of farming, forestry, and fisheries

• To better the condition of rural people

The FAO organized a Freedom from Hunger Campaign (FFHC) in 1960. Its main objective was to combat malnutrition and to disseminate information and education.

The FAO logo is given below.

questions.question: Which agency of the United Nations has the following logo?
options: United States Agency for International Development
questions.explanation:
The given logo is of the World Bank.

It helps less developed countries raise their living standards with economic support. The allocation of funds is decided by its Board of Governors.

questions.question: What does the branch of medicine known as nosology deal with?
questions.explanation: Nosology is the branch of medicine that deals with the classification of diseases.

questions.question: Study of which of the following is known as emporiatrics?
questions.explanation:
Emporiatrics is the study of the health of travelers.

It is also called travel medicine. It deals with the prevention and management of health problems of international travelers.

questions.question: Quarantine measures were implemented for the first time to prevent the spread of:
questions.explanation:
Quarantine was introduced for the first time to prevent the spread of the plague, also known as the black death.

Quarantine is the restriction on the movement of people, animals, and goods that may have been exposed to a communicable disease. It is intended to prevent the spread of communicable diseases.

Quarantine is distinct from medical isolation, in which those confirmed to be infected with a communicable disease are isolated from the healthy population.

questions.question: Which of the following is not included in the Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Disease (TDR) strategy of the WHO?
questions.explanation:
Tick-borne encephalitis is not included in the Special Programme for Research and Training in Tropical Disease (TDR) strategy of the WHO. The diseases included under this programme are:

• Chagas disease

• Dengue

• Ebola

• Helminthiasis

• Leishmaniasis

• Leprosy

• Lymphatic filariasis

• Malaria

• Onchocerciasis

• Schistosomiasis

• Trypanosomiasis

• Tuberculosis

The programme is sponsored by the WHO, UNICEF, UNDP, and World Bank.

questions.question: According to the International Health Regulations, on diagnosing a patient with which of the following diseases is notification not mandatory in all countries?
questions.explanation:
According to the International Health Regulations(IHR), notification is not mandatory if a patient is diagnosed with tuberculosis in all countries.

It needs to be notified only by the countries where the public health impact is serious and there is a risk of international spread.

The government of India made the reporting of new cases of TB mandatory for all medical practitioners from 2012. An online web-based application named Nikshay is available for this purpose. Treatment providers are given a nominal cash incentive of Rs.1000/- per TB patient reported.

questions.question: Which of the following disease is not under international surveillance by the WHO?
questions.explanation:
Chagas disease is not under international surveillance by the WHO.

Surveillance is usually done for infectious diseases and diseases that have the potential to become epidemics or pandemics.

questions.question: Patients with which of the following diseases do not require isolation or quarantine?
questions.explanation:
Patients with West Nile fever do not require isolation or quarantine.

Isolation and quarantine are used for highly infectious diseases that are at risk of becoming epidemics or pandemics.

questions.question: You are asked to investigate a possible act of terrorism using anthrax. Which of the following is false regarding this category of bioterrorism agent?
questions.explanation:
Anthrax falls under category A of bioterrorism agents. These organisms are usually easy to disseminate.

Category A refers to high priority agents. They have high case-fatality rates and high transmissibility. Thus, a specialised public health response is required to combat such attacks.

questions.question: How many goals does the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) comprise of?
questions.explanation:
The Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) are comprised of 17 goals.

These were set as part of the official Sustainable Development Goals of the Agenda 2030. These goals consist of a total of 169 targets. SDGs replaced the Millennium Development Goals on 1st January 2016.

The 2030 agenda consists of five P's:

• People

• Planet

• Prosperity

• Peace

• Partnership

questions.question: Which of the following is false about mental health?
options: Mental disorders are universal, not specific to any group
Mental health is the mere absence of mental illness
Heredity can contribute to mental illnesses
Substance abuse is a type of mental illness
questions.answer: B. Mental health is the mere absence of mental illness
questions.explanation:
Mental health is a state of well-being in which an individual realizes his or her own abilities and not merely the absence of mental illness. It is the ability to cope with stress, be productive, and contribute to the community.

Mental disorders are universal and are not specific to any particular group. They are associated with hereditary (family history of psychiatric disorders) and environmental factors. Substance abuse and alcohol addiction are considered types of mental illness.

questions.question:
Which of the following are sociopathological factors associated with mental health?

1. Economic insecurity

2. Anxiety

3. Substance abuse

4. Frustration

5. Radiation
questions.explanation:
Economic insecurity, anxiety, and frustration are the sociopathological factors associated with mental health.

The factors leading to mental health illnesses include:

• Organic - cerebral arteriosclerosis, neoplasms, endocrine, metabolic and chronic diseases

• Hereditary - schizophrenia

• Socio-pathological factors - worries, anxiety, frustration, emotional stress, tension, unhappy marriages, broken homes, poverty, industrialization, urbanization, changing family structure, population mobility, economic insecurity, cruelty, rejection, neglect.

• Environmental - environmental toxins, substance abuse, radiation, nutritional factors, mineral deficiencies, infectious diseases during prenatal, perinatal, and postnatal periods (like rubella), road traffic accidents.

questions.question: The incidence of mental illness is higher in individuals who are exposed to causal factors during which period of life?
questions.explanation:
Exposure to causal factors during the initial 5 years of life leads to an increased incidence of mental illness.

This period is critical for lifelong mental health behavior and learning, even more crucial than adolescence. During early childhood, the growth and development of children are most vulnerable to external environmental stressors. A continuous, intimate, and warm relationship with the child's parents during infancy and childhood is very important.

questions.question: All of the following can be used for the secondary prevention of mental illness in patients except:
questions.explanation:
Improving the social environment is a method of primary prevention of mental illness, not secondary prevention.

The levels of prevention of mental illness and measures are given below:

• Primary prevention - improving the social environment and the promotion of mental health awareness

• Secondary prevention - early diagnosis and family-based health services like casework and family counseling

• Tertiary prevention - measures to reduce the duration of mental illness as well family and community stresses to prevent further breakdown and disruption

questions.question: Patients with which of the following conditions are considered to have a major mental illness?
questions.explanation:
Patients with manic depressive psychosis are considered to have a major mental illness.

Mental health disorders are classified as:

• Major (psychotic or not in touch with reality) - include schizophrenia, manic depressive psychosis, and paranoia

• Minor (non-psychotic, remain in touch with reality) - include neuroses (like OCD), personality and character disorders

Dementia occurs secondary to organic causes.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a service offered to patients with mental health disorders?
questions.explanation:
Employment services are not included under mental health services.

Mental health services include:

• Early diagnosis and treatment

• Group and individual psychotherapy

• Mental health education

• Use of modern psychoactive drugs

• Rehabilitation

• After-care services - help drug-dependent persons to adapt to regular life following treatment and rehabilitation

questions.question: A 32-year-old man is brought to the casualty with a suspected drug overdose. His sister tells you that he has recently started taking a 'superman drug' after hearing about it from his friends. What drug is she referring to?
questions.explanation:
Amphetamines are also known as the superman drug.

This is because their effects include increased self-confidence and endurance. However, its usage leads to tolerance and dependence.

questions.question: What is currently the most widely used illicit substance in the world?
questions.explanation:
Cannabis is the most widely used illicit substance in the world.

Cannabis is obtained from Cannabis sativa, C. indica, and C. americana. It is colloquially called marijuana. Other forms of this drug are charas or hashish and bhang.

The image given below shows the cannabis plant.

questions.question: What is the most widely used legal addictive substance in India?
questions.explanation: Tobacco is the most widely used legal addictive substance in India, followed closely by alcohol as the second most widely consumed substance.

questions.question: Which of the following is not an objective of the National Mental Health Programme of 1982?
options: Ensure equal human rights to mentally ill
Promote community participation in mental health services
Promote application of mental health knowledge
Provide accessibility of mental health care
questions.answer: A. Ensure equal human rights to mentally ill
questions.explanation:
Ensuring equal rights to mentally ill people is not an objective of the National Mental Health Programme (NMHP). It was launched in 1982 with the following objectives:

• Ensure availability and accessibility of minimum mental health care

• Encourage the application of mental health knowledge in general care

• Promote community participation in mental health services development

The National Mental Health Programme was relaunched as The Mental Health Care Act, 2017 which includes provisions for equal rights for those with mental illness.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a component of the District Mental Health Programme?
questions.explanation:
Screening is not a component of the District Mental Health Programme. It includes the following components:

• Training of all mental health workers at the nodal institute in the state

• Increasing public awareness by education to reduce stigma

• Early detection and treatment

• Providing data for future planning, improvement in service and research

Activities by the DMHP for positive mental health include:

• School mental health services

• College counseling services

• Workplace stress management

• Suicide prevention services

questions.question: Which of the following is not included in the Mental Healthcare Act of 2017?
options: Advance directive rights of the mentally ill
Procedure for admission, treatment and discharge of the mentally ill
questions.answer: C. Establishing mobile mental health camps
questions.explanation:
Establishing mobile mental health camps for the benefit of mentally ill patients is not included under the Mental Healthcare Act of 2017.

This act encourages the mobilization of resources to improve mental health care across the country as well as reduce stigma and improve social inclusion/support for those with mental illness. It also has provisions to improve outcomes and protect their rights.

The provisions of this act include:

• Rights of persons with mental illness to access health care, live without discrimination and enjoy confidentiality.

• Advance directives to allow mentally ill people to make decisions about their treatment

• Procedures for admission, treatment (behavioral and interpersonal therapy, medications), and discharge

• Decriminalizing suicide and prohibiting electroconvulsive therapy unless anesthesia is used

The act also has clear instructions for the central and state mental health authorities and other mental health establishments on their endeavors.

questions.question: The National Suicide Prevention Strategy aims to reduce suicide mortality by _______ in the country by 2030.
questions.explanation:
The National Suicide Prevention Strategy (NSPS) aims to reduce suicide mortality by 10% in India by 2030. It is a multisectoral approach that will involve national and international government ministries, families, communities, and educational institutes to help prevent suicide.

India has a high burden of suicide. It is the leading cause of death among individuals between 15-29 years of age.

Epidemiology

• Young and middle-aged adults between 18-45 years

• Males more than females

• Daily wage earners and people who earn <1,00,000 per annum

• Individuals with family issues and illnesses

Hanging and poisoning were the most common methods of suicide. It accounts for >3/4th of all suicides.

Risk factors for suicide

• Psychiatric illnesses- Depression, BPD, schizophrenia, and anxiety disorders

• Alcohol and other substance abuse disorders

• Major physical illness

• Job or financial loss

• Relationship or social loss

• Domestic violence or abuse

• Lack of social support

• The stigma associated with help-seeking behavior of mental disorders

• Lack of social support and sense of isolation.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a component of the REDS path in the National suicide prevention strategy?
options: Reduce suicidal deaths by 2% in the next 5 years
Enhance health services to provide suicide prevention strategies
Develop community resilience, and societal support for suicide prevention
questions.answer: A. Reduce suicidal deaths by 2% in the next 5 years
questions.explanation:
The National Suicide Prevention Strategy (NSPS) is a multisectoral approach that will involve national and international government ministries, families and communities, and educational institutes. It aims to reduce suicide mortality by 10% in India by 2030.

It recommends REDS path for suicide prevention.

• Reinforce leadership, partnership, and institutional capacity in the country

• Enhance the health services capacity to provide suicide prevention services

• Develop community resilience, societal support for suicide prevention and reduce stigma against suicidal behaviours

• Strengthen surveillance and evidence generation.

Objectives

• To establish effective surveillance mechanism for suicide prevention in next 3 years

• To establish psychiatric OPDs that provide suicide prevention services through District Mental Health Programme, within next 5 years

• To integrate mental well-being curriculum in all educational institutes within next 8 years.

questions.question: A 42-year-old male prisoner is being evaluated for aggressive tendencies and antisocial behavior. Which of the following genotypes is associated with these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
XYY genotype is often associated with aggressive tendencies, antisocial, and often, criminal behavior. It is called Jacob’s syndrome.

Option A: XXY genotype is associated with Klinefelter's syndrome.

Option B: XO genotype is associated with Turner's syndrome.

Option C: Triple X syndrome is associated with genotype XXX. It is also called super female.

questions.question: What is the risk of developing Down's syndrome in a baby born to a 45-year-old woman?
questions.explanation:
The risk of developing Down’s syndrome in a baby born to a 45-year-old woman is 1 in 50.

The risk of developing of Down's syndrome in a baby born to a 20-year-old woman is around 1 in 3000 and it increases with rising maternal age. It is an autosomal disorder caused by trisomy of chromosome 21.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is not autosomal dominant?
questions.explanation:
Ataxia-telangiectasia or Louis-Bar syndrome is an autosomal recessive condition.

Autosomal dominant conditions include:

• Neurofibromatosis

• Marfan’s syndrome

• Retinoblastoma

• Huntington's chorea

• Polycystic kidney disease

questions.question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding autosomal recessive disorders?
options: Both male and female offspring are affected
Most inborn errors of metabolism have this form of inheritance
It affects more people at a later age than in childhood
questions.answer: D. It affects more people at a later age than in childhood
questions.explanation:
Autosomal recessive disorders usually manifest in childhood or earlier.

Heterozygotes are unaffected by the disease. When both parents are heterozygous, each offspring (both male and female) has a 1:4 chance of being affected. Examples of autosomal recessive disorders include several inborn errors of metabolism like phenylketonuria, cystic fibrosis, and galactosemia.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy with recurrent hemarthrosis was found to have deficiency of factor VIII. He was adopted and his family history is unknown. What is the inheritance pattern of this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hemophilia A. It is an X-linked recessive disorder.

Hemophilia is of two types:

• Hemophilia A - due to mutations in the F8 gene leading to factor VIII deficiency

• Hemophilia B - due to mutations in the F9 gene leading to factor IX deficiency

Affected children often present with prolonged bleeding after procedures like circumcision or major bleeds like intracranial hemorrhages. When the child begins to walk, bleeding into the joint (hemarthrosis) may occur, causing painful swellings and reddening.

Laboratory investigations show elevated aPTT, with normal PT and platelet count. It is treated by the administration of factor VIII or factor IX concentrates.

questions.question: A pathologist is examining the peripheral smear of a patient with anemia. Which of the following is incorrect about the epidemiology of this disease?
options: It is prevalent in areas with high frequency of malaria
It is an autosomal dominant disorder
Couples at risk can undergo prenatal testing and diagnosis
It manifests during the first year of life
questions.answer: B. It is an autosomal dominant disorder
questions.explanation:
The given peripheral smear shows sickling of RBCs, suggestive of sickle cell anemia. It is an autosomal recessive disorder.

The prevalence is high among Africans. This disorder usually has its onset during the first year of life. Couples at risk can opt for prenatal testing and diagnosis as well.

questions.question: What was the primary goal of the Human Genome Project?
options: To introduce a gene sequence into a cell
To develop new diagnostic techniques for genetic disorders
To determine the sequence of nucleotide base pairs in human DNA
To study the precise genetic composition of specific populations
questions.answer: C. To determine the sequence of nucleotide base pairs in human DNA
questions.explanation:
The primary goal of the Human Genome Project was to determine the sequence of nucleotide base pairs that make up human DNA and to map all genes from the human genome (20,500 genes).

The project was launched in 1990 and deemed complete in 2003.

questions.question: What is Hardy-Weinberg law related to?
questions.explanation:
The Hardy-Weinberg law is related to population genetics. Population genetics is the study of the precise genetic composition of a population and various factors determining the incidence of inherited traits in them.

Founder effect is a violation to this law. It is due to difference in expression of the genes in founding population. This is responsible for the difference in the distribution of disease in population.

questions.question: The Hardy-Weinberg law is applicable in populations with which of the following?
questions.explanation: The Hardy-Weinberg law is applicable for infinitely large, static populations with random mating.

questions.question:
Match the following.

Term
Definition

1) Positive eugenics
a) Environmental manipulation to enable genes to express themselves

2) Negative eugenics
b) Making phenotypic improvements to humans after birth

3) Euthenics
c) Encouraging the breeding of those with desirable phenotypes

4) Euphenics
d) Discouraging the breeding of those with undesirable phenotypes
questions.explanation:
Positive eugenics encourages the breeding of those with desirable phenotypes.

Negative eugenics discourages the breeding of those with undesirable phenotypes.

Euthenics is the environmental manipulation to enable genes to express themselves.

Euphenics is the science of making phenotypic improvements in humans after birth, generally to affect a problematic genetic condition.

questions.question: A young woman with a family history of beta-thalassemia is planning to marry her first cousin. Which of the following will you recommend for this woman?
questions.explanation:
This young woman must be advised to undergo prospective counseling.

It refers to the process explaining to heterozygous individuals the risk of having affected children if they marry another heterozygous individual. It is performed prior to conception.

Retrospective counseling is performed after the genetic disorder has already occurred in the first child.

questions.question: A 40-year-old pregnant woman is planned for amniocentesis. What is the gestational age at which it can be done at the earliest?
questions.explanation:
Amniocentesis can be done as early as 14 weeks of gestation.

It refers to the examination of a sample of amniotic fluid to diagnose chromosomal disorders and some metabolic errors. It is indicated in the following cases:

• Pregnant women aged 35 years or above

• Family history of:

• Chromosomal abnormalities

• Metabolic errors

• Chromosomal translocation

• Sex-linked genetic disease

questions.question: What is a Punnett square used for?
questions.explanation:
A Punnett square is a diagram used to predict the probability of a particular genotype in an offspring.

It is a standard tool for genetic counselors. The image given below shows a Punnett square.

questions.question: Which of the following is not included in the format of the death certificate recommended by the WHO?
options: Other significant conditions contributing to death
Age of person at the time of death
questions.answer: D. Age of person at the time of death
questions.explanation: Age at the time of death is not included in the WHO format for a death certificate.

questions.question: You are filling the death certificate of a patient who died from rupture of the myocardium following an acute myocardial infarction. This was because of thrombosis in the coronary artery due to longstanding atherosclerosis. What will you record in line I (c) of the death certificate?
questions.explanation:
Coronary artery thrombosis is to be filled in line I (c) of the death certificate as one of the antecedent causes in the order of the events that took place.

The flow of events in this patient is as follows:

As per the recommendations of Forty-Third World Health Assembly 1990, an additional line (d) was added below (c) in part I of the death certificate, as approved by the WHO.

Part II will only be filled up with a significant condition contributing to the death but not related to the disease or condition causing it.

questions.question: An HIV positive patient was suffering from multi-drug resistant tuberculosis. He died of respiratory failure due to lobar pneumonia. Which of the following options is the most appropriate for the line I (a) of the death certificate?
questions.explanation:
Lobar pneumonia is appropriate for line I (a) of the death certificate. Line I (a) consists of the immediate cause of death such as the disease/condition. Immediate cause is the immediate/terminal event leading to death

In this patient:

• I(a) - Disease directly leading to death: Lobar pneumonia

• I(b) - Antecedent cause: MDR tuberculosis.

• II- HIV

Respiratory failure is a mode of dying in this patient. It is not the cause of death.

Terminal events like circulatory failure and respiratory failure, are modes of dying. They should not be written as the immediate cause of death in the death certificate because they are just signs of death.

Simply put, respiratory failure is 'how he died' whereas lobar pneumonia is 'why he died'. Therefore, lobar pneumonia (why he died) is the cause of the death.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a morbidity indicator?
questions.answer: B. Years of potential life lost
questions.explanation:
Years of potential life lost is not a morbidity indicator. It is a mortality indicator. It is the years of potential life lost through premature death.

Notification rates, spells of sickness and incidence are examples of morbidity indicators.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about rate is false?
options: It measures the occurrence of an event in a population.
It has no specification of time.
It's numerator is mostly part of the denominator.
questions.answer: B. It has no specification of time.
questions.explanation:
Rate is the measurement of the occurrence of a particular event in a given time. Hence, rates have a specification in time.

Examples include crude death rate, incidence rate etc.

questions.question: To calculate the crude death rate of a country, at what time of the year is the population assessed?
questions.explanation:
The crude death rate is a mortality indicator, which uses the mid-year population as its denominator. The mid-year population is always attributed as the population on 1st July of any year.

Hence for calculating the crude death rate, the population is assessed on the 1st of July.

questions.question: For which of the following purposes is age-specific death rates not used?
options: Identifying specific age groups at risk
Comparison for different causes within the same population
Comparison between different sexes in relation to accidents
Comparison between different age groups in relation to accidents
questions.answer: C. Comparison between different sexes in relation to accidents
questions.explanation:
Sex-specific death rates are used for the comparison between sexes and not age-specific death rates.

Age-specific death rates are used for:

• Comparison for different causes within the same population.

• Comparison between different age groups in relation to a particular event.

• Identifying specific age groups at risk.

questions.question: An epidemiologist is assessing an outbreak of acute diarrhoeal disease in a region. He wants to predict the virulence of the causative agent. Which of the following parameters will he use for this purpose?
questions.explanation:
Case fatality rate is used in this scenario as it is the most useful parameter to predict the virulence of an acute illness. It represents the killing power of disease.

Note:

Case fatality rate is an incidence proportion and not a true rate as no time interval is used for its calculation.

questions.question: Case fatality rate is ______.
options: Killing power of a disease in time
Killing power of a disease with no time interval
questions.answer: D. Killing power of a disease with no time interval
questions.explanation: Case fatality rate reflects the killing power of a disease with no specific time interval.

questions.question: A village has a population of 30,000 people. 500 of them contracted a disease X, out of which 75 died. What is the case fatality rate?
questions.explanation:
Case fatality rate is given by the formula:

The total number of cases of disease X= 500

The total number of deaths= 75

Hence the case fatality rate= 75/500 x 100 = 15%

questions.question: In a village of 5000 people, an outbreak of cholera led to 200 cases with 50 deaths. What is the case fatality rate?
questions.explanation:
The case fatality rate is 25%.

Case fatality rate: (Total number of deaths due to a particular disease)/(Total number of cases due to the same disease)x 100

 : 50/200 * 100 = 25%

questions.question: Which of the following is the simplest measure of the burden of a disease in a community?
questions.explanation:
The proportional mortality rate is the simplest measure to estimate the burden of a disease in a community.

It is commonly used for broad disease groups and when population data is not available.It is of limited value in making comparisons between populations and in identifying risk groups.

questions.question: Among the following, which measurement can be used as a yardstick for the assessment of standards of therapy?
questions.explanation:
The survival rate can be used as a yardstick for the assessment of standards of therapy.

It is used as a method of describing prognosis and is widely employed in cancer studies.

The survival rate is given by the following formula.

questions.question: Standardisation was done before comparing the mortality rates of two countries. What is the rationale behind this?
options: Due to difference in number of deaths.
Due to difference in age distribution.
Due to difference in the population density.
Due to difference in cause of death.
questions.answer: B. Due to difference in age distribution.
questions.explanation:
While comparing the mortality rates of two countries, the standardization of rates is done due to differences in age distribution.

The two types of standardisation include direct and indirect.

In both methods, a standard population is chosen where the numbers in each age and sex group are known and its choice is arbitrary.

The commonly used standard populations are the Segi world population and the European standard population.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about the standardized mortality ratio?
options: It is a form of direct standardization.
Observed deaths and expected deaths are part of its formula.
It can be used if the event of interest is occurrence of disease.
questions.answer: A. It is a form of direct standardization.
questions.explanation: Standardized mortality ratio is a form of indirect standardization.

questions.question: A party was attended by 110 people out of which, 40 did not eat fruit salad. Among the rest of those who ate fruit salad, 55 developed food poisoning. What is the attack rate?
questions.explanation:
The attack rate is calculated by the formula:

In this scenario, the number of new cases is 55 and the total number of those at risk is 70 as they ate the fruit salad.

Therefore attack rate = 55/70 X 100 = 78.6%.

 Attack rate is an incidence rate. It is used only when the population is exposed to risk for a limited period.

questions.question: Out of a family of 4 members, one of them developed COVID-19 infection. Four days later, 2 other members developed the same. What is the secondary attack rate?
questions.explanation:
Secondary attack rate is calculated by the following:

In this scenario, there is one primary case. The total exposed contacts are the other 3 members of the family. The number of persons developing the disease is 2.

So, secondary attack rate = 2/3 x 100 = 66%.

Note: The primary case is excluded from both the numerator and denominator.

questions.question: Which of the following study designs would you prefer for calculating the incidence of a disease?
questions.explanation: The study designs which can be used to calculate incidence are cohort studies and longitudinal studies.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements about incidence are true?

1. It is more than prevalence.

2. It measures new and old cases.

3. It is not affected by the duration of disease.

4. It is a type of proportion.

5. It gives insight into the effectiveness of health services.
questions.explanation:
Incidence is not affected by the duration of the disease. Analysis of incidence rates may provide useful insights into the effectiveness of the health services provided.

Incidence is the number of new cases occurring in a defined population during a period of time.

Prevalence is more than incidence as it is the product of incidence and duration.

Incidence is a type of rate and not a proportion.

questions.question: A medical officer noticed that there were 300 new cases of cholera in an area in a year. The total population in that area is 30,000. What is the incidence of cholera?
questions.explanation:
The incidence of cholera is 10 per 1000.

Incidence is given by the formula:

In this scenario number of new cases = 300

Total population = 30,000

Hence the incidence rate = (300/30,000) × 1000 = 10

Therefore it is 10 per 1000 per year.

questions.question: Which of the following is a good indicator of efficacy of health programs?
questions.explanation: Incidence is a good indicator of the efficacy of health services and programs.

questions.question: Which of the following is false with regard to prevalence?
options: It is a product of incidence and duration.
It can be determined by a cross-sectional study.
It is an example of rate.
It is point prevalence unless specified.
questions.answer: C. It is an example of rate.
questions.explanation:
Prevalence is a proportion, not a rate.

Prevalence is the proportion of all cases, old and new, of a particular disease at a given point in time or over a period of time in a given population. It can be determined from cross-sectional studies.

Types of prevalence:

• Point prevalence is the prevalence at a point in time. Usually, prevalence is point prevalence unless otherwise specified.

• Period prevalence is the prevalence over a period of time.

questions.question: A village has a total population of 100,000 with an under-16 population at 3%. The prevalence of goitre in the under-16 population is (0.3/100). What is the total number of under-16 population affected by goitre?
questions.explanation:
The total number of persons in the under-16 with goitre is 9.

Number of total under-16 population = 3% of 100,000 = 3000.

Thus, total number of goitre patients who are under-16 with the prevalence at the given value = 3000*0.3/100= 9

questions.question: In a population of 5000, new cases of TB are 500 and old cases are 50. What is the prevalence of TB in this case?
questions.explanation:
Prevalence is given by the formula:

In the given scenario total no.of cases :50(old)+ 500(new) =550.

Hence prevalence = (550/5000) x 100 = 11%

questions.question:
In a village having a population of 5000, a diagnostic test for a particular disease showed the following results. What is the prevalence of the disease?

Disease present
Disease absent

Test positive
1000
50

Test negative
500
3450

Total
1500
3500
questions.explanation:
Prevalence is given by the formula:

In this scenario, the number of cases: 1000+500 = 1500.

Total population: 5000

Prevalence= 1500/5000 × 100 = 30%.

questions.question: A randomized control trial showed an effective treatment against an infectious disease. It was then incorporated by the health system. Which of the following is subsequently expected to happen?
questions.explanation:
A new effective treatment for infectious disease would reduce the duration of the disease, thereby reducing prevalence.

Note: Both prevalence and incidence decrease but prevalence is the first to show a change in pattern. Hence, ‘prevalence decreases’ is the better answer.

questions.question: There was an outbreak of hepatitis A infection in your town. Proper prevention strategies were enforced. What is expected to happen at first to the number of cases of hepatitis A?
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, prevention of hepatitis A would lead to decrease in incidence at first.

Prevention of an acute disease would prevent new cases, thus first decreasing incidence.

questions.question: A new drug was approved for the treatment of prostate cancer. It has been shown to prevent early deaths but not cure the cancer. What is expected to happen to the cases of prostate cancer over a period of time?
options: Increase in incidence, no change in prevalence
Decrease in incidence, increase in prevalence
Increase in incidence, decrease in prevalence
Increase in prevalence, no change in incidence
questions.answer: D. Increase in prevalence, no change in incidence
questions.explanation:
A new drug that prevents death yet does not cure the disease will cause an increase in prevalence but the incidence remains the same.

In the given scenario, the drug reduces early deaths but does not cure prostate cancer. Hence, there is a paradoxical increase in the prevalence while the incidence remains the same.

Prevalence depends on two factors, the incidence and duration of illness. If the population is stable and incidence and duration are unchanging, the relationship between incidence and prevalence can be expressed as:

P = I X D

(I - Incidence and D - Mean duration)

This equation shows longer the duration of the disease, the greater the prevalence.

Note:

• In chronic diseases like TB, prevalence will be higher than incidence.

• If a new treatment for a disease is effective, incidence does not change but prevalence decreases as the duration of disease decreases.

• If the treatment only prevents death but doesn’t cure the disease, it may cause a paradoxical increase in prevalence.

questions.question: A researcher is planning to study the etiology of certain painful idiopathic peripheral neuropathies. Which of the following study methods shall he choose?
questions.explanation: Diseases of unknown etiology or new diseases can be studied with descriptive epidemiology.

questions.question: The preliminary observations made by Burkitt in Africa eventually found that the Epstein-Barr Virus is an etiological factor for Burkitt lymphoma. What is this study an example of?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is an example of a descriptive study.

Descriptive studies are used to describe a disease of unknown etiology. These studies also led to the discovery of prions as the etiological agents of chronic degenerative neurological disorders (Kuru) in humans. This is also an example of a descriptive study.

Types of epidemiological studies:

• Observational studies - allow nature to take its own course, the investigator measures but does not intervene.

1. Descriptive studies - limited to the description of the occurrence of a disease in a population.

2. Analytical studies - go further by analyzing the relationship between health status and other variables.

• Ecological studies

• Cross-sectional studies

• Case-control studies

• Cohort studies

• Experimental studies or intervention studies involve an active attempt to change a disease determinant or the progress of a disease and are similar in design to experiments in other sciences.

1. Randomized controlled trials

2. Field trials

3. Community trials

questions.question:
Which of the following are included in descriptive epidemiology?

1. Time

2. Controls

3. Place

4. Person

5. Intervention
questions.explanation: Descriptive epidemiology involves describing the disease in terms of time, place, and person distribution.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the term hypothesis?
questions.explanation:
An epidemiological hypothesis is a supposition or variable. It is arrived at from observation and needs to be tested.

Descriptive studies primarily focus on the formulation of a hypothesis.

Analytical studies which include study designs like case-control and cohort are used to test the formulated hypothesis. The hypothesis can subsequently be rejected or accepted.

Experimental studies involve an intervention to provide scientific proof for etiological risk factors of diseases and to measure the efficiency of health services.

questions.question: The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases is planning to study the natural history of COVID-19. Which of the following studies can be used?
questions.explanation:
Longitudinal studies are useful to study the natural history of a disease.

It is also used to identify risk factors, and to find the incidence rate. In longitudinal studies, observations are repeated in the same population over a prolonged period of time by follow-up examinations. Their disadvantage is that they are difficult to organize and take a very long time.

questions.question: What are prevalence studies also known as?
questions.explanation:
Cross-sectional studies help in obtaining the prevalence of a disease. Hence, they are also known as prevalence studies.

Cross-sectional study is a type of observational study where a cross-section of a population is examined once at one point in time. It is more useful in studying chronic diseases than acute ones. They do not provide information on the natural history of disease or incidence and also do not establish the time sequence.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about point source epidemic is false?
options: Clustering of cases occur within a short period of time
It occurs only due to an infectious agent
All cases usually develop within one incubation period
questions.answer: C. It occurs only due to an infectious agent
questions.explanation:
Point source epidemics are caused not only due to infectious agents but also by environmental pollution and contamination of food.

Point source epidemics belong to the common source type of epidemics. Exposure to disease agents is brief so they are also called single exposure epidemics.

All cases develop within one incubation period. In the epidemic curve, there is a sharp rise and fall as all cases are clustered within one incubation period. There are no secondary waves and these epidemics tend to be explosive.

questions.question: Identify the type of epidemic depicted from the following epidemic curve.
questions.explanation:
Point-source epidemic is depicted in the given image.

In the epidemic curve for a point-source epidemic, there is a sharp rise and fall of the curve with no secondary waves. It tends to be explosive as all the cases are clustered in a narrow period of time. It occurs within one incubation period of the disease.

questions.question: An outbreak of viral hepatitis A was reported from a town between June and September of a particular year. The peak of the outbreak occurred in July. What is this an example of?
questions.explanation:
This outbreak of viral hepatitis A is an example of a common source, multiple exposure type of epidemic.

The incubation period of hepatitis A is approximately 28 days (range 15 to 50 days). In this scenario, the cases of viral hepatitis A have occurred over a period from June to September (120 days) which is more than one incubation period of the disease. This is suggestive of multiple exposures from a common source.

If the period of the outbreak falls within one incubation period, then the type of epidemic is common source ,single exposure or point source epidemic.

Difference between single exposure and multiple exposure epidemics:

Common source, single exposure epidemic
Common source, multiple exposure epidemic

Nature of exposure
Single, brief exposure
Multiple, continuous or intermittent exposures for a prolonged time

Nature of epidemic
Explosive with clustering of cases within a short interval of time
Less chance of clustering of cases within short interval of time

Duration of epidemic
Falls <1 incubation period of a particular disease
Extends >1 incubation period of a particular disease

Example
An epidemic of food poisoning
Outbreak of cholera

Propagated epidemic results from person to person transmission of the infectious agent over a prolonged duration of time. For e.g. Polio epidemic, COVID-19.

Note: Hepatitis A epidemic is generally an example of a propagated epidemic. However, it does not always follow this pattern. In the given scenario, since the outbreak lasts for a short duration of 3 months (about 3 incubation periods for hepatitis A), it is considered to be a point source, multiple exposure outbreak.

questions.question: The sales team of a corporate company presents to the hospital with complaints of sudden onset nausea, vomiting and loose stools. They give a history of having food from a nearby bakery three hours ago. What is this an example of?
questions.answer: A. Common source, single exposure epidemic
questions.explanation: The given scenario is suggestive of food poisoning. It is a type of common-source (point-source), single exposure epidemic.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of disease following a seasonal trend?
options: Occurrence of rubella every 6-9 years in the pre-vaccination era
Occurrence of influenza pandemic every 7-10 years
Occurrence of bacterial gastroenteritis in summer
Increase in the occurrence of diabetes in developed countries
questions.answer: C. Occurrence of bacterial gastroenteritis in summer
questions.explanation:
Occurrence of bacterial gastroenteritis in summer is an example of a disease following seasonal trend.

Seasonal trend is a type of periodic fluctuation. It refers to the occurrence of a disease in seasonal variation influenced by environmental conditions like climate, rainfall, life cycle of vectors, heat, etc.

Examples are:

• Measles and varicella in early spring

• Bacterial gastroenteritis in summer

• Heatstroke in summer

• Dengue in July-November

• Respiratory infections in winter.

questions.question: The influenza pandemic is anticipated to occur every 7-10 years due to the antigenic variation of the virus. What is this an example of?
questions.explanation:
The influenza pandemic occuring every 7–10 years due to antigenic variations of the virus is an example of a disease showing cyclical trend.

Diseases occurring in cycles spread over a short period of time show cyclical trends of time distribution. Cyclical trend is a type of periodic fluctuation.

Examples include:

• Measles: every 2-3 years in the pre-vaccination era.

• Rubella: 6-9 years in the pre-vaccination era.

Non-infectious conditions can also show cyclical trends.

questions.question: How often did the cyclical trends of measles occured in the pre-vaccination era?
questions.explanation: In the pre-vaccination era, the cyclical trends of measles occurred every 2-3 years, while that of rubella occurred every 6-9 years.

questions.question: What is known as the change in the occurrence of a disease over very long periods of time?
questions.explanation:
A secular trend refers to the changes in the occurrence of a disease over long periods of time (decade).

Usually, disease distributions tend to move in one particular direction over a period of time. Examples: Decrease in diseases like polio, tuberculosis, and typhoid fever, but increase in diabetes and coronary artery disease in developed countries.

questions.question: Which of the following cannot be depicted by the image given below?
options: Rural - urban distributions of a disease
questions.answer: B. Rural - urban distributions of a disease
questions.explanation:
The given image is of a spot map. Spot maps are not used to depict rural-urban distributions of a disease. They help to understand the local distributions of a disease.

They are also called shaded maps. This method was used by John Snow to investigate the epidemic of cholera in London in 1854. They depict areas of high or low frequency, the boundaries, and patterns of disease distribution.

questions.question: What are migration studies used to evaluate?
options: Socio-demographic reasons for migration of a population
Prevalence of diseases in a population
Environmental and genetic factors of a disease in a population
Incidence of disease in the immigrant population
questions.answer: C. Environmental and genetic factors of a disease in a population
questions.explanation:
Migration studies are used to evaluate the role of genetic and environmental factors of a disease in a population.

The two methods used are:

• Comparing disease and death rates of migrants with kin who stayed at home

• Comparing disease and death rates of migrants with the local population of the host country

Limitations of these studies:

• Non-randomization of these groups

• Environmental factors may act only up to a certain age

• Not useful for diseases with long incubation periods

questions.question: What does bimodality in person distribution refer to?
options: Description of two etiological hypotheses of a disease in one person
Evaluation of two different environmental factors of a person in disease causation
Two separate peaks in the age incidence curve of a disease
Equal incidence of a disease in male and female population
questions.answer: C. Two separate peaks in the age incidence curve of a disease
questions.explanation:
Bimodality refers to the occurence two separate peaks in the age incidence curve of a disease.

Example: Hodgkin's lymphoma shows a bimodal curve with peaks at 15–20 years and 70–80 years.

The image below shows bimodality in the age incidence curve:

questions.question: You are conducting a cohort study in a group of headload workers to identify the risk factors for developing low back pain in future. This type of study falls under which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Cohort studies fall under non-experimental (observational) analytical studies.

Classification of epidemiological studies:

1. Observational studies: allow nature to take its own course, the investigator measures but does not intervene. It is further classified into:

• Descriptive studies: limited to describing the occurrence of a disease in a population.

• Analytical studies: go further by analyzing the relationship between health status and other variables. It includes:

• Ecological studies

• Cross-sectional studies

• Case-control studies

• Cohort studies

2. Experimental studies or interventional studies: it involves an active attempt to change a disease determinant or the progress of a disease, and is similar in design to experiments in other sciences.

• Randomized controlled trials

• Field trials

• Community trials

questions.question: Identify the type of study from the following design:
questions.explanation:
The design given is of a case-control study. It proceeds from effect to cause and is done after the exposure and outcome have occurred.

It tries to determine the possible exposure factors after a known disease incidence. This is the first approach to test causal hypotheses and uses controls to support or refute an inference.

Retrospective or historical cohort study, on the other hand, tries to compare the risk of developing a disease to some already known exposure factors. Ex: risk of lung cancer in uranium miners, risk of angiosarcoma in persons exposed to polyvinyl chloride etc.

Retrospective cohort studies are more economical and quicker than prospective cohort studies.

questions.question: A study was conducted among a group of 500 patients with lung cancer and another group of 300 people chosen from the general population. Both the groups were questioned about their exposure to smoking. What kind of study is this?
questions.explanation: This is a case-control study. In this scenario, 500 patients constitute the cases and 300 people from the general population constitute the controls. The study is done from effect (lung cancer) to cause (smoking).

questions.question: A case-control study was conducted to evaluate the association between lifestyle risk factors and the prevalence of dyslipidemia. Which of the following is not an advantage of this type of study?
questions.explanation: Incidence cannot be calculated from case-control studies. Incidence can be calculated from cohort studies, also known as longitudinal studies.

questions.question: A case-control study was conducted to see if symptoms of upper gastrointestinal dysfunction occurred more frequently in patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Which of the following cannot be used as controls in this study?
questions.explanation:
Siblings cannot be used as controls while studying genetic conditions because the outcome would be distorted due to their similarities.

Controls in a case-control study:

• Usually disease-free

• Can be up to 4 times the number of cases in small studies

• In large studies, a 1:1 ratio of cases and controls can be sought

• Sources: general population, hospitals, relatives (spouses and siblings), neighbors, or colleagues

• Although, siblings cannot be used as controls for studies on genetic conditions

questions.question: Which of the following is not a cause of bias in a case-control study?
questions.explanation:
Hawthorne bias is not seen in case-control studies. This bias occurs when the subjects change their attitude/ actions while under observation. This distorts the results of the cohort or experimental studies.

The bias that are seen in the case-control study are:

1. Confounding

2. Recall bias

3. Selection bias

4. Berkesonian bias

5. Interviewer's bias

questions.question: Which of the following is not true about random errors?
options: Systematic errors are different from random errors
questions.explanation:
Random errors are not causes of bias.

Random error arises when a value of the sample measurement diverges, due to chance alone, from that of the true population value. They can never be completely eliminated.

Sources of random errors are individual biological variations, sampling errors, and measurement errors.

Systematic errors are also called biases. They are different from random errors.

questions.question: Which of the following factors in a study will cause Berkesonian bias?
options: Interviewer asking leading questions to the subjects
Different rates of hospital admission of different diseases
Researcher's belief in the treatment changing the outcome of the study
Cases that are lost to follow-up
questions.answer: B. Different rates of hospital admission of different diseases
questions.explanation: Berkesonian bias occurs due to the different rates of hospital admission of people with different diseases. It is a type of selection bias termed after Joseph Berkeson who described it.

questions.question: An epidemiologist plans to conduct a prospective study instead of a retrospective study. Which of the following disadvantages does he aim to eliminate by conducting this study?
questions.explanation:
Recall bias can be eliminated in a prospective study.

Recall bias is also called memory bias. It is widely seen in retrospective (case-control) studies as extensive history is taken from the participants.

questions.question: A study conducted in a group revealed that consumption of alcohol increases the risk of esophageal cancer, but it may be actually due to cigarette smoking. This happens due to:
questions.explanation:
In this scenario, cigarette smoking is related to both the outcome of esophageal cancer and consumption of alcohol. Thus, this is an example of a confounding factor.

A confounding factor is defined as one which is associated with both exposure and outcome and is distributed unequally in study and control groups. In this study to determine the role of alcohol in the etiology of esophageal cancer, smoking is considered as a confounding factor because:

• It is associated with the consumption of alcohol (exposure).

• It is an independent risk factor for oesophageal cancer (outcome).

In these conditions, the effects of alcohol consumption can be determined only if the influence of smoking is neutralized by matching.

questions.question: A researcher is planning to conduct a study to investigate the relationship between oral contraceptives and breast cancer. He wants to remove age as a confounding factor. Which of the following methods will not help him reduce this bias?
questions.explanation:
Deletion is not a method to reduce confounding.

Methods to reduce confounding are:

• At the time of designing the study:

• Randomization

• Matching

• Restriction

• At the time of analysis:

• Stratification

• Statistical modelings like regression analysis, multivariate analysis, and the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel method.

questions.question: Matching is done for which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Matching helps only in removing the known confounding factors.

Matching is the process by which controls are selected in a way that they are similar to cases in certain pertinent variables (e.g., age) that are known to influence the outcome of the disease. If not adequately matched for comparability, these variables could confound the results.

questions.question: Which among the following is not a type of matching?
questions.explanation:
There is no type of matching called collective matching.

Types of matching:

• Group matching: It is also called frequency matching. It is done when a large stratum is used for study and a 1:1 ratio of cases and controls can be achieved.

• Individual matching: It is also called matching by pairs. It can be done when the study is small and more controls can be selected for one case.

questions.question: An epidemiologist determines to evaluate the strength of association between asbestos exposure and mesothelioma in a case-control study. Which of the following variables would he use for it?
questions.explanation:
Odds ratio (OR), also known as cross-product ratio, is used to measure the strength of association between risk factor (asbestos exposure) and outcome (mesothelioma) in case-control studies.

A case-control study yields only odds ratio and not incidence or relative risk.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about the odds ratio?
options: It is obtained from case-control studies
It is a measure of strength of association
questions.explanation: An odds ratio (OR) of 1 indicates that there is no association or that the event is likely in both the groups.

questions.question: A case-control study was done among 500 lung cancer patients and 400 controls. The study groups had 400 and 50 smokers respectively. Calculate the odds ratio.
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, the odds ratio (OR) is 28.

The given data is represented as:

Disease +

Disease -

Exposure +

400 (a)

50 (b)

Exposure -

100 (c)

350 (d)

Odds Ratio = ad/bc

= (400 x 350) / (50 x 100)

= (4 x 35)/5

= 4 x 7

= 28

questions.question: A research scholar is preparing to do a prospective cohort study in a hospital to evaluate the association of H. pylori with inflammatory bowel disease. Which of the following measures must she take, before starting the study?
options: Enrol all patients taking proton pump inhibitors
Enrol all patients on whom endoscopy was done
Exclude all patients diagnosed with inflammatory bowel disease
Exclude all patients with positive urea breath test for H. pylori
questions.answer: C. Exclude all patients diagnosed with inflammatory bowel disease
questions.explanation: All patients diagnosed with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) must be excluded from a prospective cohort study, as the study progresses from cause to effect. The study begins before the disease under study has occurred.

questions.question: Which of the following is not true about cohort study?
options: It is always a prospective study design
Outcome is not present at the start of study
questions.answer: B. It is always a prospective study design
questions.explanation:
Although cohort studies are called prospective studies, there are subtypes of cohort studies that do not follow the prospective study design like historical (retrospective) cohort studies.

Framingham Heart Study is one of the most famous long-term cardiovascular prospective cohort studies.

questions.question: Hawthorne effect is seen in which of the following studies?
questions.explanation: Hawthorne effect is seen in cohort studies. It refers to the phenomenon when study subjects change or alter their behaviour during the course of the study, which results in different outcomes and underestimation of risks.

questions.question: Calculate the risk ratio when the incidence of the disease in exposed is 30 and that in non-exposed is 5.
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, risk ratio or relative risk (RR) is 6.

Here, the incidence of disease in the exposed is 30 and that in the non-exposed is 5.
Thus, RR = 30/5 = 6.

questions.question: A cohort study was conducted among 10,000 smokers and 10,000 non-smokers. They were followed up over a period of 20 years. It was found that 100 of the smokers and 10 of the non-smokers developed oral squamous cell carcinoma. Calculate the relative risk.
questions.explanation:
The relative risk in the given scenario is 10.

Here, the incidence in exposed is 0.01 (100/10000). Incidence in non-exposed is 0.001 (10/10000).

Relative Risk = Incidence in exposed/ Incidence in non-exposed = 0.01/0.001 = 10.

questions.question: A study conducted among smokers shows that 80% of the cases of lung cancer are due to cigarette smoking. Which of the following variables indicates this?
questions.explanation: Attributable risk indicates to what extent the disease under study can be attributed to the exposure. Here, cigarette smoking is attributed to be the cause of 80% of lung cancers in smokers.

questions.question: A study found that the incidence of bladder carcinoma is 5 times higher in smokers than in non smokers. Calculate the attributable risk.
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, the attributable risk (AR) is 80%.

Taking the incidence of disease in non-exposed as x, the incidence of disease in exposed would be 5x.

Attributable risk (AR) would be given as [(5x - x)/5x] x 100 = 80%.

questions.question: In a population of 9000 people, 2100 are alcoholics. 70 alcoholics and 23 non-alcoholics developed cirrhosis. What is the attributable risk?
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, the attributable risk (AR) is 90%.

Number of people exposed (to alcohol) = 2100
Number of people not exposed (to alcohol) = 6900

Incidence of cirrhosis among exposed = 70/2100 (IExposed)
Incidence of cirrhosis among non-exposed = 23/6900 (INon-exposed)

Attributable risk (AR) = [ ( IExposed - INon-exposed) / IExposed ]*100
= [ (70/2100 - 23/6900) / (70/2100)] *100
= [ 9 / 10 ] *100
= 90

Thus, the attributable risk (AR) is 90%.

questions.question: Which of the following is the numerator in the formula for population-attributable risk?
options: Incidence among exposed minus incidence among non-exposed
Incidence among non-exposed minus incidence among exposed
Incidence in the total population minus incidence among non-exposed
Incidence in the total population minus incidence among exposed
questions.answer: C. Incidence in the total population minus incidence among non-exposed
questions.explanation:
Incidence in the total population minus incidence among non-exposed is the numerator in population-attributable risk (PAR).

Population attributable risk is obtained from cohort studies. It provides an estimate of the amount by which the disease could be reduced in that population if the suspected factor was eliminated or modified.

questions.question: A study was done in the Indian population to correlate the deaths due to myocardial infarction and dietary practices. What is this type of study known as?
questions.explanation:
This is an example of an ecological study. As the study was done in the Indian population, it can be inferred that population was taken as the unit of the study.

The study was done to correlate the deaths and dietary practices, and hence ecological studies are also called correlational studies.

questions.question: Which among the following is the weakest study design to prove causation?
questions.explanation:
Ecological studies take a population as a unit. They provide the weakest evidence for causality because of extrapolation to individuals from regional data.

Randomized control trials (RCTs) provide the strongest design amongst the options given. Case-control and cohort studies have moderate ability to provide evidence for causality.

questions.question: What kind of bias is implied by assigning group characteristics to people which they may not possess as individuals?
questions.explanation: An ecological fallacy results when characteristics of the group are assigned inappropriately to individuals.

questions.question: Which of the following study designs is the best to prove causation?
questions.explanation:
Randomized controlled trials (RCT) are the strongest and best study design to prove causation. They are the gold standard of clinical research.

Case-control and cohort studies have a moderate ability to provide evidence for causality. Ecological studies or correlational studies are considered as the weakest study design in this aspect.

The difference between analytical studies and randomised controlled trials is that in the former there is no randomisation because it requires the participants to be divided into diseased and non-diseased. This can lead to a number of biases that are avoided in RCTs.

questions.question: In a clinical trial to evaluate a drug, randomisation was done before starting the trial. What is the purpose behind this?
options: The two groups will be similar in prognostic factors
The clinician has no control over the allocation of participants in each group
The clinician can predict in advance which treatment the subjects will receive
The sample may be referenced to a known population
questions.answer: B. The clinician has no control over the allocation of participants in each group
questions.explanation:
The main purpose behind randomisation is to eliminate selection bias.

In an RCT, participants are randomly assigned to a study group or a control group. It is done only after obtaining consent. It removes both known and unknown confounding factors.

The heart of a randomized controlled trial (RCT) is randomisation. This allows comparability between the study and the control population.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about randomised control trial?
options: Baseline characteristics are similar in both arms
Investigator’s bias is minimized by double blinding
The sample size required depends upon the hypothesis
The dropouts from the trial are not included in the analysis
questions.answer: D. The dropouts from the trial are not included in the analysis
questions.explanation:
The dropouts from an RCT are included in the final analysis. This type of analysis is called intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis.

It ignores noncompliance, protocol change, withdrawal, cross-over, and anything that happens after randomization during analysis. The exclusion of dropouts may lead to the introduction of bias.

Note: Per-protocol analysis is a comparison of treatment groups that include only those patients who completed the treatment originally allocated to them. Hence, comparability between the study and control group is limited and randomisation is lost.

questions.question: A researcher decided to use double-blinding in his trial evaluating two new therapies for cystic fibrosis. What is the characteristic feature of this concept?
options: Study and control groups are blinded
Observer and group being observed are blinded
Group members and analyzer are blinded
questions.answer: C. Observer and group being observed are blinded
questions.explanation: In double-blind trials, both the group members (study and control group) and the observers are not aware of the group allocation.

questions.question: In a clinical trial, what would be the best study design that ensures comparability between experimental and control groups?
questions.explanation:
A cross-over study would be the best method to ensure comparability between the experimental and control group.

In a cross over study design, patients are randomly assigned to the study and control group, and then after a period of time, their groups are switched. Here, each patient serves as his/her own control which allows for maximum comparability.

In a concurrent parallel study design, comparisons are made between two randomly assigned groups and there is no switching of groups. This allows only for limited comparability between experimental and control groups.

Quasi-experiments are studies that aim to evaluate interventions but that do not use randomization. The lack of randomisation is the major weakness of quasi trials. The comparability in a quasi trial is limited.

A per-protocol analysis is a comparison of treatment groups that include only those patients who completed the treatment originally allocated. Hence, comparability is limited.

questions.question: A new drug for multiple sclerosis is undergoing clinical trials where its therapeutic efficacy is being confirmed and adverse reactions are being monitored. Which of the following phases is the drug most likely in?
questions.explanation:
The confirmation of therapeutic efficacy and monitoring of adverse reactions of a new drug happens in phase III of the clinical trial.

Purpose of phase III:

• Confirmation of the effectiveness of the drug in patients with the target disease

• Monitoring of adverse reactions

Phase II involves therapeutic exploration which is the evaluation of the efficacy of the drug and dose-ranging (determination of the optimum tolerated dose).

questions.question: In which of the following phases is the maximum drug failure rate seen?
questions.explanation: Maximum drug failure rates are seen in phase II followed by phase III of a clinical trial.

questions.question: The maximum tolerable dose of a new drug for Alzheimer's disease is to be evaluated. In which of the following phases is this done?
questions.explanation:
The maximum tolerated dose of a new drug is tested in phase I of a clinical trial.

Phase I trials are usually performed on healthy volunteers to check the safety and pharmacokinetic properties of a drug. The participants in this phase do not gain any direct health benefits from taking part. They are generally paid a fee for their time, with the payments being regulated and not related to the risk involved.

questions.question: A hypothesis stating that people who continue to smoke are at a higher risk of developing lung carcinoma than those who have quit is to be tested. Which of the following study designs would you choose for this purpose?
questions.explanation:
To test the given hypothesis that smokers are at a higher risk of developing lung carcinoma than those who have quit, the study design chosen is a cessation experiment.

The outcomes of termination of a habit or removal of an agent considered to be causally related to a disease can be evaluated in a cessation experiment.

It is a type of RCT and preventive trial. If the outcome is a significant reduction in disease then the association of that habit or agent to the disease is strengthened.

A trial of aetiological agents is an experimental epidemiological study to confirm or refute an aetiological hypothesis.

Clinical trials, for the most part, have been concerned with evaluating therapeutic agents, mainly drugs.

An uncontrolled trial is an example of a non-randomised trial where there is no control group for comparison.

questions.question: Which of the following is not an example of a randomised controlled trial?
questions.answer: B. Before and after comparison studies
questions.explanation:
Before and after comparison studies are a type of non-randomized trials.

These are community trials and centre around comparing the incidence of disease before and after the introduction of a preventive measure. They are of two distinct types:

• Before and after comparison studies without control.

• Before and after comparison studies with control.

Non-randomized trials include:

• Before and after comparison studies.

• Uncontrolled trials.

• Natural experiments.

questions.question: What is the suspected cause preceding the observed effect an example of?
questions.explanation: Temporality refers to the condition when the suspected cause precedes the observed effect. It is a part of Hill’s criteria for causal association.

questions.question: While investigating a new disease, you are trying to establish the aetiological agent. Which of the following criterion is the most difficult to establish?
questions.explanation:
Specificity is the most difficult criterion to establish in both chronic and acute diseases.

This is because a single factor or cause can give rise to more than one disease. Also, most diseases are multifactorial in origin with no possibility of demonstrating a one-to-one relationship which would indicate specificity.

questions.question: What does evidence-based medicine refer to?
options: Use of experiments to prove the cause of a disease
Use of clinical trials to prove safety of drugs
Use of research findings for taking decisions about patient care
Use of behavioral modification to prevent disease
questions.answer: C. Use of research findings for taking decisions about patient care
questions.explanation:
Evidence-based medicine (EBM) refers to the use of modern research findings to guide decision-making about the treatment of individual patients.

EBM integrates clinical experience and patient values with the best available research information. Research and studies are given high importance in EBM, while opinions and conventional wisdom of experts are not taken into consideration in the practice of EBM.

questions.question:
In the hierarchy of evidence, which of the following rankings is correct?

1.
Cohort study

2.
Case-control study

3.
Meta-analysis and systematic review

4.
Randomized control trials

5.
Case reports
questions.explanation:
The correct order of ranking of the hierarchy of evidence is:

Meta-analysis and systemic review > Randomised control trial > Cohort study > Case-control study > Case reports.

questions.question: Which of the following is incorrect about systematic reviews?
questions.explanation:
Meta-analysis is not always performed in systematic reviews.

A systematic review is the process of locating and synthesizing the research on a particular question using organized, transparent, and replicable procedures. It ranks high in the hierarchy of evidence in medicine.

Steps of a systematic review:

• The research question is formulated. It is always focused.

• The literature on studies is always found and appraised after criteria of eligibility are established.

• Meta-analysis is usually done in a systematic review for quantification but it is not compulsory.

These steps are depicted in the diagram below.

questions.question: A meta-analysis is being performed to evaluate the relationship between obesity and endometrial carcinoma. Which among the following is false regarding this technique?
options: File drawer effect can be seen here
It increases the statistical power by increasing sample size
Apples and oranges effect can be seen here
Its validity does not depend on the quality of the systematic review
questions.answer: D. Its validity does not depend on the quality of the systematic review
questions.explanation: The validity of the meta-analysis depends on the quality of the systematic review.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a use of epidemiology?
questions.explanation:
Ensuring community participation is not the use of epidemiology. Community participation is a principle of primary health care.

Uses of epidemiology:

• To study the rise and fall of disease in populations

• Community diagnosis

• Planning and evaluation

• Evaluation of individual’s risks and chances

• Syndrome identification

• Completing the natural history of disease

• Searching for causes and risk factors

questions.question: For what purpose were knowledge, attitude, and practice (KAP) studies first used in India?
questions.explanation:
Knowledge, attitude and practice (KAP) studies were first used in India to study family planning.

These studies help in evaluating the knowledge, attitude, and practices of a community. It also gives an educational diagnosis.

chapters.chapter: Basic Definitions In Infectious Disease Epidemiology

questions.question: What is the host in which a parasite passes through its sexual stages of maturity called?
