questions.explanation:
A host in which a parasite passes through its sexual stage of maturity is called the definitive host or primary host.

A host in which a parasite exists in the larval or asexual form is called an intermediate host or secondary host.

A host which acts as the only source of development for a parasite is called the obligate host.

Note: A host in which the organism remains alive but no development occurs is called a transport host.

questions.question: For which of the following diseases is man the dead-end host?
questions.explanation:
Among the given options, man is the dead-end host for tetanus and rabies.

A dead-end host is a host from which the infectious agent lacks a portal of exit to continue its propagation.

Humans are dead-end hosts for :

• Rabies

• Tetanus

• Bubonic Plague

• Trichinosis

questions.question: While studying a disease, you find that it affects both humans and lower vertebrates and can be transmitted in either direction. How would you classify this disease?
questions.explanation:
A disease that affects both humans and lower vertebrates and which can be transmitted in either direction is classified as amphixenosis. E.g, Trypanosoma cruzi and Schistosoma japonicum.

It is a type of zoonoses. Zoonoses are diseases that are transmitted between vertebrate animals and humans.

Other types of zoonoses include:

• Anthropozoonoses - infections that are transmitted to man from vertebrates. E.g., Rabies, plague etc.

• Zooanthroponoses - infections that are transmitted to vertebrates from humans. E.g., Human tuberculosis in cattle.

Epizootic disease refers to an outbreak or epidemic of a disease in an animal population, often with the implication that it may also affect human populations. Enzootic disease is an endemic occurring in animals.

Note: Epornithic diseases are those diseases which are epidemic in bird populations. E.g., Psittacosis.

questions.question: What is a disease imported to an area from another called?
questions.explanation:
Exotic diseases are those imported into a country where they do not occur usually. E.g, rabies in the United Kingdom.

Enzootic diseases are those which are endemic in animals. E.g, anthrax, brucellosis.

Epornithic disease refers to an epidemic in birds. E.g, psittacosis.

Epizootic disease refers to an outbreak of a disease or an epidemic in animals with the implication that it may affect humans. E.g, Q fever, influenza.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a disease that has a haphazard occurrence?
questions.explanation:
Sporadic diseases occur in a haphazard and irregular manner from time to time.

Endemic refers to the constant presence and /or usual prevalence of a disease or infectious agent in a population within a geographic area.

Epidemic refers to an increase, often sudden, in the number of cases of a disease above what is normally expected in that population in that area.

Pandemic is an epidemic occurring over a wide area, crossing international boundaries, and usually affecting a large number of people.

Note: Opportunistic infections are those that occur in the presence of immune suppression or deficiency like cytomegalovirus.

questions.question: Surveillance data of an endemic disease reveals that most of the children in the area had been affected and had to be hospitalised. However, most of the adults remained asymptomatic carriers. Which category does this disease belong to?
questions.explanation:
The disease in question belongs to the category of holoendemic diseases. In such diseases, a higher prevalence and pathogenic response are seen among the children in an area. The adults tend to be either asymptomatic carriers or show reduced damage by the disease process. E.g, malaria.

An endemic disease is a disease that is present constantly in a population or in a given area without importation from outside. E.g, kala-azar in Bihar.

A hyperendemic disease is a disease that is constantly present at high incidence and prevalence among all groups in a population. E.g, dengue in India.

A syndemic is the aggregation of two or more concurrent or sequential epidemics or disease clusters in a population with biological interactions, which exacerbate the prognosis and burden of disease. It is also known as a synergistic epidemic.

Note: Quasiendemic is not a term used in infectious disease epidemiology.

questions.question: In which of the following diseases is subclinical infection not seen?
questions.explanation:
Subclinical infection is not seen in measles. It always causes the development of overt signs and symptoms.

Subclinical infection refers to an inapparent, covert, missed or abortive case. The host harbours and sheds the infectious agent but does not develop signs and symptoms of the disease.

Subclinical infections are seen in diseases like:

• Hepatitis A

• Diphtheria

• Japanese encephalitis

• Rubella

Subclinical infections can only be detected by laboratory tests. They frequently occur during a person’s lifetime and are responsible for the immunity shown by humans to a variety of disease-producing microbes.

Note: Subclinical cases should be differentiated from latent infections. In a latent infection, the host does not shed the organism but it lies dormant without signs and symptoms.

questions.question: In which of the following states will the host not shed the infectious organism?
questions.explanation:
The host does not shed the infectious organism in case of a latent infection. This is defined as a state in which the host does not show signs and symptoms of the disease and does not shed the organism.

It can be seen in conditions like herpes simplex, ancylostomiasis, infections due to slow viruses, Brill-Zinsser disease, etc.

Subclinical infection is a state where the host harbours the infectious agent without developing signs and symptoms but sheds the infectious agent. This state is seen in conditions like hepatitis A, rubella, mumps, etc.

Healthy carriers are those who had subclinical infections and later developed a carrier state without suffering from the overt disease. This state is seen in: (mnemonic: CM - DPT)

• Cholera

• Meningitis

• Diphtheria

• Polio

• Typhoid

Convalescent carriers are those which shed the infectious agent during the convalescent phase/recovery phase. Such carriers are seen in diphtheria, typhoid, cholera, pertussis, etc.

questions.question: While in a health camp, you notice a child with fever and rash. On subsequent history, you find out that similar symptoms occurred in her friend 6 days back. How will you epidemiologically categorise the child you examined?
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, the child is categorised as the index case. It is the first case that comes to the notice of an investigator or physician.

The primary case is the first case of a communicable disease introduced into a population unit.

A secondary case is one that develops after contact with the primary case.

A suspect case refers to a patient who has all the features of the disease but has not been diagnosed with it yet.

Note: There is no such term as tertiary case.

questions.question: You are part of a research programme for COVID-19 and are asked to define the median incubation period. How will you define it?
options: Interval between onset of symptoms in primary and secondary cases
Time required for 50% of cases to occur following exposure
Interval between exposure and the occurrence of the first symptom
Time required for the start of pathogenesis following exposure
questions.answer: B. Time required for 50% of cases to occur following exposure
questions.explanation:
The median incubation period is the time required for 50% of the cases to occur following exposure. The median incubation period of COVID-19 of approximately 5 days.

Incubation period is the time interval between invasion of the infectious agent and the appearance of the first symptom or sign in the body. It is termed as the latent period in non-infectious diseases.

Incubation period depends upon:

• Generation time of pathogen

• Portal of entry

• Infective dose

• Individual susceptibility

Incubation period is useful for :

• Tracing the source of infection and contacts.

• Determining the period of surveillance or quarantine.

• Planning immunization.

• Identification of point source or propagated epidemics.

• Determining the prognosis.

questions.question: In a school of 100 children, a child developed measles. Four days later, 3 of her classmates developed measles. What do these intervening four days correspond to?
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, the first child is the primary case and her classmates are the secondary cases. Hence, the interval between them developing the disease i.e., the intervening four days, is called the serial interval.

The time interval between the onset of the primary case and the secondary case is called serial interval.

By collecting information about a whole series of such disease onsets, the distribution of the secondary cases can be made. From this information, an approximation of the incubation period can be done.

Lead time/lead interval refers to the period between the first possible time of detection and the usual time of diagnosis.

Incubatory interval/ incubation period refers to the time period between invasion of a pathogen to appearance of the first sign or symptom.

Latent interval/ latent period refers to the period between disease initiation to detection of the disease. It is usually used for non-infectious diseases and is equivalent to the incubation period.

Note :

• Primary case is the first case of a communicable disease introduced into a population unit.

• Secondary case is one that develops after contact with the primary case.

• Index case is the first case that comes to the notice of an investigator or physician.

questions.question: The time interval between which of the following is called generation time?
options: Development of primary case and secondary case
Receipt of infection by host and maximum infectivity of the same host
Infection and first sign or symptom
Infection and initiation of pathogenesis inside the host
questions.answer: B. Receipt of infection by host and maximum infectivity of the same host
questions.explanation: Generation time is the time interval between receipt of infectious agent by the host and the point of maximum infectivity of the same host.

questions.question: For which of the following diseases is soil not a reservoir?
questions.explanation:
The main reservoir of the coccobacilli belonging to the genus Brucella that cause brucellosis are animals like sheep, cattle, horses, goats, whales, and dogs.

A reservoir is the environment (e.g. soil, humans, animals, water, etc.) where the infectious agent grows and multiplies (natural habitat) and from where it can be transmitted to a susceptible host.

A source is an animal, object, human or substance which acts as an immediate mode of transmission and may or may not be a part of the reservoir.

Option A: Coccidiomycosis is also called Valley fever and the causative fungi belong to the Coccidiodes. The main reservoir of this organism is soil.

Option B: Bacillus anthracis is a soil commensal and is also found on the hides and dried skins of infected animals.

Option C: The natural reservoir for the fungi causing mycetoma is soil.

questions.question: Which of the following is not communicable during the later part of the period marked 3 in the below image?
questions.explanation:
The period marked 3 in the figure is the incubation period while the later part of the period represents subclinical infection. Rabies is not communicable during its incubation period as it is transmitted from the saliva of a rabid animal through bite or scratch.

An incubatory carrier state is one in which carriers shed the organism during the incubation period of the disease, especially during the later parts of it.

Examples of diseases showing incubatory carrier state are:

• Measles

• Polio

• Mumps

• Whooping cough

• Diphtheria

• Influenza

• Hepatitis A

Carriers of a disease are classified by the following:

1. Type: Incubatory, convalescent or healthy.

2. Duration: Temporary or chronic.

3. Portal of exit: Urinary, respiratory, intestinal or others.

questions.question: Which of the following carriers shed the organism for indefinite periods?
questions.explanation:
Chronic carriers are those who shed or excrete the organism for indefinite periods.

Carriers are classified into chronic carriers and temporary carriers based on the duration.

Organisms may be shed continuously or intermittently in chronic carriers. The duration of the carrier state also depends on the disease. Chronic carrier state is seen in typhoid, hepatitis B, gonorrhea, malaria, etc.

Temporary carriers are classified into:

• Incubatory carriers - Those that shed the organism during the incubation period of the disease, especially during the later parts of it. It is seen in measles, mumps, polio, etc.

• Healthy carriers - Those who suffer from subclinical infections and develop a carrier state without developing the overt disease. It is seen in polio, meningococcal meningitis, cholera, diphtheria, etc.

• Convalescent carriers - Those that shed the organism during recovery or convalescence. It is seen in typhoid.

Paradoxical carrier refers to a carrier who acquires the pathogen from another carrier.

Note: Pseudo-carriers are carriers of avirulent organisms.

questions.question: Which of the following diseases does not show vertical transmission?
questions.explanation:
Tetanus does not show vertical or transplacental transmission.

Transmission of diseases or non-infectious agents transplacentally is called vertical transmission. Diseases that show this type of transmission include:

• Herpes

• HIV

• Rubella

• Varicella

Apart from diseases, non-infectious agents like lithium, thalidomide, stilbestrol, etc. can cross the placenta and lead to the development of congenital anomalies in a foetus.

Note: Neonatal tetanus occurs as a result of the failure to use aseptic techniques in managing the umbilical stump, unclean hands, and instruments or contamination by dirt, straw, or other nonsterile materials in the delivery field. Immunisation of pregnant women can prevent this disease via the transplacental transport of immunoglobulins.

questions.question: Which among the following is false about droplet transmission?
options: All droplets can travel only as far as 3 feet
Droplets are usually larger than 5 microns
It is a type of direct transmission
Basic ventilation decreases the potential for this type of transmission
questions.answer: A. All droplets can travel only as far as 3 feet
questions.explanation:
Droplet nuclei can travel as far as 6 feet, whereas a droplet (particle > 5μm) travels <30-60cm, as recent studies have shown.

Droplets are a mode of direct transmission of infectious agents. They are formed from saliva and nasopharyngeal secretions released during coughing, sneezing, or speaking into the surrounding atmosphere. The expelled droplets may impinge directly upon the conjunctiva, oro-respiratory mucosa or skin of close contact. This mode of transmission is seen in common cold, diphtheria, etc.

Proper basic ventilation and prevention of overcrowding reduce the potential for this type of transmission.

questions.question: What is the maximum size of airborne droplet nuclei?
questions.explanation:
Droplet nuclei are sized less than or equal to 5 microns.

They may be formed by evaporation of droplets coughed or sneezed into the air or be generated purposefully by a variety of atomizing devices (aerosols). They are capable of indirect airborne transmission of diseases like tuberculosis, influenza, chickenpox, measles, etc.

The droplet nuclei may remain airborne for long periods of time, some retaining and others losing infectivity or virulence. These small particles when inhaled are capable of reaching the alveoli and getting retained there.

questions.question: Spread of disease via which of the following is an example of an indirect mode of transmission?
questions.explanation:
The spread of a disease through contaminated food is an example of vehicle-borne transmission. It is an indirect mode of transmission.

Vehicle-borne transmission is the transmission of infectious agents through food, water and biological products (blood, plasma etc.). Of these, food and water are more frequent vehicles of transmission because they are used by everyone.

Mother to child transmission, droplet infection and transmission via dog bite are examples of direct modes of transmission.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about fomite-borne transmission is false?
options: It is an indirect mode of transmission
Transmission via contaminated food is an example of this
Hepatitis A is transmitted in this way
Routine disinfection can prevent such transmission
questions.answer: B. Transmission via contaminated food is an example of this
questions.explanation:
Fomites are objects other than water or food that can be contaminated by infectious agents and help in transmitting the disease. They include clothes, towels, linen, cups, plates, spoons, etc.

Fomites are an example of an indirect mode of transmission.

Some diseases transmitted by fomites include diphtheria, typhoid, hepatitis A, etc.

Good public and personal hygiene can prevent this type of transmission.

questions.question: What is the lodgement and development of an arthropod on the body surface called?
questions.explanation:
The lodgement and development of an arthropod on the body surface is called infestation.

Infection is the entry and development or multiplication of an infectious agent in a host’s body.

Contamination is the presence of a disease agent on a body surface like clothes, toys, etc. and also in substances like food or water.

Colonization is the presence of a disease agent in or on a host, with growth and multiplication but without any overt clinical expression or detected immune response in the host at the time it is isolated.

questions.question: An entomologist was studying a vector and the pathogen it transmits. He found that the pathogen underwent changes in number and morphology in the vector. What is this type of biological transmission called?
questions.explanation:
This type of biological transmission where a pathogen undergoes a change in number and morphology in a vector is called cyclo-propagative transmission.

Malaria is a disease whose causative organism (Plasmodium sp.) undergoes cyclo-propagative transmission. In malaria, the parasite undergoes both developmental changes and multiplication in the Anopheles mosquito (vector).

questions.question: A patient with chronic lymphedema was found to have a positive DEC provocation test. Which type of biological transmission does the pathogen implicated here undergo?
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, the patient most likely has lymphatic filariasis. The causative organism of this disease (Wuchereria bancrofti) undergoes cyclo-developmental transmission.

Cyclo-developmental transmission is a transmission where the agent undergoes only developmental changes and not multiplication within the vector.

DEC provocation test: In this test, a small dose of DEC is given 20-50 minutes before sample collection so that the microfilaria appears in the blood even during the daytime.

questions.question:
You are a rural medical health officer investigating an epidemic. What is the correct sequence of steps you must follow?

a. confirm epidemic existence
b. verify the diagnosis
c. formulation of hypothesis
d. define the population at risk
e. rapid search of cases
questions.explanation:
Steps for the investigation of an epidemic are:

• Verification of diagnosis

• Confirmation of the existence of an epidemic

• Defining the population at risk -

• Obtaining a map of the area

• Counting the population

• Rapid search for all the cases -

• Medical survey

• Epidemiological case sheets

• Searching for more cases

• Data analysis on the basis of time, place and person

• Formulation of hypothesis

• Testing of hypothesis

• Evaluation of ecological factors

• Further investigation of the population at risk

• Writing the report

questions.question: You have been asked to write the final report following the investigation of a cholera epidemic. Which of the following will you not include in this report?
options: Usual number of cases that existed before the epidemic
questions.explanation:
The final report of an epidemic does not include the incubation period of the disease.

The final report following the investigation of an epidemic should include:

• Background information - Geography, climate, demography, socio-economic groups, health service organization, surveillance data and normal disease prevalence.

• Historical data - Previous occurrences of the epidemic, the occurrence of any related diseases and discovery of the primary case in the present outbreak.

• Methodology of investigations - Case definition, epidemiological questionnaires, collection and laboratory techniques.

• Analysis of data - Clinical and epidemiological data, modes of transmission, laboratory data and all their interpretations.

• Control measures - Strategy definitions, methodology of implementation, evaluation methods and preventive measures.

questions.question: You have been sent to an area to study the ongoing typhoid epidemic. When will you declare the area to be free of the epidemic?
questions.answer: D. No new cases for 28 days
questions.explanation:
The area will be declared free of the typhoid epidemic when no new cases are reported for 28 days.

An area is declared free of an epidemic when there are no cases reported for twice the incubation period of the disease since the last case.

The incubation period of typhoid is 14 days. So, in the given scenario, the area will be declared free of the epidemic when no new cases are reported for twice the incubation period i.e., 14 x 2 = 28 days.

questions.question: Following an outbreak of a disease, you are asked to calculate the secondary attack rate (SAR). What is the denominator you would use?
options: All people having history of contact with a case
All people susceptible in the entire area
All the people in contact with the primary case
All the close or exposed contacts those are susceptible
questions.answer: D. All the close or exposed contacts those are susceptible
questions.explanation:
The denominator used for calculating SAR is all the close or exposed contacts that are susceptible.

The secondary attack rate is defined as the probability that infection will occur among susceptible persons following contact with an infectious person within the incubation period.

It is calculated by the formula:

Secondary attack rate (SAR) = (Number of exposed or susceptible persons developing the disease within the incubation period x 100)/(Total number of close or exposed contacts that are susceptible)

Primary cases are usually excluded from the numerator and denominator.

Secondary attack rate measures the communicability of the disease.

questions.question: A village has 100 children under the age of 5. The coverage of measles vaccination is 60%. Following a case of measles, 26 children developed measles. What is the secondary attack rate?
questions.explanation:
The secondary attack rate for the given scenario is 66%.

The secondary attack rate (SAR) is given by:

(Number of exposed or susceptible persons developing the disease within the incubation period x 100)/(Total number of close or exposed contacts that are susceptible)

Here, number who developed the disease after exposure= 26

Susceptible population= 100 - 60 (vaccinated) - 1 (primary case) = 39

Therefore, SAR = 26 /39 x 100 = 66%.

SAR is a measure of communicability.

questions.question: A 28-year-old man is found to be positive for SARS-CoV-2. On contact tracing, 30 people have been identified as close contacts but none of them shows any symptoms or signs. What is the time duration for which they must be quarantined?
questions.explanation:
Quarantine is the limitation in freedom of movement of healthy contacts of cases, who have been exposed for a period that lasts as long as the maximal incubation period of the disease.

It is a primary level of prevention and falls under specific protection measures. The various types of quarantine are:

• Absolute - Complete limitation of movement

• Modified - Selective partial limitation of movement

• Segregation - Observation of a group of persons in a population after separation

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of diseases and their periods of isolation is wrongly matched?
options: Rubella – 3 days after onset of rash
Chickenpox – 6 days after onset of rash
Herpes zoster – 6 days after onset of rash
Measles – Up to 5 days after onset of rash
questions.answer: A. Rubella – 3 days after onset of rash
questions.explanation:
Patients with rubella should be isolated for 7 days after they develop the rash.

 Isolation is defined as separation, for the period of communicability of infected persons from others to prevent or limit transmission of the infectious agent.

In settings where women who are in their 1st trimester or sexually active or non-immune without contraception usage may be exposed, outbreak control measures should begin as soon as rubella is suspected and should not be postponed until laboratory confirmation of cases.

Note: Multiple sources have confimed the period of infectivity of measles which is from 4 days before the onset of rash to 5 days after the onset of rash.

questions.question:
Which of the following are true for a screening test?

1) Done on apparently healthy

2) Applied to individuals

3) Time-consuming

4) Relatively inaccurate results

5) Based on one criterion/ cut off
questions.explanation:
Screening tests are done on apparently healthy individuals, the results of the test are relatively inaccurate, the tests are based on one criterion.

The difference between screening and diagnostic tests is given below:

Screening test
Diagnostic test

Done on apparently healthy

Done on patients with signs and symptoms

Applied to groups

Applied to single patients

Based on one criterion or cut-off point

Based on evaluation of a number of symptoms, signs, and laboratory findings

Less accurate

More accurate

Less expensive

More expensive

Not a basis for treatment

Used as a basis for treatment

The initiative comes from the investigator or agency providing care

The initiative comes from a patient with a complaint

Screening tests are recommended in the following conditions:

• Early diagnosis changes the disease course

• In a disease with an asymptomatic stage

• In a disease with a test for diagnosis and treatment

• The natural history of the disease is well known

questions.question: In which of the following diseases, screening procedure increases the overall survival to the maximum?
questions.explanation:
Screening of colon cancer increases the overall survival to the maximum.

Colon cancer has a long lead time and can be detected early before pathological changes occur. It can be curable if treated early, otherwise fatal in half the cases.

Early diagnosis and treatment before the critical point have a good outcome and reduce the severity by reversing the disease process. Diagnosis beyond the critical point treatment would be unsuccessful and/or permanent damage would have occurred.

Other diseases that can be screened are:

• Cervical cancer

• Breast cancer

• Prostate cancer

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of prescriptive screening?
options: Screening of immigrants for yellow fever
questions.answer: C. Screening of infants for phenylketonuria
questions.explanation:
Screening of infants for phenylketonuria is an example of prescriptive screening.

Screening of disease is done to detect unrecognized disease or defect, in apparently healthy individuals, by means of rapidly applied tests, examinations, or other procedures.

The difference between prospective and prescriptive screening is given below:

Prospective screening
Prescriptive screening

Definition
People screened for others benefit
People screened for their own benefit

Essential purpose
Disease control
Case detection

Request for screening
Specific request from the authority
Request from physician

Example

• Immigrants for infectious diseases like tuberculosis syphilis, yellow fever, etc;

• HIV screening during antenatal visits, sex workers.

• Screening of blood donors.

• Neonatal screening for hypothyroidism.

• Pap smear for detection of cervical cancer.

• Testing of urine sugar for diabetes mellitus.

Note: Most common neonatal disease to be screened for is neonatal hypothyroidism.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of multiphasic screening?
options: Chest X-ray for TB in large populations
Pap smear in women above 40 years
Random blood sugar during antenatal visits
questions.explanation:
Annual health checkups are an example of multiphasic screening.

Types of screening:

1. Multiphasic screening is the application of two or more screening tests in combination with a large number of people at one time. Example- Annual health checkups.

2. High-risk or selective screening is done on high-risk groups. Example- MRI screening of breast done annually in 25-year old women with BRCA 1, BRCA 2 mutations in a first-degree relative.

3. Mass screening is a screening of a whole or large population like using a chest X-ray for TB screening in large populations. It is done for diseases with high prevalence.

questions.question: Colon cancer screening is being done by a hemoccult stool test in a healthcare center. Patients who test positive, undergo a repeat stool hemoccult test. If the second test comes out positive, the individual is referred for more extensive evaluation. How is this method of screening affecting sensitivity and specificity?
options: Net sensitivity and net specificity are both increasing
Net sensitivity is decreasing and net specificity is increasing
Net sensitivity is increasing and net specificity is decreasing
Net sensitivity is decreasing and net specificity remains the same
questions.answer: B. Net sensitivity is decreasing and net specificity is increasing
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, tests are being performed in series. Here, the net sensitivity is decreasing and net specificity is increasing.

Screening tests are done in series, where the result of the first test determines whether to run the second test or not. e.g. HIV screening is done using consecutive ELISA.

Screening tests are done in parallel, where the second test is independently performed regardless of what the first test result is. Both the tests are done at the same time. For e.g. In LFT, multiple tests are done together like SGOT, SGPT, total bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, etc.

Following are the trends that are observed while evaluating screening tests:

Tests in Series
Tests in parallel

Combined sensitivity
Decreases
Increases

Combined specificity
Increases
Decreases

Combined PPV
Increases
Decreases

Combined NPV
Decreases
Increases

questions.question: Blood pressure is measured in an individual 5 times a day under the same conditions by a new screening test. All 5 readings obtained are the almost same. What is the attribute of a new screening test being described?
questions.explanation:
The attribute of a new screening test to yield the same reading when repeated under the same conditions is called reliability.

Reliability is also called precision or reproducibility.

questions.question:
Ten successive readings of hemoglobin level of a single sample measured by a new method are given below. The hemoglobin level measured by the previous standard test was 10.2. What is true regarding the new method?

Readings: 9.4, 10.4, 9.6, 9.1, 10.8, 12.1, 10.1, 9.8, 9.2, and 9.5.
questions.explanation:
The new method for measuring hemoglobin has high validity and low reliability.

The new test doesn’t give the same values on repeat testing, thus it has low reliability. The mean value of all the readings is 10. The mean is close to the value of 10.2, which is obtained from the standard test, making the validity high.

The validity of a test implies that the test must give correct and accurate results. It represents the closeness to a true/ actual value.

The reliability of a test implies that the test must give consistent results when repeated on the same individual or material, under the same conditions.

questions.question: Out of 100 people having lung cancer, 60 tested positive by a new screening test. Out of 900 people who don't have lung cancer, 300 tested positive. What will be the numerator while calculating sensitivity and its value?
questions.explanation:
The numerator of sensitivity in a screening test is true positive and its value is 60.

True positives are those people who tested positive and actually have the disease. Out of 100 people with lung cancer, 60 are tested positive i.e. true positive.

The given data is represented below:

TP- true positive, FP- false positive, FN- false negative, TN- true negative

Sensitivity is the ability of a screening test to detect true positive(TP) out of the total number of people who have the disease (TP+FN).

Sensitivity= TP/ TP+FN = 60/60+40 = 60%

questions.question: A screening test was carried out among 114 people out of which 15 have a disease. The test showed 22 people tested positive for the disease among which 14 actually had the disease. What is the sensitivity of the test?
questions.explanation:
The sensitivity of the above screening test is 93%.

The given data is represented below

Sensitivity is given as TP/(TP + FN) x 100 = 14/15 = 93%.

questions.question: 1000 patients from a healthcare setup were screened for disease 'X' with a new test (biopsy). The test showed positive results in 90 patients out of the 100 who actually had the disease. What is the sensitivity of the new test?
questions.explanation:
The sensitivity of new test is 90/100.

Biopsy gives the definitive number of cases for Disease X. Hence, the given data is represented below:

Disease +
Disease -

Test +

unknown

Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) = 90/(90+10) = 90/100 = 90%

True positive is defined as a positive test result in a person who has the disease.

questions.question: Specificity of a screening test is the ability of a test to detect:
questions.explanation:
Specificity of a screening test is the ability of the test to identify correctly those who do not have the disease, i.e. true negative.

Sensitivity of a screening test is the ability of the test to identify correctly those who have the disease, i.e. true positive.

False-positive are those who don't have the disease but tested positive.

False-negative are those who have the disease but tested negative.

questions.question: 5000 persons underwent screening for a disease. Out of 500 diseased, 350 tested positive, and out of healthy people, 3000 tested negative. Which of the following is true?
questions.answer: C. Specificity is 66.6% and Sensitivity is 70%
questions.explanation:
The sensitivity of the above screening test is 70% and Specificity is 66.6%.

The given data is represented below:

Sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN) x 100 = 350/500 = 0.7 = 70%.

Specificity = TN/(FP + TN) x 100 = 3000/4500 = 0.6666 = 66.6%.

questions.question: To calculate the positive predictive value of a new screening test for breast carcinoma, what will you use for the denominator?
questions.explanation:
The denominator for the calculation of the positive predictive value of a screening test is true positives + false positives.

Positive predictive value (PPV) of a test is TP/(TP + FP) x 100.

It indicates the probability that a person with a positive test actually has the disease. It is directly proportional to the prevalence of a disease.

Predictive value is affected by sensitivity, specificity, and prevalence. However, it is affected the most by prevalence.

questions.question: Which of the following maximally affect the positive predictive value of a test?
questions.explanation:
Positive predictive value (PPV) is maximally affected by the prevalence of the disease.

If the prevalence of a disease in a population is high, the high will be the positive predictive value of a screening test, and the more accurate will be the test. If the prevalence declines, the PPV will be low.

PPV is directly proportional to the prevalence of a disease. It is affected the most by prevalence. However, both sensitivity and specificity can change the predictive value.

questions.question: Which of the following reflects the diagnostic power of a screening test?
questions.explanation:
The predictive accuracy of a screening test reflects its performance and diagnostic power.

Predictive accuracy is given by:

• Positive predictive value (PPV): the probability of a person with a positive test, actually having the disease.

• Negative predictive value (NPV): the probability of a person with a negative test, definitely not having the disease.

Sensitivity is the ability of a screening test to detect true positive out of total disease.

Specificity is the ability of a screening test to detect true negative out of total nondiseased.

The reliability of a test implies that the test must give consistent results when repeated on the same individual or material, under the same conditions.

questions.question: Screening of 100 immigrants for COVID-19 with a new test showed 48 positive and 52 people negative. Those who tested negative underwent RTPCR out of which 25 came positive. Which of the following is lowest for the new test compared to RTPCR?
questions.explanation:
The sensitivity of the new screening test is low compared to RTPCR.

The new screening test showed 52 people negative, out of which 25 are detected positive by RTPCR. i.e. 25 are false negative.

The false-negative rate is the number of false-negative out of total people having the disease.

False-negative rate = 1 - Sensitivity

The false-negative rate increases as sensitivity decreases.

In this scenario, because the new test has more false negatives, it would have low sensitivity as compared to RTPCR.

questions.question: While screening a disease with a new screening test, the test is positive in many patients who actually don't have the disease. Which of the following is true?
questions.explanation:
The given new screening test has low specificity.

The test is positive in many patients who actually don't have the disease, i.e. high false positives.

The false-positive rate is the number of false positives out of total non-diseased.

False-positive rate = 1-Specificity

The false-positive rate is inversely proportional to specificity. Hence, the given test with high false positives will have low specificity.

Positive predictive value (PPV)= TP/TP+FP. It shows the positive predictive value(PPV) of the test decreases with an increase in false positives.

An increase in the false-positive does not affect the prevalence of the disease. The prevalence of a disease depends on the incidence(I) and duration(D) of the disease.

Prevalance= I x D

questions.question: ECG findings detecting the myocardial infarction obtained from the department of cardiology are given in the table below. Which of the following is true with regard to the below table?
options: Sensitivity is the same as specificity
PPV is the same as NPV
questions.answer: D. PPV is the same as NPV

In the above scenario, PPV is the same as NPV.

questions.question: A new test for hepatitis C is performed on 200 patients with the biopsy-proven disease and 200 patients who are free of the disease. The test shows positive results on 180 of the patients with the disease and negative results on 150 of the patients without the disease. Which of the following is true?

The specificity of the above screening test is 75%.

questions.question: Due to an effective prevention program, the prevalence of a disease in a community has been reduced by 90%. However, the physicians continue to use the same screening test for that disease. Which of the following changes is expected to be seen?
questions.answer: A. Increase in negative predictive value
questions.explanation:
If the prevalence of the disease falls, the negative predictive value(NPV) increases.

The NPV of the test is inversely proportional to the prevalence of a disease.

The PPV of the test is directly proportional to the prevalence of a disease.

Sensitivity and specificity are independent of the prevalence of the disease in the area. They do not change with the change in prevalence.

questions.question: In a population of 10000, the prevalence of a disease is 20%. The sensitivity of a screening test is 95% and specificity is 80%. What is the positive predictive value of the test?
questions.explanation:
The positive predictive value (PPV) of the test is 54.3%.

The prevalence of the disease is 20% in 10000, i.e., 2000 people have the disease(TP + FN) and 8000 are disease-free (FP + TN).

The sensitivity of the test is 95%, i.e. TP/(TP + FN) = 95%.

Thus, the true positives (TP)= 95/100 x (TP + FN) = 95/100 x 2000 = 1900.

The specificity of the test is 80%, i.e. TN/(FP + TN) = 80%.

Thus, the true negatives (TN)= 80/100 x (FP + TN) = 80/100 x 8000 = 6400.

The given data is represented below:

TP- true positive, FP- false positive, FN- false negative, TN- true negative

From the above table, PPV is calculated as TP/(TP + FP) x 100 = 1900/3500 = 54.3%.

An alternate formula(Bayes theorem) that can be used is PPV = (Sn x P) / (Sn x P)+[(1-Sp)(1-P)]

Sn- Sensitivity, P- Prevalence, Sp- Specificity

questions.question: The prevalence of the disease 'X' in a population is 30%. The diagnostic test for this disease has a specificity of 0.80 and a sensitivity of 0.90. What is the negative predictive value of the test?
questions.explanation:
The negative predictive value of the above test is 95%.

For convenience, let us assume that the total population in this scenario is 100.

The prevalence of the disease is 30%. So the total number of people with the disease is 30(TP+FN) and disease-free(FP+TN) is 70.

Since sensitivity is 0.90, i.e. TP/(TP + FN) = 90%.

The total true positives (TP) = 90/100 x (TP+FN) = 90/100 x 30 = 27

False-negative(FN) = 30-27 = 3

Since specificity is 0.80, i.e. TN/(FP+TN) = 80%.

Total true negatives (TN) =(FP+TN) x 80/100 = 70 x 80/100 = 56

False-positive(FP) = 70-56 = 14

The given data is represented below:

Disease +

Disease -

Total

Test +

27 (TP)

14 (FP)

41

Test -

3 (FN)

56 (TN)

59

Total

30(TP+FN)

70(FP+TN)

100

Negative predictive value (NPV) = TN/(FN + TN) x 100 = 56/59 = 0.949 = 95%.

An alternate formula(Bayes theorem) that can be used is NPV = (1-P) x Sp /[P x (1-Sn)] +[(1-P) x Sp]

Sn- Sensitivity, P- Prevalence, Sp- Specificity

questions.question: Which of the following is best for determining the threshold for diagnosis of a positive test?
questions.explanation:
The receiver operator characteristic curve is the best for determining the threshold for the diagnosis of a positive test. It is also used for the comparison of two or more screening/ diagnostic tests of disease with each other.

The following is an example of a ROC curve for a screening test.

questions.question: Which curve from the given image reflects a better test?
questions.explanation:
Test A is the best test among the four given, as it has the highest sensitivity and the lowest false positive rate (100-specificity).

A receiver operating characteristic curve(ROC) is obtained by plotting a test's true positive rate (sensitivity) against its false-positive rate ( 100- specificity) for different diagnostic cut-off points.

The shape of the curve reflects the quality of the test. The better the test, the more it moves to the upper left (more the area under the curve). For a good test, sensitivity comes close to 100% on the y-axis, and the false positive rate comes close to 0% on the x-axis.

questions.question: The fasting blood glucose levels of a population from two overlapping distributions are shown in the below graph. A test was done with the cutoff of 120mg/ dl for diagnosing diabetes. What does the shaded area represent?
questions.explanation: The shaded area represents the false positives (Non-diabetics incorrectly classified as diabetics).

questions.question: Which of the following is false about herd immunity?
options: It refers to group protection beyond what is afforded by the protection of immunized individuals
Vaccination allows the possibility of 100% herd immunity against a disease
It is affected by presence and distribution of alternative animal hosts
It doesn’t protect the individual in the case of tetanus
questions.answer: B. Vaccination allows the possibility of 100% herd immunity against a disease
questions.explanation:
It is not possible to achieve 100% herd immunity against a certain disease but studies have shown this is not necessary for disease control.

Herd structure is never constant. It is subject to constant variation because of new births, deaths and population mobility. An ongoing immunization programme will keep up the herd immunity at a very high level.

questions.question: Herd immunity threshold does not vary with which of the following?
options: Efficacy of the vaccine for the disease
Number of vaccines for the disease
questions.answer: C. Number of vaccines for the disease
questions.explanation: Herd immunity threshold does not vary with the number of vaccines for the disease. It varies only due to the virulence of the disease, efficacy of the vaccine and contact parameter for the population.

questions.question: Which of the following is false about normal human immunoglobulin (NHIG)?
options: All live vaccines can be given simultaneously with NHIG.
They are used against measles and hepatitis A.
There should be a low IgA concentration in NHIG preparations.
Each NHIG fraction is obtained from at least 1,000 donors.
questions.answer: A. All live vaccines can be given simultaneously with NHIG.
questions.explanation:
Live vaccines should generally be avoided for 12 weeks following an injection of normal human immunoglobulin (Ig). If a live vaccine has already been administered, the injection of normal human Ig should be delayed for 2 weeks.

NHIG is an antibody-rich fraction that is usually obtained from a pool of at least 1,000 donors. AN NHIG preparation must contain at least 90% intact IgG and minimal IgG aggregates with low IgA concentration. NHIG is commonly used to prevent measles and hepatitis A infections.

Specific human immunoglobulins are made from the plasma of patients who have recently recovered from an infection or are obtained from individuals who have been immunized against a specific infection. These preparations have a high antibody content against an individual infection and provide immediate protection.

questions.question: Which of the following is false about specific human immunoglobulins?
questions.explanation:
Specific human immunoglobulins or hyperimmune human Igs are obtained from selected donors that have high titres of the antibodies to the disease like those who have recovered from the disease.

It is commonly used in prophylaxis of chickenpox in highly susceptible individuals and in post-exposure prophylaxis of hepatitis B.

questions.question: Which of the following is not true about secondary booster immune response in comparison with primary response?
options: Antibody elicited tends to have a greater avidity to bind to the antigen
Antibody response is at a higher level
Antibody response is maintained for a longer period of time
questions.answer: D. Production of antibody is slower
questions.explanation:
Production of antibodies is faster in secondary booster response.

Primary response is the immune response developed when an antigen is administered for the first time to a person who has never been exposed to it. There is a latent period of 3-10 days before antibodies appear in the blood.

Secondary booster response is the immune response elicited by a booster dose. In comparison to a primary immune response, it has a shorter latent period, faster production of antibodies, and an abundance of antibodies. The antibody response is maintained at higher levels for a longer period of time, and the antibody elicited tends to have a greater avidity or capacity to bind to the antigen.

questions.question: Which of the following is false about live vaccines?
options: Simultaneous administration of two live vaccines should be done in the same syringe
Two live vaccines can be administered simultaneously
Immuno-compromised state poses a contraindication to live vaccines
Live vaccines contain both major and minor antigens
questions.answer: A. Simultaneous administration of two live vaccines should be done in the same syringe
questions.explanation:
Simultaneous administration of vaccines is defined as administering more than one vaccine on the same clinic day, at different anatomic sites. They are not combined in the same syringe.

Simultaneous administration of the most widely used live and inactivated vaccines does not result in decreased antibody responses or increased rates of adverse reaction. However, in children with functional or anatomic asplenia pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) and Menactra brand meningococcal conjugate vaccines should not be administered at the same visit; separate these vaccines by at least 4 weeks.

Advantages of simultaneous administration of vaccines:

• The organisms multiply in the host and thus, the antigenic dose is larger than what is injected.

• They have all the major and minor antigenic components.

Live vaccines should not be administered to those with an immunocompromised state, since they may cause severe systemic disease by way of viremia/bacteriemia.

Note: If live vaccines are not given simultaneously, they must be spaced as follows-

• The administration of two live parenteral vaccines or live intranasal influenza vaccines must be separated by at least 4 weeks (28 days).

• If two live vaccines are given less than 4 weeks apart, the second vaccine should be repeated in four weeks. This is because the live vaccine given first can interfere with the second vaccine, and the person may not develop active immunity to the second vaccine.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a killed vaccine?
questions.explanation:
Yellow fever vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine.

Injectable polio vaccine (Salk vaccine), pertussis vaccine, and rabies vaccine are killed vaccines.

questions.question: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to administration of inactivated or killed vaccines?
questions.explanation:
The only absolute contraindication to administration of an inactivated or killed vaccine is severe local or general reaction to a previous dose of the vaccine.

Inactivated or killed vaccines are made from growing cultures of the organism and then inactivating them with heat or chemicals.They activate the channels of active immunity after injection and are less efficacious than live vaccines. Multiple doses or booster doses are usually required to produce an adequate antibody response.

Killed vaccines can be given to immune-compromised individuals and in pregnancy as the infective agent is inactivated and cannot grow.

Egg allergy is not an absolute contraindication to the administration of an inactivated or killed vaccine.

questions.question:
Which of the following are live vaccines?

1. Hepatitis B vaccine

2. Yellow fever vaccine

3. HPV vaccine

4. Tetanus vaccine

5. Sabin vaccine
questions.explanation:
Yellow fever vaccine and Sabin vaccine (oral polio vaccine) are live vaccines.

HBV and HPV vaccines are recombinant vaccines. Tetanus vaccine is a toxoid vaccine.

questions.question: In which of the following diseases should active and passive immunisation not be done together?
questions.explanation:
Active and passive immunization should not be done together for measles as the vaccine used is a live vaccine.

Live vaccines should generally be avoided for 12 weeks following an injection of normal human immunoglobulin (Ig). If a live vaccine has already been administered, the injection of normal human Ig should be delayed for 2 weeks.

Note: In the case of measles alone, the recommended interval between administration of Measles immunoglobulins and Live measles vaccine is about 6 months in a non-immunocompromised individual and 8 months in an immunocompromised individual.

questions.question: What is the main drawback of polysaccharide-based vaccines?
options: They cause severe pain at the injection site
The immune responses elicited are serotype specific
It cannot be conjugated with proteins to enhance immunogenicity
The rate of adverse reactions is very high
questions.answer: B. The immune responses elicited are serotype specific
questions.explanation:
Polysaccharide-based vaccines stimulate an antibody response against the surface polysaccharide of the pathogenic-capsulated bacteria. The polysaccharide structure varies not only between bacteria of different species but also between different strains within a single species. Thus, a limitation of these vaccines is that the immune responses are serotype-specific.

If these vaccines are conjugated with proteins, they are given the capability of eliciting a stronger immune response. Multivalent formulations of both polysaccharide-based vaccines and conjugated vaccines are required to achieve protection against multiple serotypes.

questions.question: Which of the following is a subunit vaccine?
questions.explanation:
Hepatitis B vaccine is an example of a subunit vaccine made using HBsAg.

Subunit vaccines are produced from macromolecules derived from immunogenic components of organisms by recombinant DNA technology. E.g., HPV vaccine (uses L1 major capsid protein) and hepatitis B vaccine (uses HBsAg).

BCG is a live attenuated vaccine, IPV is an inactivated vaccine and DPT has diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and a killed pertussis component.

questions.question: You are a medical officer conducting an ANC camp in a rural village near Hubli, Karnataka. Which of the following vaccines would you not administer to a pregnant woman?
questions.explanation:
Yellow fever vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy in non-endemic areas. It is a live vaccine and most live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy unless the risk of infection is much greater than the risk of harm to the fetus.

Note: Yellow fever vaccine is not an absolute contraindication as it is administered in certain endemic areas and in outbreaks

questions.question: A patient is diagnosed to have an allergy to eggs. Administration of which of the following vaccines is contraindicated in this patient?
questions.explanation: Influenza and yellow fever vaccines are contraindicated in patients having an allergy to eggs.

questions.question: A newborn baby is HIV + and symptomatic. Which of the following vaccines must not be given to her?
questions.explanation:
BCG vaccine must not be administrated to HIV-infected infants who are symptomatic despite the presence of high TB prevalence. Since BCG is a live vaccine, it significantly increases the risk of disseminated TB in a symptomatic HIV+ infant.

However, asymptomatic infants who are HIV+ can be given BCG, provided the risk of contracting TB is high in that region. In areas of low TB prevalence or risk, the BCG vaccine is avoided.

WHO recommendations for administering live vaccines in symptomatic HIV+ patients:

• Measles vaccine (or MMR) is allowed even in the symptomatic stage of HIV infection (except in the terminal phase), so as to prevent serious and life-threatening wild measles virus disease. Avoid MMR only if CD4+ < 15% (severely immunocompromised).

• IPV is an inactivated vaccine and must be used as an alternative to OPV.

questions.question: Which of the following side effects is most likely to develop in a newborn, following BCG vaccination?
questions.explanation:
Ulceration is the most common side effect post BCG vaccination.

Following vaccination, the local tissue response begins in 2-3 weeks and results in scar formation and healing within 3 months. Side effects most commonly seen include ulceration at the vaccination site and regional lymphadenitis. Some vaccine strains may also rarely cause osteomyelitis.

In immunocompromised states, disseminated BCG infection can occur.

The image below shows the typical adverse effcts seen following BCG vaccination:

1. Regional lymphadenopathy

2. Suppurative lymphadenopathy with fistula

3. Ulcer at injection site

4. Cold abscess at inject site

questions.question: A child who had recently received the BCG vaccine comes to you with complaints of fever, pain and swelling at the injection site. You suspect a localised abscess formation. Which of the following steps should be avoided in the treatment of this child?
options: Incision and application of INH powder
Incision and application of PAS powder
questions.explanation:
There is no need for systemic treatment with INH in case of a local abscess formation after BCG vaccination.

If there is a local abscess formation following BCG vaccination, it should be treated by aspiration. If it does not clear, then it should be incised and INH or PAS powder should be applied daily to the site. The patient should be assured of the harmless nature of the lesion.

questions.question:
A complete blood count was obtained for a patient after they were administered vaccine X. The report is shown below. Which of the following options is most likely to be vaccine X?

Hemoglobin - 13 g/dl
RBC count - 5 million cells per microlitre
WBC count - 8000 per microlitre
Platelet count - 90000 per microlitre
questions.explanation: The lab report shows a low platelet count or thrombocytopenia. This is a possible adverse effect of the MMR vaccine.

questions.question: Persistent inconsolable crying can be a result of administration of which of the following vaccines?
questions.explanation:
Persistent inconsolable crying is usually seen after DPT vaccine. It is mostly attributed to the pertussis fraction of the vaccine.

It usually lasts for 3 hours and settles after a day or so. Other adverse effects of the DTP vaccine include neurologic effects like encephalitis and encephalopathies.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about the DPT vaccine?
options: Adult preparation contains a lower dose of diphtheria than the pediatric version
Whole killed bacteria of Bordetella pertussis has an adjuvant effect
The whole-cell killed B. pertussis component is encephalogenic
Presence of H. influenzae type b component increases its immunogenicity
questions.answer: D. Presence of H. influenzae type b component increases its immunogenicity
questions.explanation:
H. influenzae type b (Hib) is not a component of the DPT vaccine and hence cannot affect its immunogenicity. It is a component of the pentavalent vaccine.

The DPT vaccine is made up of diphtheria, pertussis and tetanus vaccines. The pertussis component in DPT vaccine enhances the potency of the diphtheria toxoid. Both whole-cell killed B. pertussis and acellular pertussis component have this adjuvant effect. The only difference is that whole-cell killed B. pertussis is encephalitogenic and immunity is short-lasting, while the acellular pertussis component (DTaP) is devoid of neurological complications.

There are two types of DPT vaccines - plain and adsorbed. Adsorption is usually carried out on a mineral carrier like aluminium phosphate or hydroxide. Adsorbed vaccines are more immunogenic and recommended by WHO for national vaccination programmes.

questions.question: A worried mother brings her baby to your PHC saying her child has gone limp. She mentions the child had recently been given some oral drops as part of a mass vaccination campaign. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the baby's symptoms?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of paralysis and the likely cause is vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis following OPV administration.

This is a rare side effect of OPV. Acute-onset flaccid paralysis occurs within 4 to 30 days of receipt of the vaccine in these cases or within 4 to 75 days after contact with a vaccine recipient.

questions.question: A patient presents with complaints of severe aching pain and weakness in his left arm and shoulder. He mentions he had recently been administered a vaccine in his left arm, but he does not remember the name of the vaccine. Which of the following could be the most common cause of his symptoms?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of brachial neuritis which is a known complication of the tetanus vaccine.

Brachial neuritis is a dysfunction of nerves supplying the arm and shoulder without the involvement of the rest of the nervous system. It presents with a deep, steady, severe aching pain in the shoulder and arm followed by weakness and wasting in arm and shoulder muscles. Sensory loss may also be present. It is treated symptomatically by analgesics.

questions.question: Select the wrongly matched pair of excipients and vaccines.
questions.explanation:
Formaldehyde is not used in the BCG vaccine. It is used in IPV and diphtheria and tetanus vaccines.

Excipients (other vaccine constituents) include: Adjuvants: serve to enhance the immune reaction to the vaccine , Stabilizers : stabilize and prolong the shelf-life of the vaccine and

Preservatives : preserve the components. Some examples are listed below:

• As stabilizing agents-

• MgCl2 - OPV

• MgSO4 - measles

• Lactose-sorbitol and sorbitol-gelatine

• To prevent microbial growth and contamination-

• Thiomersal- DPT, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), rabies, influenza, and meningococcal diseases. It contains very small amounts of organic mercury.

• Neomycin- MMR and IPV

• Other preservatives-

• 2-phenoxyethanol - IPV

• Phenol - Typhoid vaccine

questions.question: Which of the following is false about adjuvants in vaccines?
options: Immune response is increased by degree or duration by their use
They are used in HPV vaccines
There is a high incidence of side effects with their use
They help in the reduction of amount of immunogens in vaccines
questions.answer: C. There is a high incidence of side effects with their use
questions.explanation:
Side effects are rare with the use of adjuvants in vaccines.

Adjuvants are substances that are added to vaccines to enhance their immunogenicity by degree and/or duration. They help in the reduction of the amount of immunogen in vaccines or in the number of doses required to achieve immunity.

Aluminium salts are the most commonly used adjuvants.

Adjuvants are used in many vaccines like:

• Anthrax vaccine

• Hep A vaccine

• Hep B vaccine

• Japanese encephalitis vaccine

• DT and DTaP

• HPV vaccine

• Pneumococcal vaccine

questions.question: Which adjuvant is used in the DPT vaccine?
questions.explanation:
Aluminium is the adjuvant used in DPT vaccines.

The table below lists adjuvants used in human vaccines:

Name

Class

Components

Vaccine

Alum

Mineral salts

Aluminium phosphate, aluminium hydroxide

Diphtheria, tetanus, pneumococcus, HAV, HBV, anthrax, tick-borne encephalitis, MenC, HPV

MF59
