Squalene, Tween 80, Span 85

Seasonal and pandemic influenza

AS03

Oil-in-water emulsion

Squalene, Tween 80, alpha tocopherol

Pandemic influenza

AF03

Oil-in-water emulsion

Squalene, Montane 80, Eumulgin B1PH

Pandemic influenza

Virosomes

Liposomes

Phospholipids, cholesterol, haemagglutinin

Seasonal influenza, HAV

AS04

Alum-adsorbed TLR4 agonist

Alumnium hydroxide, monophosphoryl lipid A (MPL)

HBV, HPV

RC-529

Alum-adsorbed TLR4 agonist

Aluminium hydroxide, synthetic MPL

HBV

questions.question: A child has come to you for the administration of the IPV vaccine, as part of his routine immunisation schedule. Which of the following antibiotics may be found in this vaccine?
questions.explanation:
IPV may contain trace amounts of streptomycin, neomycin or polymyxin B.

MMR contain small amount of neomycin.

Antibiotics are used during vaccine manufacture to prevent bacterial contamination of tissue culture cells.

questions.question: Which of the following are the most and least heat-sensitive vaccines respectively?
options: Sabin vaccine and hep B vaccine
Japanese encaphalitis vaccine and pneumococcal vaccine
Salk vaccine and hep B vaccine
questions.answer: A. Sabin vaccine and hep B vaccine
questions.explanation: Oral polio (Sabin) vaccine is the most heat-sensitive vaccine. Hepatitis B vaccines are the least heat-sensitive alongside meningococcal A vaccine, freeze-dried Hib vaccine and pneumococcal vaccines.

questions.question: Which of the following vaccines should be protected from sub-zero temperatures?
questions.explanation:
Hepatitis B vaccine is sensitive to freezing and should be protected from sub-zero temperatures.

Vaccines to be protected from freezing are as follows:

• Hepatitis B

• Cholera

• DTaP-hepB-Hib-IPV (hexavalent)

• DTwP-hepB-Hib (pentavalent)

• Liquid Hib

• IPV

• Influenza, pneumococcal vaccines

• Tetanus, DT, Td

• Rotavirus (freeze-dried, least sensitive), the liquid form is resistant to freezing

• HPV

questions.question: What vaccines are supplied in the type of bottle given below?
questions.explanation: The image shows an amber-colored vial. Vaccines like BCG and measles vaccine are sensitive to light and thus are supplied in such vials.

questions.question: Which of the following is a non-electrical cold-chain equipment?
questions.explanation:
Cold boxes, vaccine carriers, and ice packs are some of the non-electrical components of the cold-chain system.

Cold boxes are insulated containers used for transportation and temporary storage of vaccines and ice packs. Vaccine carriers are usually not used for the storage of vaccines but for their transportation. Ice packs generally have two holes in them for placing vaccines. They are filled with water.

The below image shows a cold box containing vaccines and ice packs.

questions.question: What is the temperature maintained in the freezer compartment of the solar refrigerator battery drive?
questions.explanation:
The freezer compartment of the solar refrigerator battery drive is maintained at – 7 °C, and it is used to store mainly ice packs.

The vaccine storage compartment of this solar cold chain equipment is maintained at 2 to 8 °C. The other solar cold-chain equipment commonly used is the solar refrigerators direct drive, which uses the sun’s energy to freeze phase-change materials like water and then uses this formed ice bank to keep the refrigerator cold.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is not true about the device shown in the image below?
options: Smaller ones are given to PHCs and the larger ones to district vaccine stores
They have temperature zones for different vaccines
Kata thermometer is used to record temperature inside this device
These devices are provided with baskets to store vaccines
questions.answer: C. Kata thermometer is used to record temperature inside this device
questions.explanation:
The image shown in the question is of an ice-lined refrigerator (ILR). Dial or digital thermometers are used to record temperatures inside an ice-lined refrigerator.

ILRs are the main method of vaccine storage in primary health centers. They are an important part of the cold chain and they maintain a temperature of 2 to 8 °C for the storage of vaccines.

They have different temperature zones for different vaccines. The upper zone is for freeze-sensitive vaccines like cholera, hep B, rotavirus(liquid), etc while the lower zone is for heat-sensitive vaccines like OPV, measles, etc.

All vaccines are kept in the basket provided with ILR. Vaccines like OPV, BCG, measles, and JE can be kept at the bottom of the basket while, DPT, TT, Hep B, IPV, and pentavalent vaccines and diluents are kept in the upper part of the basket.

questions.question: While working as a medical officer in a CHC, you experience a sudden power cut in your area due to which the ice-lined refrigerator loses power. What is the time taken for the temperature inside this equipment to rise to the maximum recommended temperature limit?
questions.explanation:
Hold-over time is the time taken by cold-chain equipment to raise the temperature inside it, during loss of power, to the maximum temperature limit in its recommended range. For an ice-lined refrigerator(ILR), this time depends on:

• Ambient temperature

• Frequency of opening the equipment

• Quantity of vaccines kept inside with spacing

• Condition of ice-pack lining

The below image shows an ILR.

questions.question: At what level is the risk of cold-chain failure the highest?
questions.explanation: The risk of cold chain failure is highest at the sub-centre and village levels. Thus, vaccines are not stored at the sub-centre and are supplied on the day of use.

questions.question: Open vial policy is not applicable to which of the following vaccines?
questions.explanation:
Open vial policy is not applicable for BCG and measles vaccines.

It is applicable for:

• DPT

• TT

• Hepatitis B vaccine

• OPV

• Pentavalent vaccine

• Rotavirus vaccine (New version with the VVM on the side)

questions.question: What are the devices given below used to measure?
options: Disintegration of vaccine constituents due to temperature
questions.answer: B. Cumulative heat exposure of vaccine
questions.explanation:
The image shown is of vaccine vial monitors (VVM), which measure the cumulative heat exposure of the vaccine.

VVMs are heat-sensitive indicators that are routinely used to monitor vaccine viability as the vaccine vial moves across the supply chain. They record cumulative heat exposure through a gradual change in color. If the color of the inner square is the same or is darker than the outer circle, the vaccine has been exposed to too much heat and should be discarded.

questions.question: You are preparing to administer the BCG vaccine to a newborn at a PHC. Before administering the vaccine, you check the vaccine vial monitor. In which of the following observations on the VVM, will you discard the vaccine?
options: Inner square has the same color as the outer circle
Inner circle has the same color as the outer square
Inner circle is lighter than the outer square
questions.answer: B. Inner square has the same color as the outer circle
questions.explanation: A vaccine must be discarded if the VVM shows the inner square is the same color or darker than the outer circle.

questions.question: You are volunteering in a vaccination camp. You perform a shake test before administering a particular vaccine. Which of the following is checked by this test?
questions.explanation:
The shake test is done to check for damage to vaccines that are sensitive to freezing temperatures.

Steps to perform the shake test:

• A frozen vaccine is used as a control vial and the vial suspected to be damaged by freezing is taken as the test vial.

• Both are shaken after thawing and the rate of sedimentation is compared.

• If the rate of sedimentation in the test vial is slower than that in the control vial, then it is usable and has not been damaged.

Some of the most widely used vaccines are freeze-sensitive. These include vaccines against:

• Diphtheria

• Tetanus

• Pertussis

• Haemophilus influenza type b (Liquid )

• Hepatitis B

questions.question: Which is the process designed to prevent microorganisms from reaching a protected environment?
questions.explanation:
Asepsis is the process designed to prevent microorganisms from reaching a protected environment.

Sterilization is a process of killing or removal of all living microorganisms either in the vegetative or spore state from an area or surface or a medium.

Decontamination is the process of rendering an article or area free of contaminants, including microbial, chemical, radioactive and other hazardous materials.

Disinfection is the process by which the destruction of microorganisms is achieved with the use of physical or chemical agents. Microbial forms like spores and some viruses may be resistant to certain disinfectants.

questions.question: All of the following are methods of dry heat sterilisation except:
questions.explanation:
Autoclaving is a method of moist heat sterilization.

Dry heat sterilization

Moist heat sterilization

Flaming

Incineration

Hot air oven

Boiling

Pasteurization

Autoclaving

questions.question: What is the temperature that has to be maintained for sterilization in the device shown below?
questions.explanation:
The image shown is a sterilizing hot air oven. The temperature to be maintained is 160° C for 2 hours.

Exposure to dry heat in a sterilizing hot air oven ensures the carbonization of organic material and the destruction of microorganisms and spores. The following combinations of temperature and duration of sterilization can be applied in hot air ovens:

• 180°C for 30 mins

• 170°C for 60 mins

• 160⁰C for 2 hours

questions.question: An OT technician is sterilizing surgical instruments in the following device. What temperature should be maintained?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows an autoclave. Surgical instruments are sterilized at 121° C for 10-15 minutes.

Autoclaving is a form of moist heat sterilization which creates an increased temperature of steam under pressure. This method of sterilization is effective against spores also. Autoclaving is done for instruments that cannot withstand high temperatures of hot air oven or dry heat.

questions.question:
Which of the following materials are sterilized by a hot air oven?

1. Glasswares

2. Oils and powders

3. Surgical instruments

4. Culture media

5. Swabs and dressings
questions.explanation:
Glasswares, oils and powders, swabs, and dressings are sterilized by a hot air oven.

Surgical instruments and culture media are sterilized by autoclave.

questions.question: You have performed an upper GI endoscopy on a HbsAg positive patient. Which of the following should be used to sterilize the scope?
questions.explanation:
2% glutaraldehyde is used to sterilize endoscopes and fibreoptic scopes.

Aldehydes in 2% solutions (like glutaraldehyde and formaldehyde) have sporicidal activities.

Glutaraldehyde is usually efficacious against tubercle bacteria, fungi & viruses.

questions.question: Which of the following is false regarding the use of ethylene oxide in sterilisation and disinfection?
options: It is an inflammable and explosive gas
It is used for heat-sensitive objects
It is mixed with nitrogen for sterilization
questions.answer: C. It is mixed with nitrogen for sterilization
questions.explanation:
A mixture of ethylene oxide with carbon dioxide is used for sterilization, not with nitrogen.

Ethylene oxide is an alkylating agent and has inflammable and explosive properties. It is often mixed with the following prior to use:

• Carbon dioxide - decreases its explosive nature

• Water vapor - increases the efficiency of the gas

Sterilization using this gas is usually done at 50-60 °C. and is suitable for heat-sensitive items like plastics, heart valves, dental equipment. It is effective against bacteria, spores, and some viruses.

questions.question: The following machine was used during a cardiac bypass surgery. How is it best sterilized?
questions.explanation:
The image shown is a heart-lung machine. It is best sterilized using ethylene oxide.

Ethylene oxide gas diffuses through many types of porous materials and readily penetrates some plastics and is used for sterilizing machines.

questions.question: Povidone - iodine is an example of:
questions.explanation:
Povidone - iodine is an iodophor.

Iodophors are iodine-based disinfectants in which iodine is combined with solubilizing agents or carriers. This results in the formation of a complex that provides a sustained release reservoir of iodine and releases small amounts of free iodine in an aqueous solution.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of precurrent disinfection?
options: Chlorination of a well by village public health authorities
Disinfection of kidney tray used during delivery of placenta
Disinfection of bed linen after the death of a patient
Disinfection of artery forceps following a surgery
questions.answer: A. Chlorination of a well by village public health authorities
questions.explanation:
Chlorination of water in a well is an example of precurrent disinfection.

Precurrent disinfection refers to prophylactic disinfection prior to discharge of infectious material. This includes pasteurization of milk, chlorination of water and hand washing.

Concurrent disinfection is the application of disinfection methods after discharge of infectious material from a person or soiling. This includes disinfection of urine, faeces, vomit, contaminated linen, clothes, hands.

Terminal disinfection is done after the death of a patient or transfer or after cessation of isolation.

questions.question: Chlorine is the main disinfectant element in all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Cetrimide (trade name - Cetavlon) is a quaternary ammonia compound (QAC) that does not contain chlorine. QACs are low-level disinfectants and are sporostatic but not sporicidal. It is a bactericidal agent against vegetative gram-positive organisms.

Other QACs include cetrimide (cetavlon) and benzalkonium chloride.

Savlon contains cetrimide and chlorhexidine and is mainly used for plastic items. Clinical thermometers may be best disinfected in Savlon mixed with spirit in a 1:6 ratio.

Chlorine compounds are potent disinfectants that are bactericidal, fungicidal, sporicidal, tuberculocidal, and virucidal.

Chlorine compounds
Mechanism of action and uses

1. Bleaching powder (chlorinated lime)
Disinfection of water, feces, and urine

2. Chloramine - T
Has a prolonged bactericidal effect, used in a health care setting

3. Hypochlorites
Disinfect infectious waste and surfaces

4. Halazone tablets
Disinfect small quantities of water

5. Superoxidized water
Saline is electrolyzed to release hypochlorous acid and chlorine, which act as disinfectants

questions.question: Hydrogen peroxide is:
questions.answer: C. Bactericidal, fungicidal, sporicidal and virucidal
questions.explanation:
Hydrogen peroxide is effective against bacteria, fungi, spores and viruses.

It is used in the hospital setting to disinfect surfaces. Sporicidal activities require higher concentrations and longer contact times. A 3% solution is also used as an antiseptic and for cleaning wounds and discharging ulcers.

questions.question: Which among the following is a low-level disinfectant?
questions.explanation:
Benzalkonium chloride is a quaternary ammonium compound that is used as a low-level disinfectant.

There are 3 types of disinfectants:

• Low-level disinfectant - kills only vegetative bacteria, fungi and lipid enveloped viruses (e.g. quaternary ammonium compounds)

• Intermediate level disinfectant: kills all microbes including mycobacteria and non-enveloped viruses, but not spores (e.g. alcohol, iodophors)

• High-level disinfectant - This is a chemical that kills all microbial pathogens and some spores if the contact time is increased (e.g. glutaraldehyde, hydrogen peroxide)

questions.question: Which among the following is not a sporicidal agent?
questions.explanation:
Cresol a phenolic compound is not sporicidal.

Disinfectants that are not sporicidal are:

• Biguanides

• Alcohols

• Heavy metal disinfectants

• Organic acids

• QACs

• Phenolic compounds

Sporicidal disinfectants include:

• Aldehydes

• Chlorine disinfectants

• Hydrogen peroxide

• Ethylene oxide

• Peracetic acids

questions.question: Which of the following disinfectants has anti-viral action?
questions.explanation:
Hypochlorite is an antiviral disinfectant.

Antiviral disinfectants include:

• Chlorine compounds

• Phenol (at high concentrations)

• Aldehydes

• Hydrogen peroxide

questions.question: A nurse in a PHC is using bleaching powder to disinfect bed linen contaminated with stool. What is the amount that she should use?
questions.explanation:
Bleaching powder of 50 g/L of water is required for disinfecting feces and urine.

The agents commonly used for disinfecting faeces and urine are:

questions.question: Which of the following methods of disinfection is not effective against prions?
questions.explanation:
Benzalkonium chloride is not effective against prions.

Prions can be inactivated by following the given steps:

• Immersing the instruments in 1N NaOH or sodium hypochlorite for 1 hour

• Then they are transferred to water

• Then they are heated in a gravity displacement autoclave at 121°C for 1 hour

• After this, they are cleaned and subjected to routine sterilization

questions.question: Which of the following methods is not effective for disinfection of sputum of patients?
questions.explanation:
Chlorhexidine is not used to disinfect sputum.

Sputum can be disinfected by:

• Autoclaving or boiling - if a considerable amount of sputum is present (e.g. in TB hospitals)

• 5% cresol - patients are asked to spit in a sputum cup half-filled with cresol

• Burning - for samples received in gauze or paper handkerchiefs

questions.explanation:
The biological indicators used to check the efficiency of various sterilization methods are:

questions.question: Rideal-Walker co-efficient is employed for the assessment of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
The Rideal-Walker coefficient helps in assessing the power of a disinfectant relative to phenol.

It assesses this by determining the phenol coefficient (PC). A PC value of > 1 indicates that it is more effective than phenol. The higher the number, the greater its effectiveness in comparison to phenol and vice versa. Traditional organisms used to test the power of the disinfectant include S. aureus and Salmonella enteric subtype typhi.

Phenol coefficient = The dilution of test disinfectant which kills microorganisms in a given time ÷ The dilution of phenol which kills the microorganism in the same time under identical conditions.

Other tests that are used for disinfectants are as follows:

• Chick Martin test - modification of the Rideal-Walker test where disinfectants act in the presence of organic matter like feces or yeast to simulate natural conditions

• Kelsey-Skyes test (capacity test) - tests the capacity of a disinfectant to retain its activity when used repeatedly.

• In-use test - determines whether the chosen disinfectant is effective in actual hospital use

Joseph Lister first introduced phenol (carbolic acid) as an antiseptic to sterilize surgical instruments and clean wounds. Lister's work led to a reduction in postoperative infections and made surgery safer for patients, distinguishing him as the 'Father of Modern Surgery' and 'Father of Antiseptic Surgery'.

questions.question: Which of the following is false regarding the Spaulding classification?
options: Semi-critical items require high level disinfection
Non-critical items do not require disinfection
Cardiac catheters are classified as critical items
Critical items are associated with a high risk of infection
questions.answer: B. Non-critical items do not require disinfection
questions.explanation: Under the Spaulding classification, non-critical items require intermediate or low-level disinfection.

questions.question: A blood spill in the operation theatre must be cleaned with _____.
questions.explanation:
Sodium hypochlorite, a compound of chlorine, is the best disinfectant for surface blood spills. It is used with a concentration of 0.5-5%.

If the spill contains large amounts of blood or body fluids, clean the visible matter with disposable absorbent material and discard the contaminated materials in appropriate, labelled containment.

A 1:10–1:100 dilution of 5.25%–6.15% sodium hypochlorite (i.e., household bleach) or an EPA-registered tuberculocidal disinfectant has been recommended for decontaminating blood spills.

questions.question: When did the WHO declare that smallpox has been globally eradicated?
questions.explanation: The WHO declared the eradication of smallpox on 8th May 1980.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is not included in the case definition of smallpox?
options: Acute onset fever and malaise 2-4 days before onset of rash
Development of a maculopapular rash starting on the face and forearms
Evolution of the rash to umbilicated pustules within 48 hours
No alternative diagnosis explaining the illness
questions.answer: C. Evolution of the rash to umbilicated pustules within 48 hours
questions.explanation:
The rash of smallpox evolves within 48 hours, to first form deep-seated, firm, and well-circumscribed vesicles, which later become umbilicated or confluent pustules.

Case definition for notification of smallpox:

• An individual of any age with acute onset fever, malaise, severe prostration, headache, and backache 2-4 days before the onset of rash.

• Development of a maculopapular rash starting on the face and forearms and then spreading to the trunk and legs. Rash evolves within 48 hours to deep-seated, firm, and well-circumscribed vesicles, which later become umbilicated or confluent pustules.

• Lesions that appear at the same stage of development (i.e. all are vesicles or all are pustules) on any given part of the body.

• No alternative diagnosis explaining the illness.

• Laboratory confirmation: Identification of variola (smallpox) DNA with PCR or isolation of the virus from a clinical specimen

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy presents to you with complaints of fever and malaise. He also complains of an itchy rash which first appeared on the trunk as shown below. When is this disease the most contagious?
options: 2 days before and 5 days after the onset of rash
7 days before to 7 days after the onset of rash
4 days before to 4 days after the onset of rash
questions.answer: B. 2 days before and 5 days after the onset of rash
questions.explanation: The rash (different stages at one time) in the image and the clinical history are suggestive of chickenpox. The period of communicability for chickenpox is 2 days before and 5 days after the onset of rash.

questions.question: Which of the following is not characteristic of the rash of chicken pox?
questions.explanation:
The rash of chickenpox is superficial and the rash of smallpox is deep-seated.

Difference between the rash of chickenpox and smallpox:

Chickenpox
Smallpox

Spares palms and soles, rash mostly on flexor surfaces

Vesicles are unilocular and give dewdrop on rose petal appearance

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are true about chickenpox?

1. It is caused by HHV 3

2. The scab is infective

3. A killed vaccine is used for prophylaxis

4. The secondary attack rate is 85%

5. The virus stays latent in the sensory ganglion
questions.explanation:
Chickenpox is caused by the human herpes virus-3 (varicella-zoster virus). It remains latent in the sensory ganglion. Reactivation of the virus can cause shingles.

The secondary attack rate of chickenpox is very high, 85% (range 61%–100%).

The characteristic infective vesicle, surrounded by an erythematous halo, is described as a dewdrop on a rose petal. The scab of chickenpox is not infective.

The vaccine given for chickenpox prophylaxis is live attenuated vaccine.

questions.question: The varicella vaccine can be safely administered to which of the following individuals?
options: A HIV infected patient with CD4+ T cell levels > 15%
A patient on long term corticosteroid therapy
questions.answer: C. A HIV infected patient with CD4+ T cell levels > 15%
questions.explanation:
Varicella vaccine can be considered for clinically stable HIV infected children or adults with CD4+ T cell level ≥15%, including those receiving active antiretroviral therapy.

Varicella vaccine is contraindicated in:

• Pregnant women

• Immunocompromised patients

• Patients allergic to neomycin

Following vaccination, salicylates should be avoided for 6 weeks to prevent Reye's syndrome.

questions.question: A child with a fever and rash was brought to your OPD. Oral findings as shown in the image were observed. During which period can this disease spread to others?
options: 4 days before and 2 days after the appearance of rash
2 days before and 2 days after the appearance of rash
4 days before and 4 days after the appearance of rash
2 days before and 4 days after the appearance of rash
questions.answer: C. 4 days before and 4 days after the appearance of rash
questions.explanation: The given image shows koplik spots, which are a pathognomonic sign of measles. The period of communicability for measles is 4 days before and 4 days after the appearance of rash. The patient is isolated for 7 days from the onset of rash.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about measles?
options: Otitis media is a common complication
Large number of carriers are present
questions.answer: B. Otitis media is a common complication
questions.explanation:
The most common complication of measles is otitis media, occurring in about 10–15 % of patients.

Measles is caused by an RNA virus of the Paramyxovirus family. The incubation period of measles is 10 to 14 days. The only source of infection is a case of measles. Carriers are not known to occur.

The complications of measles include:

• Otitis media (most common)

• Measles-associated diarrhea

• Pneumonia

• Conjunctivitis

• Febrile seizures

• Subacute sclerosing pan encephalitis (rare but is fatal) - occurs several years after primary infection

questions.question: During a measles epidemic in the community, an eight-and-a-half-month-old child was vaccinated for measles. What is the correct immunisation schedule to be followed for her, regarding measles?
options: The child should be given a second dose after 4 weeks.
The child should be given a second dose as soon as she reaches 9 months of age.
The child should directly be given the second dose of measles at 16 months.
The child should be given the second dose of measles at 12 months of age.
questions.answer: A. The child should be given a second dose after 4 weeks.
questions.explanation:
In this child, the next dose of measles vaccine should be given after 4 weeks.

While the scheduled age of receiving a measles vaccine is 9 months, it can be lowered up to 6 months during a measles epidemic in the community.

For infants immunized between 6 to 9 months of age, a second dose should be administered as soon as the child reaches the age of 9 months. It is to ensure adequate immunity has developed, provided that 4 weeks have elapsed since the last dose.

In this child, the first dose was given at the age of 8 and a half months, and there must be a gap of 4 weeks between the two doses. If the child were to be vaccinated as soon as she turns 9 months old, only two weeks would have been elapsed.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct about the criteria for elimination of measles?
options: There should be an absence of transmission of epidemic measles
The duration of absence of transmission should be ≥ 6 months
A well-performing surveillance system should be present
Absence of transmission should be seen in multiple geographical areas
questions.answer: C. A well-performing surveillance system should be present
questions.explanation: Measles elimination is operationally defined as the absence of endemic measles transmission in a defined geographical area (region or country) for ≥12 months in the presence of a well-performing surveillance system.

questions.question: Which of the following is not true about the Measles-Rubella campaign?
options: It is a mass vaccination campaign organised to introduce MR vaccine
Follow-up campaign is organised every 3-5 years
It covers children from 9 months to 15 years of age
Mop-up strategy is a part of the campaign
questions.answer: D. Mop-up strategy is a part of the campaign
questions.explanation:
Mop-up strategy is not a part of the Measles-Rubella campaign.

Measles-Rubella vaccine introduction campaign:

• A mass vaccination campaign to introduce an MR vaccine

• Targets a wide age group of children: 9 months to < 15 years

• All children in the target age group receive an additional dose of the vaccine

• Regardless of previous vaccination status or history of illness.

Measles-Rubella follow-up campaign:

• A mass vaccination campaign as a periodic event every 3–5 years guided by country-specific surveillance data

• Target age group for immunization: all children aged > 9 months, who were born after the previous MR vaccination campaign

questions.question: According to the WHO, which of the following tests cannot be used to confirm a case of swine flu?
options: 4-fold rise in virus specific neutralizing antibodies
questions.explanation:
ELISA is not included in the criteria for confirming a case of H1N1.

The ELISA is an easy to perform, highly specific, and fairly sensitive diagnostic tool for the 2009 pandemic influenza A (H1N1) virus infections. However, it is not included in the WHO 's list of confirmation tests.

According to WHO, 2009 pandemic (H1N1) virus infection is confirmed by one or more of the following tests:

• Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

• Viral culture

• 4‐fold rise in H1N1 virus‐specific neutralizing antibodies

questions.question: What is the route of administration of avian influenza vaccine?
questions.explanation:
The avian influenza H5N1 vaccine is administered intramuscularly.

H5N1 avian influenza vaccine was approved in 2017 for the age group of 18 to 64 years of age who are at increased risk of exposure to the H5N1 influenza virus subtype contained in the vaccine.

It is administered intramuscularly in the upper arm and given in 2 doses, 28 days apart.

Note: The live attenuated H1N1 influenza vaccine is given intranasally.

questions.question: Vaccine that requires strain change due to evolving organism is?
questions.explanation:
Influenza vaccine requires periodic strain change due to antigenic change in the surface glycoprotein of the virus.

The change may be gradual (antigenic drift) or drastic (antigenic shift).

questions.question: Which of the following is the most important factor in reduction of diphtheria cases?
questions.explanation: Vaccination is the most important factor responsible for the reduction of diphtheria cases over the past decade.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about pertussis?
options: Most of the infections are subclinical
Secondary attack rate is 90 % in unimmunized individuals
Cerebellar ataxia is a common chronic complication
questions.answer: C. Secondary attack rate is 90 % in unimmunized individuals
questions.explanation:
The secondary attack rate in pertussis is about 90% in unimmunized individuals.

The source of infection in pertussis is a case of pertussis. There is no evidence of subclinical infections. The patients are most infectious during the catarrhal stage.

The chief complications of pertussis are:

• Bronchopneumonia

• Bronchitis

• Bronchiectasis

questions.question: According to IMNCI, which of the following is a key clinical sign for pneumonia classification?
questions.explanation:
According to the IMNCI, three key clinical signs are used to assess a sick child with suspected pneumonia:

• Respiratory rate (RR): distinguishes children who have pneumonia from those who do not. Children are classified under pneumonia if:

• > 50/min RR for infants 2 months to 12 months

• > 40/min RR for children 12 months to 5 years of age

• Lower chest wall indrawing indicates pneumonia

• Stridor indicates those with severe pneumonia requiring hospital admission.

The following image gives the IMNCI classification for cough/difficulty in breathing in children.

Signs of severe pneumonia are :

• Not able to drink

• Persistent vomiting

• Convulsions

• Lethargic or unconscious

• Stridor in a calm child

• Severe malnutrition

questions.question: Which of the following tests is used to determine the prevalence of TB infection?
questions.explanation:
Mantoux or tuberculin testing is used to detect the prevalence of TB infection.

Infection of tuberculosis does not always lead to disease. In latent infections, the Mantoux test can be positive without any clinical symptoms. Therefore, the prevalence of TB infection is detected by the Mantoux test.

However, the prevalence of TB disease is confirmed by a sputum smear.

questions.question: A 24-year-old patient has been given an intradermal injection of 0.1ml PPD (5 tuberculin units) over the forearm. After 72 hrs, the site is examined as shown in the image below. What is the interpretation of the result obtained?
options: Tuberculin test negative, suggesting immunity from TB
Tuberculin test positive, suggesting an active infection
Tuberculin test negative, suggesting a recent or past infection
Tuberculin test positive, suggesting a recent or past infection
questions.answer: D. Tuberculin test positive, suggesting a recent or past infection
questions.explanation:
The above image shows an induration of >10 mm after 72 hrs of intradermal PPD injection suggesting a positive tuberculin test(TST), indicating recent or past infection.

In TST, 0.1 ml of PPD (purified protein derivative) containing 5 TU (tuberculosis unit) is injected intradermally and induration is read after 48-72 hours. An induration of 10 mm or more is considered positive in patients from countries with a high prevalence of tuberculosis. Surrounding erythema is not considered.

A positive tuberculin test indicates hypersensitivity to tuberculoprotein, denoting either latent infection with tubercle bacilli, or BCG immunization, or recent or past infection with or without clinical disease.

False positives may be seen in infections with related mycobacteria and false negatives in miliary tuberculosis, severely immunosuppressed states, etc.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate method to assess the incidence of tuberculosis in the community?
options: Identify all positives to tuberculin test
Identify new converter to tuberculin test
Screen all under 5 years children with tuberculin test
questions.answer: C. Identify new converter to tuberculin test
questions.explanation:
Identification of new converters to the tuberculin test is a marker of the incidence of tuberculosis. Identification of all positives to the tuberculin test is a marker of the prevalence of tuberculosis.

Tuberculin conversion refers to the situation where an individual’s tuberculin skin test (TST) results in changes from negative (0–4 mm diameter induration) to positive (equal to or >10 mm diameter induration) within a 24-month period. TST conversion is considered presumptive evidence of acquired latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) and potential risk for progression to active tuberculosis disease.

questions.question: Tuberculin testing is done at which anatomical site?
questions.answer: C. Ventral aspect of left forearm
questions.explanation:
Mantoux/ Tuberculin testing is carried out by injecting 1 TU of PPD in 0.1 ml intradermally on the flexor (ventral) surface of the left forearm, midway between elbow and wrist.

The result of the test is usually read after 48-96 hours, but reading it after 72 hours is ideal.

The horizontal transverse diameter of induration is measured, based on which the following diagnosis can be inferred:

• < 6 mm – Negative

• 6–9 mm – Doubtful

• ≥ 10 mm – Positive

questions.question: The approach shown in the image is a part of which of the following?
questions.answer: B. National Strategic Plan for TB, 2017 -2025
questions.explanation:
Detect – Treat – Prevent – Build approach for eliminating TB in India is part of the National Strategic Plan for TB (2017-2025). The components of this approach are:

• Detect - Early identification of presumptive TB cases, at the first point of care, be it private or public sectors, and prompt diagnosis using high sensitivity diagnostic tests.

• Treat - Provide sustained, equitable access to high quality TB treatment, care and support services.

• Prevent - Prevent the emergence of TB in susceptible populations.

• Build - Undertake critical management reforms, restructuring of HR and financial norms, pathways for private sector participation, in order to improve efficiency, effectiveness.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most rapid diagnostic test for pulmonary TB?
questions.explanation:
The most rapid diagnosis of pulmonary TB can be done by sputum microscopy, with results in 30 minutes.

It has the least sensitivity and specificity. Smears are stained by Ziel Neelson acid-fast stain.

CBNAAT gives results within 90 minutes. Cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test is a Mycobacterium tuberculosis-specific automated, cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification assay, having fully integrated and automated amplification and detection using real-time PCR.

Quantiferon TB gold plus takes 24 hours to give the result. The radiometric BACTEC method takes approximately 2-3 weeks. Sputum culture takes approximately 2 to 8 weeks.

questions.question: What is the next step in management of a TB smear positive patient with no significant findings on a chest X ray?
questions.explanation:
The next best step in a smear-positive patient with no findings on chest-xray is to perform a CB-NAAT. This patient is a microscopically confirmed case of tuberculosis (TB).

According to the TB annual report, CBNAAT has been tried to be established in all centres. Ideally, drug sensitivity status via NAAT is to be done following a sputum smear before initiation of treatment. This helps in the early detection and treatment of drug-resistant TB. This has been integrated into the regular TB services to detect rifampicin resistance at the time of diagnosis. Depending on the sensitivity of the tubercle bacilli, appropriate ATT is started.

If NAAT is not done and sputum is positive, patient is considered as Microbiologically positive with sensitivity status unknown.

questions.question: You are posted in a TB clinic. You need to start an intensive phase (HRZE 75/150/400/275) regimen for a patient weighing 70 kgs. How many tablets of the FDCs are to be taken by him on a daily basis?
questions.explanation:
An adult weighing 65-75kg needs to take 5 tablets of FDC (fixed-dose combinations) containing HRZE 75/150/400/275 in the intensive phase.

Note: A TB patient kit contains the full course of treatment for a single patient and thus assures the TB patient that his or her medications will be available throughout treatment. The kit provides health workers with a container that has all the required drugs in the necessary strengths and quantities. This helps limit confusion and wastage and makes it easier to monitor the regularity of treatment; avoiding stock-outs also helps to maintain patient confidence in the health system.

questions.question: According to NTEP, how will you classify a TB patient who had taken antitubercular drugs for only 3 weeks in the past?
questions.explanation: Under NTEP, a new case is defined as a TB patient who had never taken ATT previously or taken ATT for <1 month.

questions.question: Which of the following drugs is not used in the management of a patient with MDR-TB under NTEP?
questions.explanation: PAS (para-aminosalicylic acid) is not included under the MDR-TB regimen.

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding the duration for treatment of XDR TB?
options: Intensive phase is for 6 to 9 months
A combination of oral and injection drugs are used
questions.answer: C. Total duration is for 20 months
questions.explanation:
All oral longer MDR-TB regimen is used for the treatment of XDR-TB patients for a duration of 20 months.

Regimen class
Drugs

All oral longer MDR TB regimen
Bdq(6 months) Lfx Lzd Cfz Cs for 18-20 months

questions.question: Which of the following is not a criteria for the bedaquiline conditional access programme under RNTCP?
options: Patient below 5 years can be included
Post menopausal females can be included
Patients with stable controlled arrhythmia can be included
questions.answer: A. Patient below 5 years can be included
questions.explanation:
Patients under 5 years are excluded from the bedaquiline conditional access programme.

The criteria to be met under the bedaquiline conditional access programme are as follows:

• Children aged 5 to <18 years of age and weighing at least 15 kg (in consultation with a paediatrician)

• Females on non-hormone-based contraceptive or post-menopausal females can be included.

• Patients with controlled stable cardiac arrhythmia can be considered after cardiac consultation.

• Pregnant women to be excluded

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding TB is false?
options: The Index TB guidelines are used for extra pulmonary TB.
X-pert MTB/RIF assay is an adjunct for diagnosis of lymph node TB.
Steroids may be used in patients with pleural TB without HIV for 4 weeks.
Duration of ATT for TB meningitis is 9 months.
questions.answer: C. Steroids may be used in patients with pleural TB without HIV for 4 weeks.
questions.explanation:
Steroids may be used in HIV-negative patients with TB meningitis and pericarditis for 4 weeks, but not for pleural TB.

The Index TB guidelines for extrapulmonary TB are as follows:

• Duration of ATT in TB meningitis is for 9 months and lymph node and abdominal TB is 6 months.

• X-pert MTB/RIF assay may be used as an adjunct in the diagnosis of lymph node TB and TB meningitis.

• Steroids may be used in HIV-negative patients with TB meningitis and pericarditis for 4 weeks.

questions.question: Where is the National Tuberculosis Institute located?
questions.explanation:
National Tuberculosis Institute is located in Bangalore.

Important national centers for tuberculosis in India:

• Tuberculosis Research Center: Chennai

• National Tuberculosis Institute: Bangalore

• National Institute of Tuberculosis and Respiratory Diseases: Delhi

• JALMA Institute for Leprosy and Other Mycobacterial Diseases: Agra.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of disability limitation for polio?
options: Polio immunization drives for infants to reduce the occurence.
Arranging for schooling for a child suffering from residual polio paralysis.
Resting the limbs affected by polio in neutral position.
Providing calipers for walking to patients affected by polio.
questions.answer: C. Resting the limbs affected by polio in neutral position.
questions.explanation:
Resting the limbs affected by polio in a neutral position is an example of disability limitation. It is an intervention done to either halt or prevent the transition of the disease process from impairment to handicap.

Rehabilitation has been defined as the use of medical, social, educational, and vocational measures for training the individual to the highest possible level of functional ability. Like providing calipers for walking to patients and arranging schooling after being affected by polio.

Immunization drives are examples of specific protection.

questions.question: A person is involved in unsafe sexual practices. Which of the following viruses is least likely to get transmitted via this route?
questions.explanation:
Hepatitis E has feco-oral or waterborne transmission. It does not transmit sexually. Transmission of Hepatitis A, C, and D can occur sexually.

Transmission of the hepatitis A virus can occur from any sexual activity with an infected person and is not limited to fecal-oral contact. People who are sexually active are considered at risk for hepatitis A if they are MSM, live with or are having sex with an infected person, or inject drugs.

questions.question: For how long is Hepatitis A excreted in the feces?
options: One week before the symptoms appear
Two weeks after the symptoms appear
Two weeks before the symptoms and two weeks thereafter
One week before the symptoms and one week thereafter
questions.answer: C. Two weeks before the symptoms and two weeks thereafter
questions.explanation:
HAV is excreted in the feces for about 2 weeks before the onset of jaundice and for up to 2 weeks thereafter.

The risk of transmitting is greatest at 2 weeks before to 1 week after the onset of jaundice.

questions.question: An intern sustains a needlestick injury while drawing blood from a Hepatitis B positive patient. Assuming he has been infected, which among the following will be the first to rise?
questions.explanation: HbsAg is the first serological marker to be detected in Hepatitis B infection.

questions.question: A 30-year-old pregnant woman is rushed to the hospital with labor pains at 34 weeks of gestation. She did not attend any prior antenatal visits. On further evaluation, she is found to be positive for HbsAg. Which of the following should be administered to the newborn after delivery?
options: Immunoglobulin, followed by vaccine 1 month later
questions.explanation:
The simultaneous administration of hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) and hepatitis B vaccine is more efficacious than HBIG alone for the prevention of the carrier state in newborn babies of HBV-positive mothers.

HBIG does not interfere with the antibody response to the hepatitis B vaccine. This combined procedure is ideal both for postexposure prophylaxis of persons accidentally exposed to blood known to contain hepatitis B virus and for the prevention of the carrier state in the newborn babies of carrier mothers.

HBIG (0.05–0.07 mL/kg) IM

• As early as possible, preferably within 24 hours of exposure

Hepatitis B vaccine (20 mcg/1.0 mL), IM

• 1st dose: within 7 days of exposure

• 2nd and 3rd dose: at one and six months, respectively

questions.question:
HCV screening is done for which of the following people?

1. A 19-year-old boy with a history of IV drug abuse.
2. A 30-year-old commercial sex worker who was diagnosed with HIV.
3. A 47-year-old man who received a blood transfusion 32 years ago.
4. A 62-year-old woman with CKD recently started on hemodialysis.
5. A 20-year-old hemophiliac man regularly receiving clotting factor concentrates.
questions.explanation:
Patients with a history of IV drug abuse, HIV, and a history of blood transfusion 32 years ago are screened for HCV.

Since the screening of blood for Hepatitis C was started after 1992, hence people who have received a blood transfusion before 1992 (in this MCQ, the year is 1992 in point 3) have to be screened.

HCV screening is done for people who may be at risk for infection. These include:

• People who received blood, blood products, or organs before screening for hepatitis C virus was implemented

• Current or former injecting drug users

• People on long-term hemodialysis

• Health-care workers

• People living with HIV

• People with abnormal liver tests or liver disease

• Infants born to infected mothers.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about Rotavirus?
options: Severe rotavirus infections are limited to children aged 5-7 years.
Rotavirus is shed in high concentrations for several days in the stools and vomit of infected children.
Rotavirus diarrhoea increases in frequency during drier, cooler months.
Clean water supplies and good hygiene are unlikely to have a substantial effect on viral transmission.
questions.answer: A. Severe rotavirus infections are limited to children aged 5-7 years.
questions.explanation:
Severe rotavirus gastroenteritis is largely limited to children aged 6-24 months, not 5-7 years.

Rotavirus is the leading cause of severe, dehydrating diarrhea in children aged <5 years globally. In developing countries, 75% of the children acquire their first rotavirus infection in the first 12 months.

The universal occurrence of rotavirus infections shows that clean water supply and good hygiene are unlikely to have a substantial effect on virus transmission. In tropical areas, rotavirus diarrhea occurs throughout the year, increasing in frequency in drier, cooler climates.

Transmission is through the feco-oral route, person-to-person contact, or indirectly through fomites. Infected individuals shed very high concentrations of the virus for many days in their stool and vomit.

questions.question: A mother brought a 2 month old child with complaints of diarrhea and vomiting. As a part of management, you advise her regarding vaccination for rotavirus. Which is the false statement regarding the same?
options: Rotarix is administered in 2 oral doses.
It cannot be given in an immunocompromised child.
The first dose of Rotarix is contraindicated for infants <12 weeks.
It is not a part of catchup vaccination programmes due to its risk of intussusception.
questions.answer: C. The first dose of Rotarix is contraindicated for infants <12 weeks.
questions.explanation:
The first dose of the Rotarix vaccine is contraindicated for infants > 12 weeks of age due to the potential risk of intussusception. Hence, it is not a part of catch-up immunization programs as the age is difficult to ascertain in such programs.

Rotavirus vaccines are live, attenuated, and are administered orally. So, it is not given to an immunocompromised child.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false for carriers of cholera?
options: A convalescent carrier may continue to excrete vibrios for 2-3 weeks.
The gall bladder is infected in chronic carriers.
The antibody titres of a contact carrier is normal while the stool culture is positive.
questions.answer: D. The antibody titres of a contact carrier is normal while the stool culture is positive.
questions.explanation:
The antibody titers of all carriers are risen and positive till the person harbors the organism.

A cholera carrier is defined as an apparently healthy person excreting V.cholerae O1 in stools. Selective media and enrichment is needed for their diagnosis. In cholera, 4 types of carriers are described.

1. Incubatory/Pre-Clinical carriers: The duration of carrier state is 1-5 days (incubation period). They present with symptoms later.

2. Convalescent carriers: Recovered from an attack of cholera, continues to excrete vibrios for 2-3 weeks, due to ineffective antibiotic treatment.

3. Contact/Health carrier: Due to subclinical infection contracted through a case or an infected environment, may excrete for 10 days.

4. Chronic carriers: Gallbladder is infected, duration may be as long as 10 years.

questions.question: A convalescent carrier of cholera will remain infectious for how many days after recovery?
questions.explanation:
A convalescent carrier of cholera will remain infectious for 14-21 days after recovery.

This type of carrier continues to excrete vibrios after being recovered from an attack of cholera. It is seen due to ineffective antibiotic treatment. These carriers can often become chronic or long-term carriers.

questions.question: A child is brought to the PHC with acute diarrhea. The doctor based on the history suspects that the child may be suffering from an infection due to shigella over cholera. Which of the following points on the history, apart from bloody stools, favors the doctor's suspicion?
questions.explanation:
Among the given options, the presence of fever favors the suspicion towards Shigella as the infectious agent.

The absence of rectal pain and the presence of vomiting favors cholera while abdominal cramps are present in both of these conditions.

Symptomatic differential diagnosis of shigella and cholera:

questions.question: Which of the following guidelines will you follow to treat a child diagnosed with cholera?
options: A cardiotonic should be added if shock persists even after treating with iv fluids.
If the diarrhoea persists after 48 hours of treatment, suspect resistance.
Antidiarrheals and antiemetics should be started.
questions.answer: C. If the diarrhoea persists after 48 hours of treatment, suspect resistance.
questions.explanation:
In patients with cholera, if diarrhea persists after 48 hours of antibiotic therapy, resistance to the antibiotic should be suspected.

Treatment for cholera:

• Rehydration therapy - is started immediately, either oral or intravenous.

• Antibiotic therapy - As soon as vomiting has stopped (usually after 3-4 hours of rehydration). Fluoroquinolones, tetracycline, azithromycin, ampicillin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are commonly used.

• Shock in diarrhea must be corrected by intravenous fluids only.

Antidiarrhoeals, cardiotonics, antiemetics, antispasmodics, and corticosteroids are not used.

questions.question: A 36-year-old man is diagnosed with cholera. Which of the following drug would you prescribe to his family members to prevent the spread of the disease?
questions.explanation:
Tetracycline is the drug of choice for chemoprophylaxis of cholera.

It should be given for:

• Adults - a 3-day period in a twice-daily dose of 500mg

• Children (4-13 years) - 125mg

• Children (0-3 years) - 50mg

Alternatively, the long-acting tetracycline (doxycycline) may be used for chemoprophylaxis, if the prevailing strains are not resistant. A single oral dose of doxycycline (300 mg for adults and 6 mg/kg for children under 15 years) has proved to be effective.

Chemoprophylaxis is advised only for household contacts or a closed community in which cholera has occurred.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most effective prophylactic measure against cholera?
questions.explanation:
The most important effective measure against cholera is health education.

The prophylactic measures against cholera include:

• Health education

• Food hygiene practices

• Hand washing practices after defecation

• Drinking safe water

• Knowledge about ORS

questions.question: You are a medical officer posted in a village 'X'. The village has been affected by the epidemic of cholera. What is the first step that should be taken to decrease the incidence of the disease?
options: Cholera vaccination to all uninfected individuals
Treat everyone in the village with tetracycline
questions.answer: A. Safe water supply and sanitation
questions.explanation:
Safe water supply and sanitation is the first step to be taken to decrease the incidence of cholera.

Steps taken to decrease the incidence of cholera include:

• Safe water supply

• Excreta disposal

• Food sanitation

• Disinfection

• Early case detection

Cholera Vaccines: available in oral forms

• Dukoral

• Sanchol and mORCVAX

• Euvichol

• Vaxchora

• CVD103-HgR - no longer produced

Sanchol and Euvichol are available for mass vaccination campaigns. The campaigns have been implemented in areas experiencing an outbreak, in areas at heightened vulnerability during humanitarian crises, and among populations living in highly endemic areas, known as hotspots.

Vaxchora is given for adults (18 – 64 years) who are traveling to an area of active cholera transmission, at least 10 days before the trip.

Mass chemoprophylaxis is not recommended for the control of cholera. This is because the drug's effect is only short-lived (a few days). Moreover, for preventing 1 case of cholera, around 10,000 individuals must be given the drug. Chemoprophylaxis is recommended for only household contacts of confirmed cases with tetracycline.

questions.question: In the ward, a patient with cholera soils the bed with stools. Which chemical should be used to disinfect the bed?
questions.explanation:
The most effective disinfectant for cholera stool is a coal tar disinfectant with Riedel-Walker (RW) coefficient of >10 such as cresol. Bleaching powder, if used, should be of good quality.

For disinfection, attention should be paid to the following: patient's stools and vomit; clothes and other contaminated personal items; the latrine, the patient's house, and neighborhood.

questions.question: Cholera is a notifiable disease locally and nationally. Which of the following statements is true regarding the international health regulations for the notification of Cholera?
options: Cholera is notifiable to the WHO by the National Government within 72 hours of its occurence.
The number of cases and deaths are to be reported daily and weekly till the area is declared free of cholera.
An area is declared free of cholera when 1 month has elapsed since the last case.
Mass chemoprophylaxis must be initiated immediately.
questions.answer: B. The number of cases and deaths are to be reported daily and weekly till the area is declared free of cholera.
questions.explanation:
The number of cases and deaths due to cholera are to be reported daily and weekly till the area is declared free of cholera.

International health regulations for the notification of Cholera:

• Cholera is notifiable to the WHO by the National Government within 24 hours of its occurrence.

• The number of cases and deaths due to cholera are to be reported daily and weekly till the area is declared free of cholera.

• When twice the incubation period (5 days) i.e. 10 days has elapsed since the death, recovery, or isolation of the last case, an area is declared free of cholera.

• Mass prophylaxis is not advised in cholera, as it fails to stop the spread of the disease. Chemoprophylaxis is only advised for household contacts or a closed community.

questions.question: A 5-year-old boy has had 15 episodes of loose stools in the last 24 hours and vomited twice in the last 4 hours. The child is restless and has sunken eyes. On examination, he is irritable but is drinking fluids. What is the optimal therapy for the child?
options: Intravenous fluid initially for 4 hours followed by oral fluids
questions.explanation:
Oral rehydration therapy is the optimal therapy to treat acute diarrheas in some dehydration patients.

Recommended formulation: Reduced osmolarity ORS solution, which has a reduced concentration of sodium (75 mmol/liter) and glucose (75 mmol/liter). It helps in reducing the adverse effect of hypertonicity on net fluid absorption.

According to IMNCI guidelines, irritable child who is able to drink fluids come under some dehydration category.

questions.question: A mother brings her child with complaints of acute diarrhea. After an initial assessment, you diagnose that the child has some dehydration. You counsel the mother to give ORS. After how many hours shall she be advised to discard the old solution and prepare a new one?
questions.explanation:
The freshly prepared ORS should not be used after 24 hours.

Guidelines for administering ORS:

• After each loose stool, give:

• Children <2 years of age - 50-100 ml (a quarter to half a large cup) of fluid

• Children 2 to 10 years - 100-200 ml (a half to one large cup)

• Older children and adults - as much fluid as they want

• For children <2 years, give a teaspoon every 1 to 2 minutes and offer frequent sips out of a cup for older children. Try to give the estimated required amount within a 4-hour period.

• If the child vomits, wait for 10 minutes, then give a spoonful every 2 to 3 minutes.

• If the child wants to drink more ORS solution than the estimated amount and does not vomit, there is no harm in feeding him/her more.

• If the child is breastfeeding, continue breastfeeding with ORS solution.

questions.question: A baby is brought with complaints of diarrhea and vomiting. The weight of the baby is 12 kgs. What is the estimated amount of fluid to be replaced in 4 hours?
questions.explanation:
According to the guidelines of ORS by WHO, a child with a weight of 11-15.9 kg has to be treated with 800-1200 ml of ORS solution within the first 4 hours.

questions.question: Which among the following home remedies are not advised for a child with diarrhea?
options: A mixture of 1 teaspoon of salt and 6 teaspoons of sugar in 1 L of drinking water
Unsalted water in which a cereal has been cooked
Soup with 3g/litre salt added to it
questions.answer: B. Unsalted water in which a cereal has been cooked
questions.explanation:
Salted water in which cereal has been cooked can be given to a child with diarrhoea.

If the WHO ORS mixture is not available, a simple mixture of 1 teaspoon of salt and 6 teaspoons of sugar must be dissolved in 1 L of drinking water and given to the child.

Fluids that do not contain salt in water, for eg: rice water, unsalted soup, yoghurt drinks, green coconut water, etc, must not be given. 3g/litre of salt must be added to such drinks before giving it to the child with diarrhoea.

The infant's usual diet of cereals, vegetables and other foods should be continued and never be diluted. The child should be given as much nutrient-rich food as acceptable.

Avoid the following:

• Sweetened drinks with sugar, like commercial fruit juices and sweetened tea, as they lead to osmotic diarrhoea and hypernatremia.

• Fluids with a stimulant and purgative effect like coffee and medicinal tea infusions.

questions.question: A child with severe dehydration is being treated with intravenous fluids for the past 2 hours. Which of the following will be used as an early indicator for adequate rehydration?
questions.explanation:
Skin elasticity and pulse strength are the most helpful indicators for adequate intravenous rehydration.

The urine output may be unchanged even after 3-4 hours of adequate rehydration. Hence, it cannot be a criterion for continuous examination.

The initial rehydration must be fast until an easily palpable pulse is present. Reassess the patient every 1-2 hours.

After 1-2 liters of fluid have been infused, the drip should be slowed down till the blood pressure and pulse return to normal. Rehydration must be continued otherwise till all signs of dehydration have disappeared. ORS should be given when the patient can drink oral fluids.

Puffy eyelids are a sign of excess rehydration and intravenous fluids must be stopped when it occurs.

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy is referred from a sub-center due to a feeble pulse and low BP. The patient has had diarrhea for 2 days. He has sunken eyes and is lethargic. On examination, BP is 90/60 mmHg. Which of the following fluids cannot be used for resuscitation in this patient?
questions.explanation:
This patient has severe dehydration which is treated by giving IV fluids. Plain glucose and dextrose solutions should not be used as they worsen the hyperosmolar state.

Intravenous rehydration: Used for initial rehydration for patients in shock or those who are unable to drink.

• Ringer's lactate solution/Hartmann's solution - Used for injection. Best commercially available solution.

• Diarrhea treatment solution- Recommended as an ideal polyelectrolyte solution for intravenous infusion.

• Normal saline- Used if nothing else is available. It is the poorest fluid, as it does not correct the acidosis and will not replace the potassium losses.

questions.question: What is the recommended dosage for zinc supplements in children with diarrhea?
options: 20 mg of zinc daily for infants < 12 months of age for 10-14 days
20 mg of zinc for children > 6 months of age for 7 days
10 mg of zinc for children > 12 months of age for 20 days
10 mg of zinc for children < 6 months of age for 10-14 days
questions.answer: D. 10 mg of zinc for children < 6 months of age for 10-14 days
questions.explanation:
According to WHO and UNICEF, 10 mg of zinc is given to infants < 6 months of age for 10-14 days.

20 mg of Zinc is given to infants > 6 months of age for 10-14 days during an episode of acute diarrhoea. This is done to reduce the duration and severity of the episode and prevent recurrence in the following months.

Intensified Diarrhea Control Fortnight : The goal is to attain zero child deaths due to childhood diarrhea. The overall objective of IDCF is to ensure high coverage of ORS and Zinc use rates in children with diarrhoea. It also complements awareness activities (including Swachh) for prevention and management of diarrhoea in under-five children.

questions.question: For a child with SAM, what should be the sodium content of his rehydration fluid?
questions.explanation:
The sodium content of the rehydration solution to treat SAM is 45mmol/L.

ReSoMal (rehydration solution for malnourished children) contains a lower amount of sodium (45mmol/L) and a higher amount of potassium (40 mmol/L) than the standard WHO-ORS.

ReSoMal is used in in-patient centers for the treatment of children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM). It is useful in correcting hypokalemia, and in lowering the risks of excess sodium and/or overhydration.
