questions.question: What is the average incubation period of typhoid fever?
questions.explanation:
The average incubation period of typhoid is 10-14 days.

However, it can vary from 3 days to 3 weeks depending on the dose of bacilli ingested.

questions.question: In a boys hostel, there has been an outbreak of typhoid. The hostel cook is identified as the carrier of the disease. Which is true among the following statements regarding her condition?
options: Gallbladder is usually not involved in carrier state
Chronic carriers are those who excrete the bacilli for more than a year
Tetracycline is the drug of choice for carriers
To treat the carrier state, treatment should be given for 4 weeks
questions.answer: B. Chronic carriers are those who excrete the bacilli for more than a year
questions.explanation:
Chronic carriers of typhoid are those who excrete the bacilli for more than a year.

Convalescent carriers excrete bacilli for 6-8 weeks and chronic carriers excrete for more than a year. The carrier rate in females is higher. Gallbladder and biliary tract are affected.

To treat the carrier state, an intensive course of ampicillin or amoxicillin (4-6 g a day) together with Probenecid (2 g/day) for 6 weeks is given. Cholecystectomy with concomitant ampicillin therapy is the most successful treatment for the carrier state.

questions.question: In which of the following patients can the Ty21a vaccine be administered?
options: A 50-year-old HIV patient who is asymptomatic with CD4+ count 240/mm3
A 42-year-old patient with fever and cough for 3 days
A 64-years-old alcoholic on colchicine therapy for acute gout
questions.answer: A. A 50-year-old HIV patient who is asymptomatic with CD4+ count 240/mm3
questions.explanation:
Ty21a vaccine can be administered in an HIV-positive asymptomatic patient as long as the CD4+ count is >200/ cubic mm.

Ty21a is an oral vaccine for individuals ≥5 years of age. It is given in 3 doses on the 1st, 3rd, and 5th day. Repeat every 3 years for endemic areas, and every year for traveling individuals.

It is not recommended in:

• Patients on antimitotic drugs and immunosuppressants

• Acute febrile illness

• Acute intestinal infestation

Proguanil and antibacterial drugs should be stopped from 3 days before to 3 days after the vaccine.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding dracunculiasis?
options: Niridazole prevents transmission of the disease.
The disease is limited to tropical and subtropical regions.
No animal reservoir has been proved.
questions.answer: B. Niridazole prevents transmission of the disease.
questions.explanation:
Niridazole does not prevent transmission of the disease.

Dracunculiasis is treated by removing the worm by sequentially rolling them out over a small stick. Wet compresses may relieve discomfort. Occlusive dressings limit shedding of infectious larvae.

Metronidazole and mebendazole are used to limit inflammation and facilitate worm removal.

Dracunculiasis or Guinea-worm disease is amenable to eradication. The eradication strategy comprises the following elements :

• Provision of safe drinking water.

• Control of cyclops.

• Health education regarding drinking boiled water.

• Surveillance: Active search for new cases.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about hookworms?
options: Blood loss due to Necator americanus infection is more compared to Ancylostoma infection.
Malnutrition is a predisposing factor for this chronic disabling disease.
Chandler’s index is used in epidemiological studies of hookworm.
Chronic blood loss in pregnant women may lead to abortions, stillbirth and low birth weight babies.
questions.answer: A. Blood loss due to Necator americanus infection is more compared to Ancylostoma infection.
questions.explanation:
The blood loss due to Ancylostoma (0.2 ml/day) is more compared to Necatur americanus (0.03ml/day)

Malnutrition is a predisposing factor. The chronic disabling disease does not occur in individuals who are well-nourished and whose iron intake is adequate.

Chandler's index is used to identify importance of hookworm infestation as a public health problem. It is calculated as average number of hookworm eggs/gram of stool.

• <200: no significance

• 200-250: the potential danger

• 250-300: minor public health problem

• >300: major public health problem

Hookworm inection causes chronic blood loss and depletion of body's iron stores leading to iron deficiency anemia. This in pregnant women can lead to abortions, stillbirth and low birth weight babies.

questions.question: Which malarial parasite has the shortest incubation period?
questions.explanation: Plasmodium falciparum has the shortest incubation period of 12 days.

questions.question: A patient from a hilly area was diagnosed with malaria. Which vector is most likely responsible for this?
questions.explanation:
Anopheles fluviatilis is the vector for transmitting malaria in hilly areas, forests and forest fringes.

Vector

Area

Anopheles stephensi

Urban

Anopheles culicifacies

Rural

Anopheles fluviatilis

Hilly areas and forests

questions.question: Individuals with Duffy negative RBCs are resistant to:
questions.explanation:
People with Duffy negative RBCs are resistant to P.vivax.

Resistance to P.falciparum is seen in:

• Individuals with sickle cell trait

• Neonates, as fetal hemoglobin suppresses the development of P. falciparum

questions.question: Which is the most sensitive index of recent transmission of malaria?
questions.explanation:
The infant parasite rate is regarded as the most sensitive index for recent transmission of malaria in a locality.

It is defined as the % of infants showing malarial parasites in their blood films. The transmission of malaria is considered absent if the infant parasite rate is zero for 3 consecutive years in a locality (even though the Anopheline vectors responsible for the previous transmission may remain).

questions.question: In a town with a population of 1,00,000, a total of 50,000 slides were examined for malaria. Among these, 100 cases of malaria were confirmed. What is the annual parasite incidence of this town?
questions.explanation:
The annual parasite incidence of this town (API) is 1.

API = Confirmed cases in a year

 ----------------------------------- x 1000

 Population under surveillance

In this scenario, API = 100 x 1000/100000 = 1

API is based on the number of slide-confirmed cases that are found through active and passive surveillance. It is a measure of malaria incidence in a community and helps in determining the burden of the disease. Areas with API ≥ 2 / 1000 population are classified as high-risk areas and are eligible for vector control.

Note: The number of slides examined is used to determine the annual blood examination rate (ABER).

questions.question: Which parameter is used to measure the operational efficiency of the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme?
questions.explanation: The annual blood examination rate (ABER) is used to measure the operational efficiency of the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP).

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman from Assam presented with fever and chills recurring every 48 hours. On examination, she was conscious, oriented, and febrile. CBC, LFT, and RFT were normal. Peripheral smear revealed the following. What is the drug of choice?
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario and peripheral smear showing crescent-shaped gametocytes are suggestive of uncomplicated falciparum malaria. As this woman is from a North-Eastern state, the drug regimen of choice is ACT-AL (artemisinin combination therapy):

• Artemether (20mg)

• Lumefantrine (120mg)

This regimen is followed in the North-Eastern states of India due to documented resistance to sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine in these areas. ACT-AL is contraindicated in:

• 1st trimester of pregnancy

• Children < 5 kg

questions.question: A 23-year-old pregnant woman at 11 weeks of gestation was diagnosed with falciparum malaria. What is the drug of choice?
questions.explanation:
Quinine is the drug of choice for falciparum malaria during 1st trimester of pregnancy.

The treatment of falciparum malaria during pregnancy is as follows:

• 1st trimester - quinine

• 2nd and 3rd trimester - ACT-AL in North-Eastern states and ACT-SP in other states

questions.question: Which of the following patients with malaria can be treated with primaquine?
options: A 24-year-old pregnant woman at 30 weeks of gestation
A 10-year-old boy diagnosed with G6PD deficiency
A 40-year-old woman recently treated for a flare-up of SLE
A 60-year-old man who had a myocardial infarction 4 months ago
questions.answer: D. A 60-year-old man who had a myocardial infarction 4 months ago
questions.explanation:
Cardiac disease is not a contraindication for the use of primaquine. It is contraindicated in:

• Infants

• Pregnant and lactating women

• Patients with G6PD deficiency

• Patients at risk of developing granulocytopenia:

• Systemic diseases including active RA and SLE

• Drugs that cause hemolysis or bone marrow depression

questions.question: What is the dose of mefloquine given for chemoprophylaxis of malaria?
questions.explanation:
Mefloquine 250 mg weekly is given for chemoprophylaxis against malaria in adults. It should be administered 2-3 weeks before travelling.

Chemoprophylaxis is recommended for travellers from non-endemic areas and as a short term measure for soldiers, police and labour forces serving in highly endemic areas. It should be complemented by personal protection and vector control.

 The following drugs are used for malaria chemoprophylaxis:

• Chloroquine - 300 mg/week

• Proguanil - 200mg/day

• Mefloquine - 250mg/week

• Doxycycline - 100mg/day

Mefloquine is contraindicated in cases with a history of convulsions, neuropsychiatric problems and cardiac conditions.

questions.question: What is the most important strategy for the control of malaria in endemic areas?
questions.explanation: Vector control is the most important strategy to control malaria in endemic areas. Proper measures should be taken to kill both adult mosquitoes and larvae.

questions.question: Which of the following was a component of the Roll back malaria programme?
options: Development of larvivorous fish for eradication of larvae
questions.explanation:
Ensuring proper and expanded use of insecticide-treated mosquito nets was a component of the Roll Back Malaria (RBM) programme.

The other components of the RBM initiative included:

• Strengthening the health system to ensure better delivery of health care

• Ensuring adequate access to basic health care and training of health workers

• Encouraging the development of more effective and new anti-malaria drugs

questions.question: Which sequence of infection poses the highest risk of dengue hemorrhagic fever?
questions.explanation:
The DENV-1 --> DENV-2 sequence of infection is associated with the highest risk of dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF).

Multiple infections with different serotypes of the dengue virus lead to severe forms of dengue such as DHF/DSS. The first infection probably sensitizes the patient, while the second infection with a different serotype appears to produce immunological catastrophe.

• DENV-1 --> DENV-2 - 500-fold risk (compared to primary infection alone)

• DENV-3 --> DENV-2 - 150-fold risk

• DENV-4 --> DENV-2 - 50-fold risk

questions.question: What is the extrinsic incubation period of the dengue virus?
questions.explanation:
The extrinsic incubation period of the dengue virus is 8-10 days. This refers to the period necessary for the development of the disease agent in the arthropod host.

Aedes mosquitoes become infective when they feed on infected patients from 1 day before onset of illness to the 5th day (viremia stage) of illness. After 8-10 days of extrinsic incubation of the virus in a mosquito, Aedes becomes infective and can transmit the infection. Higher temperature results in shortening of the extrinsic incubation period, allowing mosquitoes to remain infectious for a longer duration.

questions.question: In patients with dengue fever, platelets should be transfused if the platelet count falls below which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Prophylactic platelet transfusion in dengue is to be initiated when the platelet count is <10,000/cu.mm.

Indications for platelet transfusion in dengue are as follows:

• Platelet count <10,000/cu.mm

• Prolonged shock with coagulopathy

• Systemic massive bleeding

questions.question: Which of the following is a WHO-approved dengue vaccine for individuals seropositive for dengue virus?
questions.explanation:
Dengvaxia is a WHO-approved vaccine for individuals seropositive for dengue virus. It is currently licensed in 20 countries.

A pre-vaccination screening strategy must be adopted so that only dengue-seropositive individuals are vaccinated. It is indicated for individuals between 9 to 16 years. It is given in 3 doses, 6 months apart. Booster doses are not required.

However, it carries an increased risk of severe dengue in those who experience their first natural dengue infection after vaccination (seronegative individuals).

Note: TV003, a live, attenuated, tetravalent dengue vaccine is currently in Phase-3 trials. It has shown efficacy in promoting immunity in both seropositive and seronegative individuals between 2-59 years of age.

questions.question: The prepatent period in lymphatic filariasis is the time interval between:
options: Invasion of infective larvae and blockage of lymphatics
Inoculation of infective larvae and detection of microfilaria
Ingestion of microfilaria and development of third stage larva
Inoculation of infective larvae and maturation into adult worm
questions.answer: B. Inoculation of infective larvae and detection of microfilaria
questions.explanation:
The prepatent period in lymphatic filariasis is the time interval between inoculation of the infective larvae and the first appearance of detectable microfilaria.

The clinical incubation period is the time interval from the invasion of infective larvae and the development of clinical manifestations. It is usually 8-16 months.

questions.question: A 44-year-old man presented with high-grade fever, chills, and pain in his groin area. Examination revealed reddish streaks over his lower limbs and bilateral non-pitting edema to the level of the knee. Swelling and tenderness in his scrotum was also noted. To diagnose the condition, when will you draw blood from the patient?
questions.explanation: This patient has features of lymphangitis, lymphedema, and epididymo-orchitis, which are suggestive of acute filariasis. Blood must be drawn between 10 pm to 2 am. This is because the maximum density of microfilaria are present in the peripheral blood at this time.

questions.question: Which is the most sensitive method to detect low-density microfilaremia in blood?
questions.explanation:
The most sensitive method to detect low-density microfilaremia in the blood is by membrane filter concentration.

The thick film is the most commonly used method for epidemiological assessment. The DEC provocative test is used to induce microfilaria to appear in the blood in the daytime.

questions.question: What is the dose of diethylcarbamazine for the treatment of Bancroftian filariasis?
questions.explanation:
The dose of diethylcarbamazine (DEC) for treatment of Bancroftian filariasis is 6 mg/kg/day orally for 12 days.

Medicated common salt with 1-4g DEC/kg is a special form of mass treatment, particularly in endemic areas. By this method, very low doses of DEC are given over a long period of time.

questions.question: A man is referred for fever and agitation for the past 4 days. Examination reveals a disoriented man who is unable to swallow water due to involuntary inspiratory muscle spasms of the pharynx. He had been bitten by a dog 3 months ago but was not treated. What genus does the causative organism of this condition belong to?
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario with hydrophobia and a history of an untreated dog bite is highly suggestive of rabies. The causative virus belongs to the genus Lyssavirus.

Rabies virus is an RNA virus that belongs to the family Rhabdoviridae. This family has 3 genera:

• Lyssavirus

• Vesiculovirus

• Ephemerovirus

questions.question: Which of the following is false about the fixed virus of rabies?
options: Does not multiply in extra neural tissues
questions.answer: A. Has a long incubation period
questions.explanation:
The fixed virus has a short incubation period.

There are 2 types of rabies viruses:

Fixed virus
Street virus

Isolated after several intracerebral passages in rabbits

Isolated from naturally occurring cases of rabies

Short, fixed, and reproducible incubation period of 6 to 7 days

The incubation period is long and highly variable between 1 to 12 weeks

Does not form Negri bodies or multiply in extraneural tissues

Forms Negri bodies and multiplies in extraneural tissues

Used in the preparation of live-attenuated anti-rabies vaccine

It is the primary cause of rabies disease

questions.question: Which of the following does not lead to the transmission of rabies to humans?
options: Nibbling by an infected animal on abraded skin
Direct contact of infected saliva with the mucosa
Ingestion of raw meat of infected animal
questions.answer: D. Ingestion of raw meat of infected animal
questions.explanation:
Ingestion of the raw meat of the infected animal does not lead to the transmission of rabies.

Mammals like dogs and bats are important animal sources. The important modes of transmission of rabies are as follows:

• Scratches or deep bites

• Exposure of infected saliva to intact mucosa or fresh skin wounds

Human–to–human transmission through bites has never been confirmed.

questions.question: You have witnessed your neighbor being bitten by a rabid dog. You should advise him to wash the wound with soap and water for a minimum of:
questions.explanation:
Following dog bites, the bite wound should be washed with soap under running tap water for 15 minutes.

Local treatment of the bite wound is essential for the prevention of rabies and can reduce the infection rate by up to 80%. The following steps must be followed:

• Cleansing: Washing under running water with soap or irrigation with a catheter in case of deep wounds

• Chemical agent: Alcohol or tincture /0.01% aqueous solution of iodine or povidone-iodine is effective for inactivation of residual virus

• Suturing: Must be done only following 24-48 hours if necessary, under the cover of rabies immunoglobulin locally and minimal stitches

• Antibiotics and anti-tetanus measures when indicated

questions.question: A worker at a veterinary hospital has just received the 1st dose of rabies vaccine as a pre-exposure prophylactic measure. When should he return for the remaining doses?
questions.explanation:
Pre-exposure prophylaxis for rabies consists of 3 doses to be given on days 0, 7, and 21 or 28. They are given intramuscularly or intradermally in the deltoid area of the arm.

High-risk groups like laboratory staff, wildlife wardens, veterinarians, animal handlers, and travelers to endemic regions are candidates for pre-exposure prophylaxis.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy was bitten by a suspected rabid dog . On examination, there are minor scratches and abrasions without bleeding. Which of the following is true about the category and management of the wound?
options: Category II - Local treatment of wound with povidone and follow up
Category III - Local treatment of wound and give ARV and antibiotics
Category II - Local treatment of wound and give ARV
Category III - Give ARV and anti-rabies immunoglobulin
questions.answer: C. Category II - Local treatment of wound and give ARV
questions.explanation:
Minor scratches and abrasions without bleeding are classified under category II wounds. Category II wounds are managed by immediate local treatment of wound and vaccination (ARV).

Antibiotics are not required in case of minor scratches and abrasions.

questions.question: A public health worker was brought with multiple transdermal dog bites. He tells you that he had received pre-exposure prophylaxis 6 months ago. What is the next best step in management?
options: Wound washing and ARV with half dose of RIG
Wound treatment and ARV; RIG is not required
questions.answer: D. Wound treatment and ARV; RIG is not required
questions.explanation:
This given clinical scenario of a patient with multiple transdermal dog bites would be categorised under category III. As the patient received pre-exposure prophylaxis 6 months ago, his line of management includes the following:

1. Wound treatment with soap and running water for 15 minutes and application of antiseptic

2. Anti-rabies vaccine 2 doses on day 0 and day 3, with either intradermal vaccine(0.1ml, 1 site) or intramuscular vaccine(1 vial, 1site).

There is no requirement for Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG), if previous pre-exposure prophylaxis or post exposure prophylaxis documentation is available. If documentation of PEP or PrEP is unavailable, patient should be treated as fresh case and given full PEP.

questions.question: An 8-year-old child was brought with an unprovoked dog bite. Which of the following measures should be taken?
options: Withhold the vaccine and observe the dog for 10 days
Give half the dose of the vaccine
questions.answer: D. Give cell culture derived vaccine
questions.explanation: This child should be given immediate post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) by administering a cell culture-derived vaccine to reduce the chances of getting rabies.

questions.question: What is the incubation period of yellow fever?
questions.explanation: The incubation period of yellow fever is 3–6 days.

questions.question: According to the International Health Regulations, an Aedes aegypti index of which of the following must be maintained to achieve zero risk of spread of yellow fever?
questions.explanation:
The Aedes aegypti index should be < 1% in endemic areas to achieve zero risk of spread of yellow fever.

The Aedes aegypti index is a type of house index. It refers to the percentage of houses and premises in a limited well-defined area with actual breeding of Aedes aegypti larvae.

questions.question: A woman is planning a trip to Morocco, which is endemic for yellow fever. As per travel regulations, she receives the yellow fever vaccine. After how many days following vaccination is she eligible to travel?
questions.explanation:
This woman is eligible to travel to the endemic area 10 days after being vaccinated for yellow fever. This period is required for the majority of vaccine recipients to develop immunity.

The 17D vaccine for yellow fever is given subcutaneously. Unvaccinated people are required to remain quarantined for 6 days (maximum period of incubation).

questions.question: Which of the following is the yellow fever reference center in India?
questions.explanation:
The reference centers for yellow fever in India are as follows:

• Central Research Institute, Kasauli

• National Institute of Virology, Pune

questions.question: An outbreak of Kyasanur forest disease occurred among a group of forest officers in Karnataka. Which of the following vectors should be targeted to prevent the further spread of the disease?
questions.explanation:
Kyasanur forest disease (KFD) is transmitted by the bite of infective hard ticks of Haemaphysalis species. Hence, control of ticks must be done to prevent spread of the disease.

KFD is a hemorrhagic febrile disease caused by a flavivirus. Man is an incidental dead-end host in the life cycle of the vector (hard tick). Small mammals like rodents and squirrels are the reservoirs while monkeys serve as the amplifier hosts. KFD is endemic in 4 districts of Karnataka (Shimoga, North Kannada, South Kannada, Chikmagalur).

The incubation period is between 3 to 8 days. The disease presents with sudden onset of fever, headache, myalgia. In severe cases, gastrointestinal disturbances and hemorrhages from the nose, gums, stomach, and intestine may occur. The case fatality rate is 5 to 10%.

questions.question: Which of the following organisms follow a bird-arthropod-human transmission route?
questions.explanation:
Japanese encephalitis follows bird-arthropod-human transmission.

JE virus infects several extra-human hosts, e.g., pigs and birds (like pond herons). The basic cycles of transmission are:

 (a)Pig → Mosquito → Pig

(b) Bird → Mosquito → Bird

Humans are incidental "dead-end" hosts and are infected by the bite of infected Culex mosquitoes.

questions.question: Which following is false about Japanese encephalitis?
options: Man is the incidental dead-end host
Culicines act as vectors for this condition
It is caused by a group B arbovirus
questions.answer: C. The incubation period is 1-2 days
questions.explanation:
The incubation period of Japanese encephalitis (JE) in man following a mosquito bite is 5-15 days.

JE is mosquito-borne encephalitis caused by a group B arbovirus (Flavivirus). It is transmitted by Culex (culicine) mosquitoes mainly C.tritaeniorhynchus and C.vishnui. Ardeid birds (herons) are the reservoirs while pigs are the amplifier hosts. Man is an incidental dead-end host. Man-to-man transmission has not been recorded.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about Japanese encephalitis?
options: SA-14-14-2 strain vaccine is commonly used
Diagnosis is confirmed by CSF culture
Patients usually recover without any sequelae
questions.answer: A. SA-14-14-2 strain vaccine is commonly used
questions.explanation:
SA-14-14-2 strain vaccine is used for the prevention of Japanese encephalitis (JE).

Japanese encephalitis (JE) is mosquito-borne encephalitis caused by a group B arbovirus (Flavivirus) and transmitted by Culex mosquitoes. Most individuals develop subclinical infection.

The course of disease in man divided into 3 stages:

• Prodromal stage - fever, headache, gastrointestinal disturbances, lethargy, and malaise

• Acute encephalitic stage - high-grade fever, nuchal rigidity, convulsions, signs of raised intracranial pressure, paralysis, altered sensorium

• Late-stage and sequelae - neurological or psychiatric sequelae seen in up to 50% of survivors

Diagnosis is serological, using blood or CSF samples. The virus rarely grows in culture. The case fatality rate varies between 20-40%. There are 3 types of JE vaccines available:

• Nakayama or Beijing strain - purified inactivated vaccine

• Beijing P-3 strain - inactivated vaccine

• SA-14-14-2 - live attenuated vaccine

Note: Killed JE vaccines (Inactivated SA 14-14-2 cell culture-derived and inactivated Vero cell culture-derived) are gradually replacing live attenuated vaccines. According to the national immunisation schedule, both live attenuated, killed-inactivated vaccines are now used for vaccination against the JE virus.

questions.question: Which of the following are transmitted biologically by invertebrate vectors?
questions.explanation:
Metazoonoses are a type of zoonoses where the infective agents are transmitted by invertebrate vectors. They multiply and develop within the invertebrates (extrinsic incubation period) before transmission to a vertebrate host.

A zoonosis is any disease or infection that is naturally transmissible from vertebrate animals to humans. They can be classified based on their reservoir hosts into:

• Anthropozoonoses - transmitted from lower vertebrates to man

• Zooanthroponoses - transmitted from man to lower vertebrates

• Amphixenoses - may be transmitted in either direction

They can also be classified based on the life cycle of the infecting agent:

Category

Mode

Example

Direct zoonoses

Direct contact, fomites, mechanical vector

No developmental or propagative changes during transmission

Rabies, brucellosis, trichinosis

Cyclo-zoonoses

Require > 1 vertebrate host to complete the developmental cycle

Human taeniasis, Echinococcosis, Pentastomid infections

Meta-zoonoses

Transmitted by invertebrate vectors

Infective agent develops and multiplies within the invertebrate (extrinsic incubation period) after which it is transmitted to another vertebrate host

Arboviral infections, plague and schistosomiasis

Sapro-zoonoses

Has both a vertebrate host and a non-animal (food, soil, plants) developmental site or reservoir

Various forms of larva migrans and mycoses

questions.question: Multiple members of the same community presented with sudden-onset fever, chills, and painful inguinal swellings as shown below. Further questioning leads to the identification of a rat infestation in the locality. Which of the following is the likely source of transmission of this disease?
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario and image showing buboes are suggestive of bubonic plague. It is transmitted by the bite of the infected rat flea, Xenopsylla cheopis. Rodents, including rats, are the reservoirs of infection.

On the other hand, the pneumonic plague spreads from man to man by droplet infection.

questions.question: Which of the following indices is the best determinant of a potential plague outbreak?
questions.explanation: Cheopis index is the best determinant of potential plague outbreaks. If this index is > 1, it indicates there is a high likelihood of an outbreak.

questions.question: All of the following are causes of different types of typhus except:
questions.explanation:
R.rickettsii causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever. It is a type of spotted fever, not typhus.

*Note:- Orientia tsutsugamushi was previously known as Rickettsia tsutsugamushi.

questions.question: Which of the following rickettsial diseases is correctly matched with their respective vectors?
questions.explanation:
Endemic typhus is caused by the bite of an infective flea.

This condition, also called murine typhus or flea-borne typhus, is caused by Rickettsia typhi. Rats serve as reservoirs. The incubation period is 1–2 weeks. The Weil Felix reaction is positive in 2nd week.

The drug of choice is tetracycline. Rodent control is most important and is best done by BHC and malathion.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman is being evaluated for fever and rash. All of the following can be included in the differential except:
questions.explanation:
Rashes and local lesions are not a feature of Q-fever.

It is caused by Coxiella burnetii. The mode of transmission is the inhalation of infected dust, entry through abrasions, or ingestion of contaminated milk. Rarely, ticks can be involved in transmission. The incubation period is 2 to 3 weeks.

The drug of choice is prolonged treatment with doxycycline. Pasteurization is advised to inactivate the causative agent.

questions.question: Which of the following is false about scrub typhus?
options: Adult mite feeds on vertebral host
questions.answer: B. Adult mite feeds on vertebral host
questions.explanation:
Both adult and nymphal stages of the mite are free-living in nature. They do not feed on the vertebral host.

Scrub typhus is the most widespread rickettsial disease. It is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi (previously known as Rickettsia tsutsugamushi) and transmitted by the bite of trombiculid mite. The incubation period is 10-12 days.

It presents with a typical eschar at the bite site. It is diagnosed by the Weil Felix reaction, which is strongly positive with proteus strain OXK. It is treated by tetracyclines.

questions.question: Which of the following are the causative agent and vector of epidemic typhus respectively?
questions.explanation:
The causative agent of epidemic typhus is Rickettsia prowazekii and the vector is a louse.

The incubation period is 10 to 14 days. Brill-Zinsser disease refers to the recurrent form of epidemic typhus.

questions.question: Which of the following is not true about Leishmania?
options: Extrinsic incubation period of kala-azar is 4 to 25 days
Post kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis is caused by L. donovani
questions.answer: A. Leishmania is an extracellular parasite
questions.explanation:
Leishmania is an intracellular parasite in the macrophages.

The vector is Phlebotomus (sandfly). Man is the reservoir in the Indian kala-azar. The incubation period is 10 days to 2 years, whereas the extrinsic incubation period is 4 to 25 days. The following conditions are caused by Leishmania:

• Visceral leishmaniasis or kala-azar – L. donovani

• Cutaneous leishmaniasis or oriental sore – L. tropica

• Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis - L. braziliensis

• Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis - L. donovani

The image below is a microscopic image of the LD body.

According to the NVBDCP, the management is as follows:

• First-line - single-dose liposomal amphotericin B (10 mg/kg IV infusion)

• Alternate - paromomycin + miltefosine for 10 days

Monotherapy with antimonials (sodium stibogluconate) is no longer recommended due to resistance and toxicity. Synthetic pyrethroid is used for indoor residual spraying in all the endemic areas.

questions.question: In patients with vagabond disease, which of the following is implicated?
questions.explanation:
Vagabond’s disease or pediculosis corporis is caused by the body louse.

The following image shows the body louse.

questions.question: When is World AIDS day observed?
questions.explanation:
The World AIDS Day is observed on December 1st. The theme for 2021 is 'Ending the HIV epidemic: Equitable Access, Everyone’s Voice'.

Option A: The World Tuberculosis Day is on March 24.

Option B: The World Cancer Day is on February 4.

Option D: The World Malaria Day is on April 25.

questions.question: What are the most common modes of transmission of HIV in India in descending order?
questions.explanation:
The most common mode of transmission of HIV in India is heterosexual transmission, followed by transplacental and homosexual contact, respectively.

The common modes of transmission of HIV are:

• Heterosexual (83.7%)

• Injecting drug users (5.6%)

• Transplacental transmission (3.8 %)

• Homosexual (2.5%)

• Blood and blood products (0.8%)

• Unknown (3.6%)

The highest risk of transmission is seen in homosexuals due to the increased risk of abrasions during anal sex.

questions.question: Health care workers will require post-exposure prophylaxis after exposure to which of the following body fluids of an HIV patient?
questions.explanation:
Health care workers exposed to the menstrual blood of an HIV-positive patient will require post-exposure prophylaxis. The risk of transmission of HIV during vaginal intercourse is higher when the woman is menstruating.

Tears, non-blood-stained saliva, urine, and sweat do not pose a significant risk. Exposure to these fluids does not require post-exposure prophylaxis.

questions.question: As per WHO staging of HIV, which of the following HIV-positive patients cannot be classified as stage IV?
options: A 29-year-old man diagnosed with cerebral toxoplasmosis
A 56-year-old woman with significant weight loss and muscle wasting
A 43-year-old lady being treated for Pneumocystis pneumonia
questions.answer: D. A 32-year-old man with oral candidiasis
questions.explanation:
Oral candidiasis is seen in stage 3, not stage 4 of HIV.

The following conditions are included in the WHO stage IV of HIV:

• HIV wasting syndrome (Slim disease)

• HIV encephalopathy

• HIV-associated nephropathy or cardiomyopathy

• Infections:

• Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia (previously known as Pneumocystis carinii)

• Chronic herpes simplex infection, cytomegalovirus disease

• Oesophageal/ tracheal candidiasis

• Extrapulmonary TB or disseminated M. avium infection

• CNS toxoplasmosis

• Extrapulmonary cryptococcosis

• Chronic cryptosporidiosis or isosporiasis

• Disseminated fungal infections (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis)

• Recurrent severe bacterial pneumonia or septicemia

• Atypical disseminated leishmaniasis

• Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy

• Neoplasms:

• Kaposi sarcoma

• Lymphoma (cerebral or B cell non-Hodgkin)

• Invasive cervical carcinoma

questions.question: A 45-year man with a high-risk sexual history now presents with prolonged fever for the past 1.5 months. On examination, the following finding is noted. Which one of the following additional features is required to diagnose this patient with AIDS?
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario is suspicious for HIV infection. As per the WHO definition, the presence of chronic diarrhea > 1 month is needed to diagnose this patient with AIDS.

The WHO clinical definition is used for AIDS surveillance in the clinical setting. Patients > 12 years of age are said to have AIDS if they have at least 2 major and 1 minor signs, provided other clinically similar conditions are be ruled out.

Major signs:

• Weight loss ≥ 10% of body weight

• Chronic diarrhea > 1 month

• Prolonged fever for > 1 month (intermittent or constant)

Minor signs:

• A persistent cough > 1 month

• Generalized pruritic dermatitis

• History of herpes zoster

• Oropharyngeal candidiasis

• Chronic progressive or disseminated herpes simplex infection

• Generalized lymphadenopathy

For surveillance purposes, the presence of either of the following is also considered sufficient to diagnose AIDS:

• Generalized Kaposi's sarcoma

• Cryptococcal meningitis

questions.question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding the epidemiology of HIV?
options: HIV infected infants and children do not progress rapidly to AIDS
Seminal secretions are more infectious than vaginal secretion
People are infectious during the window period
HIV prevalence has not exceeded 5% in any subpopulation
questions.answer: A. HIV infected infants and children do not progress rapidly to AIDS
questions.explanation:
Infants and children infected with HIV progress rapidly to AIDS.

Semen is more infectious than vaginal or cervical fluids as it has a higher concentration of HIV.

HIV-infected patients are highly infectious during:

• Window period (very early stages before antibody production)

• Advanced stages of infection (due to higher levels of viremia)

 HIV prevalence has consistently remained < 5% in all defined subpopulations.

questions.question: In individuals exposed to HIV, within how many hours should prophylaxis be initiated?
questions.explanation: Post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV should ideally be initiated within 72 hours. It is recommended that it be started as even as early as < 2 hours.

questions.question: Which of the following HIV-infected patients would you start on cotrimoxazole prophylaxis?
options: A 24-year-old pregnant woman with WHO stage 2 disease.
A 47-year-old man in a malaria-endemic area with WHO stage 1 disease
A 2-week-old HIV-exposed infant who is being exclusively breastfed
A 7-year-old girl with a CD4 count of 400 cells/cubic mm
questions.answer: B. A 47-year-old man in a malaria-endemic area with WHO stage 1 disease
questions.explanation:
All HIV infected adults and children in malaria-endemic areas should be given cotrimoxazole prophylaxis regardless of CD4 count or WHO clinical stage.

Cotrimoxazole is also indicated in areas with a low prevalence of malaria as shown below:

Age group
Indication
When to discontinue

HIV-exposed infants > 4-6 weeks of age
All infants
After HIV infection has been ruled out

Children < 5 years
All children

At 5 years in areas with low prevalence of malaria

(In high prevalence areas, continue till adulthood)

Children > 5 years
CD4 count <350 and/or WHO stage 3/4
When CD4 > 350 and they have been on ART > 6 months

Adults and pregnant women
CD4 count <350 and/or WHO stage 3/4
When CD4 count is rising and viral load is decreasing

HIV and TB coinfection
All patients
—

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with HIV is being screened for symptoms of TB. He reports no cough, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. What is the next step in management?
options: Start 5 mg/kg/day Isoniazid daily for 9 months
Prophylaxis does not need to be started
Start weekly dose of rifapentine + isoniazid for 3 months
questions.answer: D. Start weekly dose of rifapentine + isoniazid for 3 months
questions.explanation:
The next step in management in this patient is to provide tuberculosis preventive therapy (TPT) with rifapentine+ isoniazid weekly for 3 months.

According to the NTEP guidelines, TPT is indicated for the following groups:

 Risk group
 Criteria

• People living with HIV

• Negative 4 symptom test - start TPT after ruling out TB

• Patients with active TB - start TPT after completion of the ATT regimen

• Household contacts (HHC) of pulmonary TB patients < 5 years

• Start TPT after ruling out active TB

• Household contacts of pulmonary TB patients ≥ 5 years

• Other risk groups:

• Children/adults on immunosuppressive therapy

• Patients on anti-TNF treatment

• Patients on dialysis or post-transplantation

• Patients with silicosis

• First rule out active TB

• Start TPT if IGRA or TST is positive with a normal chest x-ray

IGRA - interferon-gamma release assay; TST - tuberculin skin test; ATT - antituberculous therapy

Target Population
Treatment option

• People living with HIV (adults and children > 2 years)

• HHC of pulmonary TB patients

• 3-month weekly Isoniazid (300 mg) and Rifapentine (300 mg) in persons older than 2 years

• Infants <12 months of age and Children < 2years of age with HIV

• 6-months daily isoniazid (6H): 10 mg/kg/day

TPT is contraindicated under the following conditions:

• Active TB

• Active hepatitis

• Peripheral neuropathy

• Regular and heavy alcohol consumption

questions.question:
Which of the following is true about the 2025 targets of the Global AIDS Strategy for 2021 to 2026?

A. 95% of women of reproductive age must have their HIV and reproductive health needs met
B. 95% of pregnant/ breastfeeding women with HIV must have suppressed viral loads
C. 75% of HIV-exposed children must be tested at 2 months of age and after stopping breastfeeding
D. 90% of people living with HIV must receive preventive treatment for TB
E. 75% of children living with HIV must have suppressed viral loads by 2023
questions.explanation:
95%, not 75% of HIV-exposed children are tested by 2 months of age and after stopping breastfeeding according to the 2025 targets.

Global AIDS Strategy 2021-2026 has the following targets for the year 2025:

Target %
Target population
Target intervention

95% of
People at risk of HIV infection
Access to effective prevention options

Women of reproductive age
Have their HIV, sexual, reproductive health service needs met

Pregnant and breastfeeding women with HIV
Suppressed viral loads

HIV-exposed children
Tested by 2 months of age and again after stopping breastfeeding

90% of
People living with HIV
Preventive treatment for TB

People living with HIV and people at risk

Linked to services for overall health and wellbeing including:

• Communicable and non-communicable diseases

• Sexual health

• Gender-based violence

• Mental health and substance abuse

75% of
All children living with HIV
Suppressed viral loads by 2023 (interim target)

95–95–95 testing and treatment targets to be achieved within all subpopulations, age groups, and geographic settings, including children living with HIV.

questions.question: A 29-year-old man comes to you with complaints of painful swelling in his right groin, as shown below. He gives a history of 3-4 painless ulcers over his penis 4 weeks ago that had resolved on its own. What is the likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario and image showing the groove sign of Greenblatt are suggestive of lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV). The causative organism is Chlamydia trachomatis.

LGV commonly presents with multiple small, painless ulcers on the genitalia that are often unrecognized and resolve spontaneously. This is followed by painful lymphadenopathy and bubo formation after 4-6 weeks. If left untreated, it can lead to extensive lymphatic damage, elephantiasis, and deformity of the genitalia.

The treatment of choice is doxycycline.

questions.question:
Match the following conditions with their causative agents:

 I. Pinta

 A. Treponema pertenue

 II. Lymphogranuloma venereum

 B. Klebsiella granulomatis

 III. Yaws

 C. Chlamydia trachomatis

 IV. Granuloma inguinale

 D. Treponema carateum
questions.explanation:
The causative organisms of the given conditions are as follows:

Condition
Organism

Pinta
Treponema carateum

Lymphogranuloma venereum
Chlamydia trachomatis

Yaws
Treponema pertenue

Granuloma inguinale
Klebsiella granulomatis

India is the first country in the world to be officially acknowledged as being yaws-free. The WHO declared India free of yaws on 5th May 2016.

questions.question:

questions.question: Which of the following is not a part of case detection in STDs?
questions.explanation:
Notification is not part of the case detection strategy for STDs. Case detection in STDs includes the following:

• Screening

• Contact tracing

• Cluster testing

questions.question: A 32-year-old man is diagnosed with syphilis. On probing, he gives you the information of other people in the same sociosexual environment as him. You then refer all these people for testing. What is this method of case detection?
questions.explanation:
This method of case detection is known as cluster testing.

The methods employed in case detection of STDs are:

• Screening - testing of apparently healthy volunteers from the general population for early detection of disease

• Contact tracing - technique by which the sexual partners of diagnosed patients are identified, located, investigated, and treated

• Cluster testing - patients are asked to name other persons who move in the same socio-sexual environment, who are then tested

questions.question: A 29-year-old man with urethral discharge is treated with the grey kit. This treatment is effective for the control of which of the following organisms?
questions.answer: C. Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis
questions.explanation: The grey kit is effective for the treatment of infections caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis.

questions.question: Which of the following is false about the epidemiology of leprosy?
options: Increased prevalence in childhood indicates that the disease is active and spreading.
Multibacillary cases are the most infectious in the community
Bacterial load is highest in patients with tuberculoid leprosy
Seldom may be transmitted by insect vectors
questions.answer: C. Bacterial load is highest in patients with tuberculoid leprosy
questions.explanation:
The bacterial load is highest in patients with lepromatous leprosy. 1 gram of leproma contains as many as 2-7 billion bacilli.

Multibacillary cases (lepromatous and borderline lepromatous) are the most important source of infection in the community. Infection can occur at any age. In general, cases rise to a peak between 10-20 years of age and then fall. In endemic areas, the disease is acquired commonly during childhood. A high prevalence in this age group indicates that the disease is active and spreading.

The organism may also be transmitted by insect vectors or by tattooing needles. However, this is not clinically significant.

questions.question: Elimination of leprosy in India is defined as the prevalence of :
questions.explanation: Elimination of leprosy in India is defined as a prevalence of < 1 per 10,000.

questions.question: What is the prevalence of leprosy in India per 10,000?
questions.explanation: The prevalence of leprosy in India is 0.41 per 10,000 as of March 2021.

questions.question: The Ridley Jopling classification for leprosy uses which of the following parameters?
questions.explanation: The Ridley Jopling classification uses clinical, bacteriological, immunological, and histological parameters.

questions.question:
A pathologist is studying the split skin smears taken from 4 sites of a leprosy patient. The following findings are noted in the samples. What is the bacteriological index?

Sample 1 - 10 bacilli in 100 oil immersion fields

Sample 2 - > 1000 bacilli in each oil immersion field

Sample 3 - 10 bacilli in 100 oil immersion fields

Sample 4 - > 1000 bacilli in each oil immersion field
questions.explanation:
The bacteriological index (BI) of the given samples is 3.5

According to Ridley’s logarithmic scale,

• 10 bacilli out of 100 oil immersion fields indicate an index of 1+

• > 1000 bacilli out of average fields imply an index of 6+

The bacteriological index is calculated by adding the index from each site examined and dividing the total by the number of sites examined.

Hence, BI = (1+1+6+6) / 4

BI = 14/4

BI = 3.5

questions.question: The lepromin test was performed on a patient with suspected leprosy. When will you ask him to come back for interpretation of the test results?
questions.answer: C. After 48 hrs and on 21st day
questions.explanation:
The patient should be asked to come back after 48 hours and on the 21st day for interpretation of the test results.

The lepromin test is a skin test for delayed hypersensitivity and is the only method to study immunity in leprosy patients. It is performed by injecting 0.1ml of lepromin reagent intradermally into the inner aspect of the forearm. The following 2 reactions are observed:

Early reaction of Fernandez
Late reaction of Mitsuda

Develops in 24-48 hours
Starts at 7-10 days, peaks at 3-4 weeks (read on day 21)

Remains for 3-5 days
Gradually subsides over the next few weeks

Poorly defined erythema and induration. Carries less significance
Considered positive if there is a nodule > 5 mm in diameter

questions.question: Which of the following is false about the lepromin test?
options: It is negative in most children in the first 4 months of life
It can be used as a diagnostic test
It is used to classify leprosy cases
False positive may be seen in those who underwent BCG vacination
questions.answer: B. It can be used as a diagnostic test
questions.explanation:
The lepromin test is not a diagnostic test. It is only used to assess the immune status, classify the cases, and estimate the prognosis.

The two main drawbacks of this test are:

1. False-positive results in those who received BCG vaccination

2. False-negative results in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous cases

questions.question: A group of public health workers is trying to identify trachoma cases at an ophthalmology camp. Which of the following is the best index to assess for trachoma inflammation?
options: Follicles on the upper tarsal conjuctiva
Vascular pannus at the superior limbus
questions.answer: A. Follicles on the upper tarsal conjuctiva
questions.explanation:
In epidemiological studies, the upper tarsal conjunctiva is the best index of trachomatous inflammation in the eye.

For the purpose of diagnosis, any 2 of the following diagnostic criteria must be present:

• Follicles on the upper tarsal conjunctiva

• Limbal follicles and Herbert's pits

• Typical conjunctival scarring (trichiasis and entropion)

• Vascular pannus, most marked at the superior limbus

 The following image shows follicles on the upper tarsal conjunctiva seen in trachomatous inflammation.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the organisms causing trachoma?
options: Morax- Axenfeld bacillus is the most widespread
Gonococcus is the most dangerous organism contributing to the disease process
Koch-Weeks bacillus is the most innocuous
C. trachomatis type D commonly causes permanent visual damage
questions.answer: B. Gonococcus is the most dangerous organism contributing to the disease process
questions.explanation:
Gonococcus is the most dangerous organism contributing to the disease process in trachoma.

Classic endemic trachoma is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis types A, B, C. Other pathogenic organisms that contribute to the disease process are:

• Morax-Axenfeld diplobacillus - most innocuous

• Kochs-Weeks bacillus - most widespread

• Gonococcus - most dangerous

The types D-K of C. trachomatis are sexually transmitted and cause inclusion conjunctivitis. It rarely causes permanent vision loss.

questions.question: The elimination of neonatal tetanus is defined as:
questions.explanation:
The elimination of neonatal tetanus is defined as <1 case per 1000 live births in every district. Maternal and neonatal tetanus (MNT) was eliminated in India in 2015.

Since July 2018, TT vaccines have been replaced by the Td vaccine for dual protection.

questions.question: Which of the following diseases is called the 8th day disease?
questions.explanation:
Neonatal tetanus is known as the 8th-day disease. This is because the clinical features are often seen after the 7th day after birth due to infection of the umbilical cord.

Option A: Trench fever is also called the 5-day fever.

Option B: Pertussis is called the 100-day cough.

Option D: Scarlet fever is also known as the 2nd disease.

questions.question: A 13-year-old girl is brought to the casualty a few hours after being injured by a rusty knife. According to her parents, her course of tetanus vaccination was completed 7 years ago. What is the next best step in management?
options: Human tetanus immunoglobulin and single dose of toxoid
questions.answer: B. Single dose of tetanus toxoid
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of a contaminated wound in a patient who received complete immunization against tetanus 7 years ago. She comes under category B of tetanus immunization and must be given a single dose of tetanus toxoid alone.

The WHO recommends a 3-dose primary vaccination series with tetanus-diphtheria-containing vaccine followed by 3 booster doses. Ideally, there should be at least 4 years between booster doses.

questions.question: The WHO has formulated a Global Action Plan for the prevention and control of non-communicable diseases. Which of the following is not a voluntary global target under this initiative?
options: 10% relative reduction in harmful use of alcohol
30% relative reduction in mean population intake of sodium
10% relative reduction in prevalence of insufficient physical activity
10% relative reduction in use of trans-fat for cooking
questions.answer: D. 10% relative reduction in use of trans-fat for cooking
questions.explanation:
A 10 percent relative reduction in the use of trans-fat for cooking is not a voluntary global target under the WHO Global Action Plan for prevention and control of non-communicable diseases.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the relationship between smoking and coronary heart disease (CHD)?
options: Smoking can cause sudden death from CHD.
Filters in cigarettes are protective against the development of CHD.
Risk of developing CHD 10-20 years after the cessation of smoking is equal in smokers and non smokers.
Degree of risk of developing CHD is directly related to the number of cigarettes smoked per day.
questions.answer: B. Filters in cigarettes are protective against the development of CHD.
questions.explanation:
Filters are probably not protective against the development of coronary heart disease in smokers.

Smoking is a modifiable risk factor for coronary heart disease (CHD). The degree of risk is directly related to the number of cigarettes smoked per day. Several mechanisms have been suggested for this:

• Carbon monoxide induced atherogenesis

• Nicotine stimulation of adrenergic drive

• Lipid metabolism with fall in levels of HDL

Cigarettes also increase the risk of sudden death in patients with CHD who are below 50 years of age. The risk of death from CHD decreases with the cessation of smoking. The risk declines quite substantially within one year of stopping smoking and more gradually thereafter until, after 10- 20 years, it is the same as that of non-smokers.

Risk factors for coronary heart disease are:

• Modifiable:

• Cigarette smoking

• High blood pressure

• Elevated serum cholesterol

• Diabetes

• Obesity

• Sedentary habits

• Stress

• Non-modifiable:

• Age

• Sex

• Family history

• Genetic factors

• Personality

questions.question: A chronic smoker was found to have a deranged lipid profile during his annual health checkup. Which of the following variables tested is most directly associated with the risk of developing coronary heart disease?
questions.explanation:
The plasma LDL level is most directly associated with the risk of developing coronary heart disease (CHD).

HDL is protective against the development of CHD. Its levels should ideally be more than 40 mg/dl.

Recent evidence shows that levels of Apolipoprotein-A-1 and Apolipoprotein-B are better predictors of CHD than HDL or LDL.

VLDL is more strongly associated with the risk of developing peripheral vascular disease.

questions.question: A 45-year-old diabetic male is concerned about his risk of developing coronary heart disease. What cholesterol/HDL ratio would you aim to achieve in this patient?
questions.explanation: A cholesterol/HDL ratio <3.5 is recommended for the prevention of coronary heart disease (CHD).

questions.question: While conducting a screening camp for coronary heart disease, you encounter the following people. Who among them is at the highest risk for developing this disease?
options: A person who is competitive and ambitious
A person who is calm and relaxed
A person who tends to suppress their emotions
An introverted person with negative affectivity
questions.answer: A. A person who is competitive and ambitious
questions.explanation:
A person who is competitive and ambitious is said to have a type A personality. Such people are more prone to develop coronary heart disease (CHD). Personality type is a non-modifiable risk factor for CHD.

Risk factors for coronary heart disease are:

• Modifiable:

• Cigarette smoking

• High blood pressure

• Elevated serum cholesterol

• Diabetes

• Obesity

• Sedentary habits

• Stress

• Non-modifiable:

• Age

• Sex

• Family history

• Genetic factors

• Personality

Option B: A calm and relaxed person is said to have a type B personality.

Option C: A person who tends to suppress their emotions, especially negative emotions, is said to have a type C personality.

Option D: A person with negative affectivity and social inhibition is said to have a type D personality.

questions.question: A 45-year-old obese woman enquires about ways she can reduce her risk of coronary artery disease. Which of the following dietary modifications would you suggest?
options: Reduction of salt intake to less than 10g per day
Consumption of saturated fats limited to less than 10% of the total energy intake
Reduction of total fat intake to less than 5% of total energy intake
Dietary cholesterol increased to above 100 mg/1000 kcal energy intake
questions.answer: B. Consumption of saturated fats limited to less than 10% of the total energy intake
questions.explanation:
Limiting the consumption of saturated fats to less than 10% of total energy intake is recommended for the prevention of coronary artery disease.

The WHO'S Expert Committee suggested certain dietary modifications for the prevention of coronary artery disease. These include:

• Reduction of the total fat intake to 20–30% of total energy intake

• Consumption of saturated fats must be limited to less than 10% of total energy intake

• A reduction of dietary cholesterol to below 100mg per 1000 kcal per day

• Increase in the complex carbohydrate consumption (i.e vegetables, fruits, whole grains and legumes)

• Avoidance of alcohol consumption and reduction of salt intake to 5g daily or less

questions.question: A 50-year-old man, under treatment for hypertension for the past two months, is found to have a blood pressure of 144/96 mmHg. How will you grade it according to the European society of cardiology guidelines-2018?
questions.explanation: According to the European society of cardiology guidelines-2018, a patient having a systolic BP≥140 and a diastolic BP≥90 mmHg is classified as having grade 1 hypertension.

questions.question: A doctor records the BP of a patient as 142/90mmHg. One hour later, another doctor records the BP of the same patient as 160/98 mmHg. Both the readings are measured with the same apparatus under the same emotional and physical state of the patient. What type of error is seen here?
questions.explanation:
Such errors can arise due to differences in hearing acuity and interpretation of Korotkoff sounds.

The types of errors that can occur during the measurement of blood pressure include:

• Observer errors - due to difference in hearing acuity and interpretation of Korotkoff sounds

• Instrumental errors - due to a leaking valve or cuffs that do not encircle the arm completely

• Subject errors - due to anxiety, fear, etc. of the patient

questions.question: What does number 2 in the given diagram related to hypertension denote?
options: Diagnosed hypertensive subjects not on treatment
questions.explanation:
The above diagram depicts the "rule of halves", which shows the distribution of hypertension in the community. The number 2 in this diagram denotes normotensive subjects.

The rule of halves is a way of depicting the iceberg phenomenon seen in hypertension. It depicts that only about half of the hypertensive subjects in the general population of most developed countries are aware of the condition and only half of those aware are being treated and only half of those being treated are considered to be adequately treated.

The circles marked by numbers in the given diagram correspond to the following parts of the population:

1. Whole community

2. Normotensive subjects

3. Hypertensive subjects

4. Undiagnosed hypertension

5. Diagnosed hypertension

6. Diagnosed but untreated

7. Diagnosed and treated

8. Inadequately treated

9. Adequately treated

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding tracking of blood pressure?
options: BP increases with age in all individuals
BP falls steadily in the elderly
Hypertensive children become hypotensive as they grow
BP of hypotensive children tends to remain low in adult life
questions.answer: D. BP of hypotensive children tends to remain low in adult life
questions.explanation:
If the blood pressure of individuals is followed up over years from early childhood to adult life, low blood pressures tend to remain low and high blood pressures become higher as the individuals grow older. This phenomenon of persistence of the rank order of blood pressure is described as tracking.

This is helpful in identifying children and adolescents who are at risk of developing hypertension in the future.

Although blood pressure is known to increase with age in both sexes, some communities have been identified whose mean blood pressure does not rise with age. This is because their salt intake and calorie consumption are at a subsistence level.

questions.question: While formulating a diet plan for a hypertensive patient, you advise salt restriction. How much reduction in systolic blood pressure is expected by this intervention?
questions.explanation:
Salt restriction or decreasing dietary sodium intake decreases the systolic blood pressure by 2-8 mmHg approximately.

questions.question: Which of the following is a minor criterion for the diagnosis of rheumatic fever in a low risk population?
questions.explanation: Polyarthralgia is a minor criterion for the diagnosis of rheumatic fever in a low risk population.

questions.question: A child having strep throat is being prescribed benzathine penicillin G. Which level of prevention of rheumatic fever does this intervention fall under?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is an example of primary mode of prevention of rheumatic fever. This is because the patient only has strep throat and rheumatic fever has not developed yet.

In case benzathine penicillin G is given to a patient with rheumatic fever to prevent further complications, then it becomes secondary level of prevention.

questions.question: A 16-year-old boy with rheumatic fever developed carditis which subsequently healed in a couple of weeks. How long will you administer benzathine penicillin G for secondary prophylaxis to him?
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, benzathine penicillin G for secondary prophylaxis should be given for 10 years from the last attack i.e, till 26 years of age. The given case is of rheumatic fever with carditis but with no residual valvular disease, for which secondary prophylaxis is given for 10 years from the last attack or till 21 years of age, whichever is longer.

Recommendations for the duration of secondary prophylaxis with penicillin:

Category of the patient

Duration of prophylaxis

Rheumatic fever without carditis

For 5 years after the last attack or until 21 years of age ( whichever is longer)

Rheumatic fever with carditis but with no residual valvular disease

For 10 years after the last attack or until 21 yrs of age (whichever is longer)

Rheumatic fever with persistent valvular disease evident clinically or on echo

For 10 years after the last attack or until 40 years of age, or sometimes lifelong prophylaxis

questions.question: Which of the following is not a protective factor for diabetes mellitus?
questions.explanation:
A higher intake of saturated fats is associated with an increased risk of diabetes mellitus.

Dietary factors that are protective for diabetes mellitus are:

• Higher intake of unsaturated fatty acids

• A minimum daily intake of 20g of dietary fibre

• Exclusive breastfeeding

questions.question: A patient's fasting plasma glucose is 122 mg/dl and postprandial plasma glucose is 138 mg/dl. According to the WHO diagnostic criteria for diabetes, which category does this patient fall under?
questions.explanation:
Fasting blood glucose of 122 mg/dl with a postprandial value of 138 mg/dl indicates the patient falls under the criteria for impaired fasting glucose.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are incorrect regarding the benefits of various interventions in diabetes?

1. Lifestyle interventions can reduce the incidence of diabetes by 50%

2. Risk of microvascular disease reduces by 30% per 1% drop in HbA1c

3. Use of ACE inhibitors reduces the risk of nephropathy by 10%

4. Risk of macrovascular disease reduces by 35% per 10 mmHg drop in blood pressure

5. Annual eye examination reduces the incidence of serious visual loss by 40%
questions.explanation:
The use of ACE inhibitors in diabetics reduces the risk of nephropathy by 42% and cardiovascular risk by 22%. Annual eye examination in diabetics reduces the incidence of serious visual loss by 60-70%.

Interventions in diabetes:

• Glycaemic control in diabetics with HbA1C > 9% reduces microvascular disease risk by 30% per 1% drop in HbA1c.

• Blood pressure control in patients with BP > 130/80 mmHg reduces microvascular and macrovascular disease risk by 35% per 10 mmHg drop in blood pressure.

• Lifestyle modification reduces the incidence of diabetes by 35-58%.

• Metformin administered as a preventive therapy reduces the incidence of diabetes by 25-31%.

• Proper foot care reduces the risk of serious foot disease by 50-60%.

questions.question: The community health officer of an area is instructed to assess the population for the risk factors of Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease under NP-NCD. Which of the following will not be a risk factor?
questions.explanation:
Low blood pressure is not a risk factor for NAFLD according to the NP-NCD.

The National Programme for Prevention & Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD), which was earlier NPCDCS, has integrated guidelines for the management of Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver disease (NAFLD) into its framework. Through a community-based assessment checklist, the community health officer along with ASHA workers will assess for the presence of the following risk factors:

1. Abdominal obesity (waist circumference of >90cm in men and >80cm in women)

2. Personal or family history of diabetes, hypertension, cancers, heart diseases, liver diseases or gallstones

3. Obesity (BMI >23 kg/m2)

4. Presence of pedal edema

Level of healthcare
Provisions

Community level

• ASHA workers assess for abdominal obesity, relevant personal or family history.

• Refer to the sub-health centre.

Sub-Health Centre

• Validate ASHA workers’ referrals.

• Further assess for pedal edema, BMI, and screen for other NCDs.

Primary Health Centre

• Assessment of SHC referrals for signs of chronic liver disease.

• Basic treatment for DM/HTN.

Community Health Centre

• Rule out other causes of liver disease, and perform CBC and LFT. Calculate FIB4 or NFS score.

• If low risk of fibrosis - Refer back to the PHC for conservative management, weight reduction etc. Reassess in 3 years.

• If indeterminate, or high risk of fibrosis - Refer to a higher centre.

District level

• Perform Fibroscan for indeterminate risk of fibrosis.

• In case of low risk of fibrosis - Refer back to the PHC for conservative management, weight reduction, etc. Reassess in 3 years.

• In case of high risk of fibrosis - Management of fibrosis, screening for HCC and portal hypertension.

• Refer complicated cases to tertiary level.

Tertiary level

• Management of complicated cases.

questions.question: Which of the following organisms is least likely to be associated with malignancies?
questions.explanation:
HPV 6 and 11 are considered low-risk subtypes and are associated mainly with genital warts (condyloma acuminata) and respiratory papillomatosis in both genders.

HPV 16 and 18 are considered high-risk subtypes and are associated with cancer cervix and pre-cancerous cervical lesions. There is also evidence linking HPV 16 and 18 with cancers of the anus, vulva, vagina, penis, and oropharynx.

Important agents associated with malignant conditions:

• HHV-8 (mainly), cytomegalovirus - Kaposi’s sarcoma

• Epstein-Barr virus - Burkitt’s lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma

• HPV 16 and 18 - Cancer cervix

• HBV and HCV - Hepatocellular carcinoma

• Schistosoma - Bladder carcinoma

questions.question: Which among the following is not a primary method of prevention of carcinoma in the population?
questions.explanation:
Screening for cancer is a secondary level of prevention.

This is because it detects the disease at a pre-invasive or pre-malignant stage when the process of carcinogenesis has already started. It thereby aids in further treatment and improved survival.

Immunization, restricting the use of tobacco and avoiding alcohol are primary levels of prevention because they prevent the start of carcinogenesis.

questions.question: Which of the following women is not at an increased risk of developing breast cancer in future?
options: A woman who attained menarche at 9 years of age
A woman who has never breastfed in her lifetime
A woman who attained menopause at 56 years of age
A woman who had her first full term pregnancy at 26 years of age
questions.answer: D. A woman who had her first full term pregnancy at 26 years of age
questions.explanation:
Women who have their first full-term pregnancy after 30 years of age are at increased risk for breast cancer.

The risk of breast cancer increases with an increase in duration of exposure to estrogen. As progesterone levels are increased during pregnancy, it reduces the risks of conditions that occur due to hyperestrogenemia.

Risk factors for breast cancer:

• Modifiable risk factors:

• Age at first live birth (First full-term pregnancy after 30 years)

• Parity

• Lack of breastfeeding

• Obesity

• Alcohol consumption

• Tobacco smoking

• Use of hormone replacement therapy

• Decreased physical activity

• Non-modifiable risk factors:

• Increasing age

• Early age at menarche (onset of menses before 12 years of age)

• Menstrual factors

• Female sex

• Older age at menopause (onset beyond 55 years of age)

• Nulliparity

• Race, ethnicity

• Genetic predisposition

• Family history

• History of radiation exposure

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman is at increased risk of breast cancer as she is on hormone replacement therapy. Which of the following is the most sensitive method of screening for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Mammography is the most sensitive and specific investigation for detecting breast cancer.

It can detect even small tumors that are missed during a self-breast examination, clinical examination by the physician and ultrasonographic examination.

questions.question: A patient with Prader-Willi syndrome needs to be evaluated for obesity but the scale for measuring height in your clinic is broken. Which of the following indices can you still use in this situation?
questions.explanation: The corpulence index can be used in this scenario as it is independent of height. The formula for corpulence index is actual weight/ desired weight.

questions.question: Which of the following indices of obesity is obtained by dividing weight in kg by square of height in metres?
questions.explanation: Quetelet's index (Body Mass Index) is obtained by dividing weight in kg by square of height in metres.

questions.question: The BMI of two Indian college students are 17 and 24.99 respectively. How will you classify them in terms of their BMI?
questions.explanation: An adult Indian with a BMI of 17 is classified as underweight and a BMI of 24.99 is classified as overweight.

questions.question: The weight of a diabetic woman is 75 kg and her height is 150 cm. Calculate her BMI.
questions.explanation:
The BMI of an individual with a weight of 75 kg and height of 150 cm is 33. It is calculated as follows,

BMI = Weight (in kg) / Height2 (in metre2) = 75 / (1.5)2 = 33.

questions.question: For which of the following conditions, an obese individual is at the greatest risk of developing in the future?
questions.explanation:
Among the given options, an obese individual is at the greatest risk of developing type 2 diabetes.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding waist circumference?

It is measured at the midpoint between the lower border of the rib cage and the iliac crest
It is an approximate index of intra-abdominal and total body fat
It is an indicator of the risk of chronic diseases
questions.answer: A. The cut-off for normal waist circumference in Indian women is 90 cm

Waist circumference is an approximate indicator of intra-abdominal and total body fat. It is measured at the midpoint between the lower border of the rib cage and the iliac crest. It is an indicator of the risk of chronic diseases.

questions.question: According to the WHO, what is the cut-off for visual acuity for blindness?
questions.explanation: According to the WHO, blindness is defined as visual acuity of less than 3/60, or a corresponding visual field loss to less than 10°, in the better eye with the best possible correction.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of blindness in India?
questions.explanation: According to the National Survey on Blindness (2015-2019), cataract is the most common cause of blindness in India accounting for 66.2% of the total cases.

questions.question: You administer vitamin A prophylactically to a 15-month-old child during a routine checkup. What is the level of prevention being achieved here?
questions.explanation: Prophylactic administration of vitamin A to a normal child is an example of primary level of prevention. It is done to prevent xerophthalmia.

questions.question: A boy is brought to the ophthalmologist with complaints of dryness in both the eyes and difficulty in reading. On examination, his eye appears as shown in the below image. What is the stage of xerophthalmia according to WHO?
questions.explanation: The finding in the given image is a Bitot's spot. It belongs to WHO class X1 B of vitamin A deficiency.

questions.question: A 2-year-old child on examination shows signs of vitamin A deficiency. What is the dose of vitamin A to be administered to this child?
questions.explanation:
2 lakh IU of vitamin A should be administered to a 2-year-old child with vitamin A deficiency.

Dosage of vitamin A in children:

• 50,000 IU for children less than 6 months of age

• 1 lakh IU for children between 6 months to 12 months of age

• 2 lakh IU for children above 12 months of age.

These doses of vitamin A are to be administered on days 1, 2 and 14 for the treatment of vitamin A deficiency.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of injury-related death?
questions.explanation: The most common cause of injury-related deaths are road traffic accidents, followed by suicide.

questions.question: You are working as the PHC Medical Officer in your village. Which of the following diseases would you not target under the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme?
questions.explanation:
The National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP) does not target the prevention and control of cutaneous leishmaniasis (also known as Chiclero's ulcer).

NVBDCP is the nodal agency for the prevention and control of the following vector-borne diseases:

• Kala-azar (also called visceral leishmaniasis)

• Malaria

• Dengue

• Lymphatic filariasis

• Japanese encephalitis

• Chikungunya.
