questions.question: What is the normal daily requirement of magnesium in adults?
questions.explanation:
The normal daily requirement of magnesium in adults is 400 mg/day

The following are the approximate daily requirements of some electrolytes in adults:

• Sodium: 1.2 to 1.5 grams (g)/day (up to 2g/day)

• Potassium: 3500 mg/day

• Calcium: 1000-1200 mg/day

• Magnesium: 400 mg/day

questions.question: Which of the following formulates food standards for the international food market?
questions.explanation:
The Codex Alimentarius Commission formulates food standards for the international market. It is the principal organ of the FAO/WHO food standards program.

The ISI standards (Indian Standards Institute) and AGMARK are the Indian food standards. They are based on the standards of Codex Alimentarius.

The PFA (Prevention of Food Adulteration) Act was introduced to provide protection from adulteration or contamination of food.

questions.question: What is the dose of vitamin A added during fortification of vanaspati?
questions.explanation:
Vanaspati is fortified with 2500 IU of vitamin A and 175 IU of vitamin D.

Note: 1g of double fortified salt contains 40 mcg iodine and 1 mg iron.

questions.question: Which of the following contributes to a significant loss of beta carotene from food?
questions.explanation:
Dehydration contributes to a significant loss in the beta carotene levels in food.

Processes that do not affect beta carotene levels in the food are:

• Boiling

• Canning

• Freezing

questions.question: In order to effectively prevent endemic goiter, what is the recommended iodine content in salt at the consumer level?
questions.explanation:
The recommended level of iodine content in salt is 15 ppm at the consumer level and 30 ppm at the production level.

The iodization of salt is used as a prophylactic measure against endemic goiter. In India, the level of iodization is fixed under the Prevention of Food Adulteration (PFA) Act.

questions.question: In a milk factory, the milk is heated at 63°C for 30 minutes and then cooled quickly to less than 13°C . Which bacteria can survive this method?
questions.explanation:
The method described above is the holder method of pasteurization. Coxiella burnetti can survive this method since it is highly heat-resistant. It causes Q fever.

The various methods of pasteurization are:

• Holder/Vat method - 63-66 °C for 30 minutes

• HTST method (high-temperature short time) - 72°C for 15 seconds

• UHT method (ultra-high temperature) - 125 °C for a few seconds

questions.question: Which of the following tests is not used to check the efficiency of pasteurization?
questions.explanation:
Methylene blue reduction test is not used to check the efficiency of pasteurization. This test is used for grading raw milk quality prior to pasteurization.

The following tests are used to check the efficiency of pasteurization:

• Phosphatase test

• Standard plate count

• Coliform count

questions.question: In a rice processing factory, paddy is soaked in hot water. After this, the water is drained and the paddy is steamed and dried. Which of the following statements is false about the above process?
options: This method is used for partial cooking of rice
It makes the rice grains resistant to insects
Vitamins and minerals are driven into endosperm during this process
questions.answer: D. It softens the rice grains
questions.explanation:
The procedure mentioned above is parboiling. It hardens the rice grains.

Parboiling is the process of partial cooking of rice in steam. It is done by the hot soaking process that was initially developed by the Central Food Technological Research Institute (CFTRI), Mysore.

The advantages of parboiling are:

• Preserves nutritive quality by driving the vitamins and minerals into the endosperm.

• Hardens the grains and makes them insect resistant.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man presented with gradually progressive muscle weakness and leg spasms for 2 months. He says that he had been consuming an inexpensive dal resembling red gram for the past 2 years. Pure motor paresis was seen on examination. Which of the following could have prevented this?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical features are suggestive of neurolathyrism. It can be prevented and treated by the administration of vitamin C at doses of 500-1000 mg.

Lathyrism is a paralyzing disease of humans and animals. It is due to the consumption of khesari dal or Lathyrus sativus. When the husk is removed, it looks similar to red gram or Bengal gram.

BOAA (beta oxalyl amino alanine) is the toxic compound causing this disease. It is water-soluble and can be removed by the following methods:

• Soaking pulses in hot water and discarding the water

• Overnight soaking in lime water followed by boiling

• Parboiling - for large-scale detoxification

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman is being evaluated for sudden onset of hypersecretory glaucoma, diarrhea, and cardiac failure. Further probing reveals that she had been purchasing groceries from a dealer who was recently arrested for food adulteration. What toxin is likely responsible for her presentation?
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of epidemic dropsy. It is caused by the toxic compound sanguinarine, which is present in argemone oil. It is commonly used as an adulterant in mustard oil.

Epidemic dropsy results in sudden onset of swelling of lower limbs, diarrhea, and breathlessness. Some patients may develop hypersecretory glaucoma. It can lead to death due to cardiac failure.

Adulteration with argemone oil can be detected by the following tests:

• Paper chromatography - most sensitive test

• Nitric acid test

chapters.chapter: Water I Sources And Purification Of Water

questions.question: Which of the following is not a component of the definition of safe and wholesome water?
questions.explanation:
Water intended for human consumption must be safe and wholesome. It must be colorless.

Safe and wholesome water is defined as:

• Free from pathogenic agents

• Free from harmful chemicals

• Pleasant to taste, free from colour and odour

• Usable for domestic purposes

Water is said to be polluted when it does not fulfill the above criteria.

questions.question: In an urban PHC, an increasing number of skin diseases are being reported due to inadequate water supply in the region. What would be the adequate supply of water for them to meet their needs for all domestic purposes?
questions.answer: B. 150–200 litres per capita per day
questions.explanation:
The given scenario of skin diseases is suggestive of water-washed diseases caused by improper hygiene related to an inadequate water supply. In urban areas, 150–200 litres per capita per day is the recommended allowance to meet the needs for all kinds of domestic purposes.
In rural areas, the set target of water supply to be achieved in India is around 50-55 litres per capita per day.

questions.question: What are the norms for the required litres of water per capita per day in rural areas?
questions.explanation:
According to the National Rural Drinking Water Programme, the requirement of water in rural areas (areas with public water posts) is 55 litres per capita per day. This is in accordance with the 12th Five Year Plan.

For reasons of comparability, the source of water provision in rural areas should be within a distance of 100 metres from the household or the time taken to fetch water should not be > 30 minutes.

Note: Park textbook mentions 40-50 litres per capita per day as the norm. However, in the 12th five year plan period, the Government of India enhanced the rural drinking water supply norms from 40 litres to 55 litres per capita per day.

questions.question: What is the purest form of water in nature?
questions.explanation:
Rain water is the purest form of water in nature. It contains a very low amount of total dissolved solids (TDS). Rain water is the origin of both surface and ground water.

Sources of water:

• Rain

• Surface water:

• Impounding reservoirs

• Rivers and streams

• Tanks, ponds and lakes

• Ground water:

• Shallow wells

• Deep wells

• Springs

questions.question: Which of the following is not a source of surface water?
questions.explanation:
Shallow wells are sources of ground water.

Sources of water:

• Rain

• Surface water:

• Impounding reservoirs

• Rivers and streams

• Tanks, ponds and lakes

• Ground water:

• Shallow wells

• Deep wells

• Springs

questions.question: What is the area from which water drains into impounding reservoirs known as?
questions.explanation:
The area draining into the impounding reservoirs are known as catchment areas.

Impounding reservoirs are also called embankment ponds. These reservoirs are artificial lake-like water bodies. They are made by building an embankment or earth fill in an area into which natural water flows and can be stored for usage. Dams are also built to create these reservoirs.

Water from these reservoirs is second in purity to rainwater but is not completely free from impurities. Catchment areas are the main sources of impurities in the water in impounding reservoirs.

The image given below shows catchment area:

questions.question: What is the most common type of well in India?
questions.explanation: Dug wells are the most common type of wells in India.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about artesian wells?
options: It is not common in India
Water is put under pressure between two impervious layers
No pump is required to bring water to surface
It is a type of shallow well
questions.answer: D. It is a type of shallow well
questions.explanation: Artesian wells are types of deep wells.

questions.question: Step wells belong to which of the following types of wells?
questions.explanation: Step wells belong to the type of pucca dug wells.

questions.question: An outbreak of guinea worm disease was reported among villagers who used step wells for drinking water. In order to arrest the spread of disease, a decision was made to replace step wells with sanitary and safe wells. All of the following measures would be considered during its construction except:
options: Must be located at least 15 metres away from sources of contamination
A partition space for washing clothes and vessels
Lining must be made to a depth of 6 metres or more
Hand-pump must be made to handle rough use
questions.answer: B. A partition space for washing clothes and vessels
questions.explanation:
Washing clothes, vessels, and bathing must be prohibited around wells to avoid contamination of the water.

Step wells are a type of pucca wells which enable people to descend into the well to fetch water. It is obsolete now, as there is considerable personal contact between the user and the water which can pose a health hazard to the community.

questions.question: What is the minimum length that the platform of a well should extend around it in all directions?
questions.explanation: The platform of a sanitary well should stretch for at least 1 metre around the well in all directions.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a water-washed disease?
questions.explanation:
Cholera is a water-borne disease and not a water-washed disease.

The diseases which are transmitted by improper hygiene and are widely related to circumstances where there is inadequate water supply are called water-washed diseases.

Some examples of water-washed diseases are:

• Conjunctivitis

• Trachoma

• Scabies

• Typhus

questions.question: A multipurpose worker is spraying herbicides on aquatic plants as part of vector control measures in your area. Which of the following water-related diseases can be controlled by this approach?
questions.explanation:
Filariasis (caused by B.malayi) is transmitted by Mansonia species of mosquito that breeds in water bodies containing aquatic vegetation. It can be controlled by the use of herbicides to destroy aquatic vegetation.

Water-related diseases are classified as:

Category

Examples

Water-borne diseases

Caused by ingestion of water contaminated by human or animal faeces, or urine containing pathogenic bacteria or viruses.

ex: Cholera, typhoid, amoebic and bacillary dysentery, and other diarrhoeal diseases.

Water-washed diseases

Caused by poor personal hygiene.

ex: Scabies, trachoma, flea-, lice- and tick-borne diseases, in addition to the majority of waterborne diseases (which are also water-washed).

Water-based diseases

Caused by parasites found in intermediate organisms living in water.

ex: Dracunculiasis, schistosomiasis and some other helminths.

Water-related diseases transmitted by insect vectors

Caused by vectors that breed in water

ex: Dengue, filariasis, malaria, onchocerciasis, trypanosomiasis and yellow fever.

questions.question: Which of the following methods of purification of water cannot be used on a large scale?
questions.explanation: Berkefeld filter is used for the purification of water on a small scale (ex: in households).

questions.question: During your posting as a rural medical officer, you conduct an awareness drive prior to the monsoon season in order to highlight the necessity of water purification. Which of the following methods would you not recommend for a household setup?
questions.explanation: Slow sand filter is a method of filtration used for the purification of water on a large scale.

questions.question: When river water is stored properly, by how much percent does the bacterial count drop in the first 5-7 days?
questions.explanation:
When river water is stored properly, the bacterial count drops by as much as 90% in the first 5 – 7 days.

Purification during the storage of water is a natural process that takes place by physical, chemical and biological phenomena. Components of water purification include storage, filtration and disinfection.

questions.question: What is the other name for slow sand filters?
questions.explanation: Slow sand filters are also called biological filters.

questions.question:
Which of the following is a part of a slow sand filter?

1. Under-drainage system

2. Sand bed

3. Filter control system

4. Supernatant water

5. Filter box
questions.explanation:
Components of a slow sand filter include:

• Under-drainage system

• Sand bed and a layer of organic matter

• Filter control system

• Supernatant water

• Filter box

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about slow sand filters?
options: The thickness of sand bed is 2 metres
It takes a longer duration for water purification
The sand grain size is 0.4 to 0.7 mm
questions.answer: C. It takes a longer duration for water purification
questions.explanation: Slow sand filters take a longer duration than most other methods for purification of water.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes Schmutzdecke?
options: Layer of alum flocculate on supernatant water
Layer of algae and diatoms on supernatant water
Layer of alum flocculate on surface of sand bed filter
Layer of algae and diatoms on surface of sand bed filter
questions.answer: D. Layer of algae and diatoms on surface of sand bed filter
questions.explanation: Schmutzdecke refers to the vital layer which is formed by algae, plankton, diatoms and bacteria on the surface of the sand bed filter.

questions.question: Which of the following is not the vital layer of a slow sand filter?
questions.explanation: The vital layer of a slow sand filter is also called the zoogleal layer, Schmutzdecke, or the biological layer.

questions.question: Where is the vital layer of the slow sand filter seen?
options: On top of the raw water
questions.explanation: The vital layer of the slow sand filter is seen on the sand bed.

questions.question: What does the venturi meter measure in a slow sand filter?
questions.explanation:
Venturi meters measure the bed resistance or loss of head in a slow sand filter.

The following image shows a venturi meter:

questions.question: Which of the following is an incorrect statement about rapid sand filters?
options: No preliminary storage of raw water is required
Can be gravity or pressure type
questions.answer: C. Frequent washing is not required
questions.explanation: Frequent washing of the filter bed is required in rapid sand filters. This is done by backwashing.

questions.question: What is the effective size of sand grains in a rapid sand filter?
questions.explanation:
Effective size of sand grains in a rapid sand filter is 0.4 – 0.7 mm.

Effective size of sand grains in a slow sand filter is 0.2 – 0.3 mm.

questions.question: Rapid sand filter is different from the slow sand filter by which of the following features?
options: Sand particles are of smaller size
questions.explanation:
Skilled labor is required for rapid sand filters. Unskilled labor is enough for slow sand filters.

Comparison of rapid and slow sand filters:

Rapid sand filter

Slow sand filter

Space

Occupies very little space

Occupies large area

Rate of filtration (million gallons per acre per day)

200 m.g.a.d
2-3 m.g.a.d.

Effective size of sand

0.4-0.7 mm
0.2-0.3 mm

Preliminary treatment

Chemical coagulation and sedimentation
Plain sedimentation

Washing

By back-washing
By scraping the sand bed

Operation

Highly skilled
Less skilled

Loss of head allowed

6-8 feet (2- 2.5 m)
4 feet (1.5 m)

Removal of bacteria

98-99%
99.9- 99.99%

questions.question: Which of the following is not a ceramic filter that can be used for small scale purification of water?
questions.explanation:
Filtration of water on a small scale is done by ceramic filters like Pasteur Chamberland, Berkefeld, and Katadyn filters.

Ceramic filters are not widely used in India. The most important parts of these filters are the filter candles. Filter candles of the fine type help in removing bacteria but not viruses. These filter candles need to be cleaned periodically as they get clogged with impurities and bacteria.

Types of ceramic filters include:

• Pasteur Chamberland filter – It has a candle made of porcelain.

Image of a Pasteur Chamberland filter is shown below:

• Berkefeld filter - it has a candle made of infusorial earth or kieselguhr.

Image of a Berkefeld filter is shown below:

• Katadyn filter - the surface of this filter is coated with a silver catalyst. The incoming bacteria are killed on contact with the surface by the oligodynamic action of silver ions which are liberated into the water.

Image of a Katadyn filter is shown below:

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect about ceramic filters?
options: Surface of Berkefeld filter is lined with a silver catalyst
Chamberland filter has a porcelain filter candle
Oligodynamic action is seen with Katadyn filter
They are not widely used in India
questions.answer: A. Surface of Berkefeld filter is lined with a silver catalyst
questions.explanation:
Berkefeld filter has a candle made of infusorial earth or kieselguhr.

Ceramic filters are used for small scale purification of water. They are not widely used in India. The most important parts of these filters are the filter candles.

Types of ceramic filters include:

• Pasteur Chamberland filter – It has a candle made of porcelain.

• Berkefeld filter - it has a candle made of infusorial earth or kieselguhr.

• Katadyn filter - the surface of this filter is coated with a silver catalyst. The incoming bacteria are killed on contact with the surface by the oligodynamic action of silver ions which are liberated into the water.

questions.question: Which of the following is the method of choice for the purification of highly polluted water on a large scale?
questions.explanation: Superchlorination followed by dechlorination is done for purification of highly polluted water on a large scale.

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding chlorination of water?
options: Orthotolidine test measures only combined chlorine
Chlorine acts best when the pH of water is around seven
It kills bacteria, viruses, spores and slime organisms
Hypochlorite ions are mainly responsible for its disinfectant activity
questions.answer: B. Chlorine acts best when the pH of water is around seven
questions.explanation:
Chlorine acts best when the pH of water is around seven because of the predominance of the hypochlorous acid. Most water sources have a pH around 6.5–7, making chlorination an effective form of disinfection.

Option A: Orthotolidine test measures both free and combined chlorine in water.

Option C: Chlorination kills pathogenic bacteria, but has no effect on spores and certain viruses.

Option D: The disinfecting action of chlorine is mainly due to hypochlorous acid.

questions.question: You assign a male health worker at a sub-centre with the task of chlorinating public water resources. What is the minimum concentration of free residual chlorine that should be maintained for effective chlorination?
options: 0.5 mg/litre for a contact period of 1 hour
0.5 mg/litre for a contact period of ½ hour
0.8 mg/litre for a contact period of 1 hour
0.8 mg/litre for a contact period of ½ hour
questions.answer: A. 0.5 mg/litre for a contact period of 1 hour
questions.explanation: The minimum recommended concentration of free residual chlorine for routine chlorination is 0.5 mg/litre for a contact period of 1 hour.

questions.question: As an epidemiologist, you are investigating an outbreak of cholera. What is the minimum free residual chlorine level that should be maintained in pipelines to prevent further spread of the outbreak?
questions.explanation:
The minimum level of free residual chlorine to be maintained in pipelines following an outbreak of cholera is 0.5 mg/litre.

After a disaster (such as a flood), the water bodies are contaminated with sewage and drainage. The mixing of faeces in drinking bodies increases the risk of numerous microbial infections. The advisable level of free residual chlorine in water bodies after a disaster is, therefore, higher i.e. 0.7-0.9 mg/litre.

questions.question: The municipal corporation in your area is performing routine chlorination of drinking water supplies. Which of the following statements about chlorination is incorrect?
options: Free chlorine is released in water after breakpoint chlorination
Chlorine demand is the amount needed to kill spores, protozoal cysts and helminthic ova
0.5 ppm of free chlorine must be present in water after the breakpoint has been reached
Contact period of 1 hour is necessary
questions.answer: B. Chlorine demand is the amount needed to kill spores, protozoal cysts and helminthic ova
questions.explanation:
Chlorine demand is the amount of chlorine that is needed to kill bacteria, and to oxidize all the organic matter and ammoniacal substances in the water. It is the difference between the amount of chlorine added to the water and the amount of residual chlorine remaining at the end of a specific period of contact (usually 1 hour) at a given temperature and pH of the water.

0.5 ppm (0.5 mg) of free chlorine must be present in water after the breakpoint has been reached.

questions.question: Which of the following tests identifies free and combined chlorine in water separately?
questions.explanation:
Orthotolidine-arsenite test determines both free and combined chlorine in water separately.

Orthotolidine test determines free and combined chlorine together.

Chick Martin test and Garrod's test are used to test the efficacy of disinfectants.

questions.question: A village health and sanitation team is planning to disinfect 100 wells. Which of the following is the most cost-effective method in this scenario?
questions.explanation: Disinfection of wells using bleaching powder is the most widely used and cheapest method.

questions.question: An outbreak of viral hepatitis A has been reported in a village. On investigating, you find a contaminated well in the locality to be the source of the outbreak. Which of the following methods would you advise for chlorinating the well in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
The double pot method is used for disinfecting wells by chlorination in emergencies like hepatitis A outbreak in a village.

Double pot method has an inner and outer pot, each with a hole in it and covered with a polyethylene foil. The inner pot is filled with bleaching powder and coarse sand. The double pot system is then lowered into a well. This device can work satisfactorily for 2 – 3 weeks in small wells containing about 4500 litres of water.

questions.question: In your community medicine practicals, you are given an apparatus as shown in the image given below. Which of the following statements regarding the apparatus is true?
options: The indicator used is bromocresol purple
It is used to estimate free chlorine levels
It is used to estimate combined chlorine levels
questions.answer: B. The indicator used is starch-iodide
questions.explanation:
The image given is that of a Horrock's apparatus. The indicator used in Horrock's apparatus is starch iodide.

Horrock's apparatus contains 6 white cups (200 ml each), 1 black cup with a circular mark, 2 metal spoons with 2 grams of bleaching powder in each, 7 glass stirring rods, 1 special pipette and 2 droppers. It is not usful in measuring free and combined chlorine. It estimates the chlorine demand of water and is used to calculate the amount of bleaching powder used to disinfect the well.

questions.question: What is the amount of bleaching powder required to disinfect 455 litres of water if the 4th, 5th, and 6th cups of a Horrock’s apparatus show distinct blue color?
questions.explanation:
The dose of bleaching powder required is 8 grams.

It is given by (n x 2) gms for 455 litres of water, where n is the number of the first cup that shows distinct blue color. In this scenario, the dose of bleaching powder required to disinfect 455 litres of water is (4 x 2) = 8grams.

questions.question: The water sample from a well is tested using Horrock’s apparatus. It is observed that the 3rd cup shows a blue color after the addition of the starch-iodine indicator. How much bleaching powder will be required to disinfect 2275 litres of the well water?
questions.explanation:
The dose of bleaching powder required is 30 grams.

It is given by (n x 2) gms for 455 liters of water, where n is the number of the first cup that shows a distinct blue color.

In this scenario, the dose of bleaching powder required to disinfect 455 liters of water is (3 x 2) = 6 grams.

Since 2275/455 = 5. The amount of bleaching powder required to disinfect 2275 litres of water = 6 x 5 = 30 grams.

questions.question:
Which of the following agents have residual germicidal effect when used for treatment of water?

1. UV radiation

2. Ozone gas

3. Chlorine

4. Iodine

5. Potassium permanganate
questions.explanation:
Chlorine has residual germicidal effect when used for treatment of water.

 UV radiation, ozone gas, iodine and potassium permanganate have good germicidal action but do not have residual germicidal effect.

questions.question: Which of the following properties of ozone makes it less suitable for the disinfection of water on a large scale?
options: Ozone requires a long time period for action
It has no residual disinfectant action
questions.answer: D. It has no residual disinfectant action
questions.explanation:
Ozone has no residual disinfectant action.

Ozone gas can be used as a primary disinfectant of water in a large scale. Ozone disinfection is usually followed by biological filtration or granular activated carbon to prevent further contamination during distribution. Chlorine residual treatment is also done as ozone does not provide for a residual disinfectant action.

questions.question: Which of the following is a lower-pressure membrane process for treatment of water?
questions.explanation:
Microfiltration is a lower-pressure membrane process used for the treatment of water.

Membrane processes are employed in the large scale treatment of water. They are classified as high-pressure processes and lower-pressure processes.

• High-pressure processes:

• Reverse osmosis - Rejects monovalent ions and organic molecules of molecular weight > 50 daltons. It is most commonly used for desalination of brackish water and sea water. The membrane pore size is < 0.002 µm.

• Nanofiltration - Allows monovalent ions such as sodium or potassium to pass but rejects a high proportion of divalent ions like calcium and magnesium and some higher molecular weight organics. The membrane pore size ranges from 0.001 – 0.01 µm.

• Lower-pressure processes:

• Ultrafiltration - Rejects organic molecules of molecular weight > 800 daltons. The membrane pore size ranges from 0.002 - 0.003 µm.

• Microfiltration - Rejects colloidal and suspended material. It does not separate molecules and is usually used before reverse osmosis. The membrane pore size ranges from 0.01 – 12 µm.

chapters.chapter: Water Iii Water Quality And Standards

questions.question: Above what level does the turbidity of water become visible to the naked eye?
questions.explanation:
Turbidity of water becomes visible to the naked eye above 4 nephelometric turbidity units (NTU).

The ideal level of turbidity is <1.0 NTU for household drinking purposes. However, in situations where this is not achievable, the maximum permissible limit is <5 NTU.

questions.question: What is the maximum permissible level of chloride in drinking water?
questions.explanation: The maximum permissible level of chloride in drinking water is 600 mg/litre.

questions.question: A detectable taste begins to appear in drinking water if chloride levels in it exceed:
questions.explanation: A detectable taste begins to appear in drinking water if chloride levels in it exceed 250 mg/litre.

questions.question: A large number of cases of methemoglobinemia were reported among infants from a municipal area. On detailed investigation, the nitrate levels in drinking water were found to be elevated in that area. This complication can occur when nitrate level in drinking water exceeds:
questions.explanation: Nitrates in the excess of 45 mg/L may cause methaemoglobinemia in infants.

questions.question: Which is the most undesirable metal in drinking water?
questions.explanation: The most undesirable metal in drinking water is lead.

questions.question: What is the acceptable level of total dissolved solids in drinking water in India?
questions.explanation:
According to the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), the acceptable level of total dissolved solids (TDS) in drinking water in India is 500 mg/L.

Note: There is a variation in the value of the acceptable level of total dissolved solids in drinking water provided by WHO and the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS). While the WHO sets the value at 600 mg/L, the BIS has set it at 500 mg/L for India.

questions.question: What is the proposed guideline for the permissible radioactivity values for drinking water?
options: Gross alpha activity up to 0.1 Bq/L and gross beta activity up to 1 Bq/L
Gross alpha activity up to 1 Bq/L and gross beta activity up to 0.5 Bq/L
Gross alpha activity up to 0.5 Bq/L and gross beta activity up to 1 Bq/L
Gross alpha activity up to 0.1 Bq/L and gross beta activity up to 0.5 Bq/L
questions.answer: C. Gross alpha activity up to 0.5 Bq/L and gross beta activity up to 1 Bq/L
questions.explanation:
The proposed guideline for the permissible radioactivity values for drinking water is:

Gross alpha activity up to 0.5 Bq/litre.

Gross beta activity up to 1.0 Bq/litre.

questions.question: In view of a hepatitis A outbreak in a hostel, samples of drinking water are collected to detect fecal contamination. Presence of which of the following organisms serves as the most reliable evidence of fecal contamination?
questions.explanation:
The presence of Escherichia coli is the most suitable and reliable evidence of fecal contamination of water.

Klebsiella aerogens is a typical example of the non-fecal group of coliform organisms.

questions.question:
A microbiologist is testing a sample of drinking water to detect fecal contamination. The presence of all of the following organisms indicates a positive test result except:

1. Staphylococcus

2. Streptococcus

3. Escherichia coli

4. Klebsiella aerogens

5. Clostridium perfringens
questions.explanation:
Presence of Staphylococcus and Klebsiella aerogens does not indicate fecal contamination of water.

 Biological indicators of fecal pollution of water are:

• Streptococcus faecalis

• Escherichia coli

• Clostridium perfringens

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect about water purification and pollution?
options: Presence of clostridial spores indicates recent contamination
Sodium thiosulphate can be used to dechlorinate water
Coliforms must not be detectable in any 100 ml sample of drinking water
Coliforms can be detected by the multiple tube method
questions.answer: A. Presence of clostridial spores indicates recent contamination
questions.explanation: The presence of clostridial spores indicates remote or intermittent contamination of water.

questions.question: Multiple tube method is done for which of the following?
options: Detecting the presence of coliform organisms in a sample of water
Detecting the presence of enteric viruses in a sample of water
Estimating the levels of mercury in a sample of water
Estimating turbidity of a sample of water
questions.answer: A. Detecting the presence of coliform organisms in a sample of water
questions.explanation:
The multiple tube method is done to detect the presence of coliform organisms in a sample of water.

In order to estimate the presumptive coliform count, water to be tested is inoculated into tubes containing a suitable liquid medium. These tubes are then incubated and examined after an appropriate period of time. The test is called presumptive because the reaction observed in the tube may occasionally be due to other organisms.

The proportion of false-positive reactions obtained depends both on the bacterial flora of the water under examination and the medium used. Lactose broth, or MacConkey's broth, with bromocresol purple as an indicator and a standardized concentration of bile salts incubated between 35°C–37°C for 48 hours, seems to be the most suitable media for presumptive tests.

questions.question: What is the acceptable bacteriological quality of drinking water in small communities?
options: No coliform bacteria in 100 ml of water
Upto 10 coliform bacteria in 100 ml of water
Upto 10 coliform bacteria in 1000 ml of water
Upto 100 coliform bacteria in 1000 ml of water
questions.answer: A. No coliform bacteria in 100 ml of water
questions.explanation: There must be no coliform bacteria in any 100 ml sample of drinking water as its presence indicates fecal contamination.

questions.question: Which of the following criteria is true for safe drinking water according to the WHO guidelines?
questions.explanation:
The desirable pH of safe drinking water ranges from 6.5 to 8.5.

The maximum permissible level of chloride in drinking water is 0.6 g/L (600 mg/L), and that of nitrates is 0.05 g/L (50mg/l).

The concentration of lead must be kept at <0.01 mg/L. It is the most undesirable metal in drinking water.

questions.question: Which of the following is a criterion included in the guidelines for drinking water quality recommended by WHO?
questions.explanation:
According to WHO, the permissible level of color in drinking water is <15 true color units (TCU).

The permissible level of turbidity in drinking water is <1 NTU. The permissible level of arsenic is up to 0.01 mg/l and nitrites is up to 3 mg/l.

questions.question: Temporary hardness of water is primarily due to the presence of which of the following?
questions.explanation: The temporary hardness of water is primarily due to the presence of calcium and magnesium bicarbonates.

questions.question: What is the level of hardness in soft water?
questions.explanation: The level of hardness in soft water is <1 mEq/litre.

questions.question: How would you classify a water sample that has a level of hardness of 200 mg/litre?
questions.explanation: When the level of hardness of water is in the range of 150 – 300 mg/litre, it is classified as hard water.

questions.question: A health worker is conducting periodic quality test for water sources in your area. What should be the hardness level of water used for drinking purposes?
questions.explanation: Water used for drinking purposes must have a hardness level of 1 – 3 mEq/L (moderately hard).

questions.question: Above what level of hardness is softening of water recommended?
questions.explanation: Softening of water is recommended when the hardness exceeds 3 mEq/l (150 mg/litre).

questions.question: Which of the following is not a method of removal of hardness of water?
questions.explanation:
Filtration is not a method of removal of hardness of water.

Methods for removal of hardness of water are:

• Boiling

• Addition of lime

• Addition of sodium carbonate (soda ash)

• Base exchange process

questions.question: What is the composition of permutit which is used for the base exchange process to remove hardness of water?
questions.explanation:
Permutit is a complex chemical compound made of sodium, aluminium and silica. It is used to remove hardness of water by base exchange process.

Permutit has the property of ion exchange and removes calcium and magnesium from water. It removes both permanent and temporary hardness.

questions.question: The water vapor and pollutants tend to get trapped in the lowermost layers of the atmosphere in winters. What is the reason behind this occurrence?
questions.explanation:
In winters, water vapor and pollutants get trapped in the lowermost layers of the atmosphere due to temperature inversion.

This results in the formation of smog, especially in the winter months, and this is a possible threat to human health.

questions.question: Which of the following is not an indicator of air pollution?
questions.explanation:
The heavy metal pollution index (HPI) is not an indicator of air pollution. It is a rating method and an effective tool to assess the water quality with respect to heavy metals.

Indicators of air pollution:

• Sulfur dioxide - best indicator

• Smoke or soiling index

• Grit and dust measurement

• The co-efficient of haze

• Air pollution index

• Suspended particle matter (SPM)

questions.question: Which agency monitors air quality in India?
questions.explanation: Central Pollution Control Board is the main body that monitors air quality in India and sets standards.

questions.question: Greenhouse gases include all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Carbon monoxide is not a greenhouse gas.

Greenhouse gases include:

• Water vapor

• Carbon dioxide

• Methane

• Tropospheric ozone

• Nitrous oxide

• Chlorofluorocarbons (non-natural)

questions.question: Which of the following protocols set the standard to reduce the emission of greenhouse gases internationally?
questions.explanation:
The Kyoto Protocol was an internal agreement to set internationally binding emission reduction targets.

It is linked to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The parties committed to reduce GHGs by 18% in the period between 2013-2020.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about global warming?
options: Carbon dioxide is the major greenhouse gas
CFC increases ozone levels in the stratosphere
Kyoto Protocol called for 10% reduction in greenhouse emissions
questions.answer: A. Carbon dioxide is the major greenhouse gas
questions.explanation:
Carbon dioxide is the major greenhouse gas.

Tropospheric ozone and chlorofluorocarbons are also important greenhouse gases. Water vapor is the most abundant greenhouse gas, but the water vapor produced directly by human activity contributes very little to the amount of water vapor in the atmosphere. Hence, its emissions have not been estimated.

Greenhouse gases lead to global warming, which is the major cause of climate change. Climate change accelerates species extinction on earth.

questions.question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding indoor air pollutants?

Radon is an indoor air pollutant
Mercury vapor is a source of indoor air pollution

Indoor air pollutants commonly arise from coal or fuel combustion. They include:

• Carbon monoxide

• Polyaromatic hydrocarbons

• Nitrogen

• Sulfur oxides

• Pesticides

• Asbestos

• Lead

questions.question: Which of the following is unlikely to be seen in individuals affected by indoor air pollution?
questions.explanation:
Indoor air pollution has not been linked with neurodevelopmental disorders. It can result in a higher incidence of the following:

questions.question: Which of the following is incorrect about cold stress?
options: Dry-cold conditions occur at temperatures above freezing
Cold stress can cause desire to sleep
Frostbite is common at high altitudes
questions.answer: B. Dry-cold conditions occur at temperatures above freezing

Dry-cold conditions occur at temperatures below freezing and are common at high altitudes. It results in complications like frostbite.

Wet-cold conditions occur at temperatures above freezing. It results in complications like trench foot. Cold stress also causes hypothermia which can induce numbness, loss of sensations, muscular weakness, desire to sleep, coma, and death.

Ventilation involves the quality control of incoming air but not quality control of outgoing air.

It also involves the replacement of vitiated air(air with decreased oxygen content) by a supply of fresh outdoor air. It aims to provide a comfortable thermal environment and reduce the risk of infections.

questions.question: What is the ideal number of air changes in a drawing-room?
questions.explanation:
The number of air changes in drawing rooms or living rooms must be 2 – 3 per hour.

The number of air changes in work rooms and assemblies must be 4 – 6 per hour.

questions.question: What is ventilation provided by wind blowing through a space called?
questions.explanation:
Ventilation provided by wind blowing through a space is called perflation.

Ventilation can be broadly classified as natural and mechanical:

Natural ventilation includes:

• Perflation is the ventilation of a space achieved by allowing wind to blow through it and removing the obstacles for this to happen (e.g., opening windows and doors).

• Aspiration occurs when there is an obstruction as wind bypasses it and creates a suction action

• Diffusion is the passage of air through small spaces or openings

• Cross-ventilation is when air is allowed a natural path through the space by providing openings at appropriate places, opposite each other.

The drawback of natural ventilation is that regulation of air quality is not possible.

Mechanical ventilation includes:

• Exhaust ventilation utilizes exhaust fans placed high up near the roof on the external walls. A vacuum is created by which fresh air enters the ventilated space.

• Plenum ventilation uses centrifugal fans to blow fresh air into the room and create a positive pressure, by which vitiated air is pushed out.

• Balanced ventilation is the combination of both exhaust and plenum methods of ventilation.

• Air conditioning can be done through mechanical ventilation. It is the simultaneous control of all or at least three factors that influence air quality in a confined room or space. These factors include temperature, humidity, air movement, distribution, dust, bacteria, odours and toxic gases.

questions.explanation:

• Family life

questions.question: Which of the following is incorrect about the requirements of good lighting?

Ceilings and roofs must have a 50% reflection factor

questions.explanation:

questions.question: Which of the following is correct about daylight factor?
options: D.F. = Instantaneous illumination outdoors x 100/ Simultaneously occurring illumination indoors
D.F. = Instantaneous illumination indoors x 100/ Simultaneously occurring illumination outdoors
D.F. = Delayed illumination indoors x 100/ Simultaneously occurring illumination outdoors
D.F. = Delayed illumination outdoors x 100/ Simultaneously occurring illumination indoors
questions.answer: B. D.F. = Instantaneous illumination indoors x 100/ Simultaneously occurring illumination outdoors

Daylight factor (D.F.) is the ratio of the illumination at a given point to illumination at a point exposed simultaneously to the whole hemisphere of the sky (taken as 500-foot candles) excluding direct sunlight.

The D.F. is used for the measurement of daylight. It is determined by a modified photo-electric meter called daylight factor meter.

In living rooms, the daylight factor should be at least 8% and in kitchens, it should be 10%.

questions.question: A watchmaker presents with symptoms of eye strain. What is the optimum illumination recommended at his workplace?
questions.explanation:

questions.question: What is the intensity of sound produced during whispering?
questions.explanation:
Whispering produces a sound of 20 – 30 dB.

questions.question: What is the upper limit of daily exposure to noise which people can tolerate without hearing damage?
questions.explanation:
The upper limit of daily exposure to noise which people can tolerate without hearing damage is 85 dB. This is the maximum acceptable noise level.

It has been observed that the human ear responds in a non-uniform way to different sound-pressure levels. A weighting curve, called curve A has been constructed which takes into account the subjective effects of sound. Sound-pressure levels are therefore expressed in dBA because this reflects the perception of that sound emission by the normal human ear.

questions.question: A steel plant worker presented with sudden onset of bilateral hearing loss after hearing a blast in the plant. On examination, both his tympanic membranes were ruptured. What would have been the minimum intensity of the blast to cause this injury?
questions.explanation: A minimum intensity of 160 dB can lead to rupture of the tympanic membrane, resulting in hearing loss.

questions.question: A 32-year-old patient presents with complaints of whistling and buzzing in both his ears since yesterday. He gives a history of being exposed to continuous noise due to construction near his house. At what intensity of noise do such conditions begin to occur?
questions.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of auditory fatigue that begins to appear with exposure to noise at 90 dB.

questions.question: An airline ground staff officer with difficulty hearing is found to have permanent hearing loss on follow up. Continuous exposure to sound above what intensity can cause this condition?
questions.explanation: Continuous exposure to sound above 100 dB can cause permanent hearing loss.

questions.question: The WHO defines disabling hearing loss in adults as a hearing loss of more than:

questions.question: Which of the following is a unit of absorbed dose of radiation?
questions.explanation: Rad is a unit of absorbed dose of radiation by tissue or material. It has been replaced by the SI unit which is gray (Gy).

questions.question: What is the SI unit of radiation dose equivalent?
questions.explanation:
The SI unit of radiation dose equivalent is sievert (Sv).

Dose equivalent (H) = Absorbed dose (D) x Quality factor (Q)

The quality factor depends upon the density of ionization produced in the tissue by radiation. The factor Q for X-rays, γ-rays and electrons is 1 and that for an alpha particle is 20.

questions.question: What is the permissible dose of manmade radiation per year?
questions.explanation: The permissible dose of manmade radiation is 5 rads per year.

questions.question: A young girl who is 1 month pregnant is concerned about a chest X-ray that she had taken 3 weeks back. What is the dose of radiation below which deterministic effects on the fetus are not seen?
questions.explanation:
Deterministic effects on the fetus are not seen below 5 rads or 50 mSv of radiation.

Dose limits of radiation exposure are:

• Occupational exposure - Effective dose should not exceed 20 mSv/year averaged over 5 consecutive years / 30 mSv in a year.

• General public exposure - Effective dose should not exceed 1 mSv/year

• Occupational exposure for pregnant staff - Effective dose to the fetus should not exceed 1mSv/year (same as the general public).

For pregnant patients who require diagnostics with exposure to ionising radiation, the radiation protection principles are followed:

• The exposure should be justified

• The dose should be as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA principle)

• The dose limit is not particularly specified as it involves a single time exposure to diagnostic radiation. Usually, the effective dose to the fetus is <1msv and deterministic effects to the fetus are not seen below 50 mSv (5 Rad).

questions.question: What was the 10 days rule in radiation related to?
questions.explanation:
The 10 days rule in radiation was related to pregnancy. It is aimed at preventing unintentional exposure of the embryo or fetus to radiation.

This rule states that if a radiograph is being done on the abdomen or pelvis of a woman in her childbearing age, then it should be done during the 10 days following the onset of menstruation.

In most situations, there is growing evidence that strict adherence to the "ten-day rule" may be unnecessarily restrictive. Since organogenesis starts 3 to 5 weeks post-conception, it was felt that radiation exposure in early pregnancy couldn't result in malformation. Based on this, it was suggested to do away with the 10-day rule and replace it with a 28-day rule. This means that radiological examination if justified, can be carried throughout the cycle until a period is missed.

questions.question: Solid wastes generally should not contain:
questions.explanation:
Solid wastes should not contain nightsoil, which is untreated human waste (feces).

Solid wastes generally contain:

• Garbage (food wastes)

• Rubbish waste (papers, plastics, etc.)

• Demolition products (bricks, masonry, etc.)

• Sewage treatment residue

• Dead animals and other waste materials

questions.question: Which of the following is not a method of solid waste or refuse disposal?
questions.explanation:
Oxidation ponds are not used for solid waste or refuse disposal. It is used for sewage treatment.

Methods of solid waste disposal are:

• Dumping

• Controlled tipping

• Incineration

• Composting

• Manure pits

• Burial

questions.question: Which of the following is the most insanitary method of waste disposal?
questions.explanation:
The most insanitary method of waste disposal is dumping.

Methods of waste disposal include:

• Controlled tipping or sanitary landfill - Most satisfactory method of refuse disposal where suitable land is available

• Incineration - Method of choice where suitable land is not available

• Composting

• Manure pits

• Burial

• Dumping

questions.question: Which method is most appropriate when suitable land for waste disposal is available?
questions.explanation:
Controlled tipping is the most satisfactory method of refuse disposal when suitable land is available.

In this method, waste materials are placed in a trench, compacted, and covered with earth at the end of the day. This method is also called a sanitary landfill. Chemical, bacteriological and physical changes occur in the buried refuse with temperatures rising to over 60 degrees Celsius within 7 days.

Methods used for controlled tipping are:

• Trench method

• Ramp method

• Area method

Sewage farming is also a method of sewage disposal in places where sufficient and suitable land is available. It is also called land treatment or broad irrigation.

questions.question: Which of the following is false about composting?
options: Bangalore method is an aerobic process
Mechanical composting uses a controlled environment
Nightsoil can also be disposed with composting
Compost has few or no disease-causing pathogens
questions.answer: A. Bangalore method is an aerobic process
questions.explanation:
The Bangalore method of composting is an anaerobic process.

Composting is a method of combined disposal of refuse and nightsoil. In this process, organic matter is broken down into compost. It has manure value and few or no disease-causing pathogens.

Bangalore method is an anaerobic method and is also called hot fermentation process. Trenches with a depth of not more than 90cm are used for this. This is done by spreading a layer of refuse (15 cm thick) at the bottom of the trench and nightsoil (5cm thick) is added next. Layers of refuse and nightsoil are added alternatively till the heap rises to 30cm above ground level. The heap is then covered with excavated earth. At the end of 4 – 6 months, decomposition will be completed.

Mechanical composting is an aerobic process. In this method, compost is manufactured on a large scale by processing raw materials and turning out a finished product. The refuse is first cleared of salvageable materials. It is then pulverised to reduce the size of particles to less than 2 inches. The pulverised refuse is then mixed with sewage, sludge or nightsoil in a rotating machine and incubated.

questions.question: All of the following are methods of disposing only excreta except:
questions.explanation:
Bangalore method, also known as the hot fermentation process, is a form of composting that is used for disposing of both solid waste and nightsoil (excreta).

Methods of excreta disposal:

• Unsewered areas:

• Service type latrines (conservancy system) - In this, nightsoil is collected manually from pail or bucket type latrines and then disposed of by burying or composting

• Non-service type latrines (sanitary latrines)

• Borehole latrine

• Dug well or pit latrine

• Water-seal latrines – Examples are P.R.A.I. type, R.C.A. type, and Sulabh shauchalaya

• Septic tanks

• Aqua privy

• Latrines for camps and temporary use

• Shallow and deep trench latrine

• Pit latrine

• Borehole latrine

• Sewered areas:

• Water carriage system and sewage treatment

• Primary treatment – Screening, removal of grit and plain sedimentation

• Secondary treatment – Trickling filters, activated sludge process

• Other methods – sea and river outfalls, sewage farming, oxidation ponds

questions.question: A military camp is being set up in an area for one month. Which of the following latrines will not be suitable here?
questions.explanation:
Septic tanks cannot be used for camps and temporary purposes.

questions.question: Which of the following is the oldest non-service type of latrines in India?
questions.explanation:
The oldest non-service type of latrines in India is the borehole latrine. It was introduced in the 1930s to combat hookworm infections.

Special equipment called auger is used to dig a borehole latrine.

Advantages:

• No special staff is needed for upkeep as after using the latrine is closed and another hole is dug elsewhere

• Breeding of flies is less

• No water pollution if located far from a water source

Demerits:

• Fills up rapidly

• Augers are not readily available

• Water pollution is still a risk

questions.question: There is an outbreak of hookworm infection in your locality. On investigation, it is found that the outbreak is a result of open-air defecation. The district council decides to construct an RCA type of latrine in every household. What is the optimum water seal required?
questions.explanation:
The optimum water seal required for an RCA type of latrine is 2 – 2.5 cm.

It was designed by the Research-cum-Action Projects (RCA) in Environmental Sanitation of the Ministry of Health. Water seals aids in preventing flies and other organisms from reaching the waste. It also prevents the escape of odors and foul gases, eliminating the nuisance from the smell.

Features of RCA type of latrine

Location
More than 15m away from the water source

Squatting plate
Should be impervious and should allow for drainage of water

Pan
Receives the nightsoil, urine, and washes water.

Trap
Holds the water and provides the water seal. A good trap has an effective seal of around 2 – 2.5 cms.

Connecting pipe
Present in indirect type and absent in direct type

Dug well
Has to be changed after it is filled

Superstructure
Built for privacy and shelter

questions.question: A health committee formed under Swachh Bharat Mission is involved in constructing septic tanks in every household. Which of the following is true about a septic tank?
questions.explanation:
The recommended retention period for a septic tank is 24 hours.

If the retention period is too short, there is insufficient treatment of sewage and if it is too long, then undue septicity results.

There are single and double-chambered septic tanks. The minimum capacity recommended for a septic tank is 500 gallons. The depth of a septic tank is usually 1.5 to 2m.

questions.question: Which of the following is false about the sewage treatment shown in the image below?
options: Desludging must be done at least once a year
Anaerobic digestion occurs inside the tank
Soap and disinfectants like phenol should not be used inside the tank
questions.answer: B. Useful for very large communities
questions.explanation: The given image is of a septic tank. It is not useful for very large communities and is used for household sewage treatment.

questions.question: What is wastewater without human excreta called?
questions.explanation:
Wastewater that doesn’t contain human excreta is called sullage. It is also called greywater. E.g., waste water from the kitchen.

Sewage is wastewater from a community that contains solid and liquid excreta along with street and yard washings. It is also called blackwater.

questions.question: What is the average amount of sewage which flows though the sewerage system in 24 hours known as?
questions.explanation: The average amount of sewage which flows though the sewerage system in 24 hours is known as dry weather flow.

questions.question: Which of the following is not used to express the strength of sewage?
questions.explanation:
E. coli count is not used to express the strength of sewage.

The strength of sewage is expressed only in terms of:

• Biochemical oxygen demand

• Chemical oxygen demand

• Suspended solids

questions.question: What does the biochemical oxygen demand of sewage indicate?
questions.explanation:
Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) indicates the organic content of sewage.

It is defined as the amount of oxygen absorbed by a sample of sewage for aerobic destruction by living microorganisms.

If wastewater contains toxic substances, the organic load is measured by the chemical oxygen demand.

questions.question: Which of the following values of biochemical oxygen demand would indicate that the sewage is weak?
questions.explanation:
Sewage with biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) of 100mg/L would indicate that it is weak.

If the BOD is ≥ 300 mg/L, sewage is said to be strong.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a part of the primary treatment of sewage?
questions.explanation: Aeration tank is not a part of primary treatment of sewage. It is a part of secondary treatment of sewage.

questions.question: What is the function of the grit chamber in modern sewage treatment plants?
options: Allow anaerobic auto-digestion of organic matter
questions.explanation: The function of the grit chamber in modern sewage treatment plants is to allow heavier particles in the sewage to settle.

questions.question: Trickling filter method is used in which of the following?
questions.explanation: The trickling filter method is used in secondary sewage treatment.

questions.question: Which of the following is the heart of the activated sludge process?
questions.explanation: The heart of the activated sludge process is the aeration tanks.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a requirement for an oxidation pond?
questions.explanation:
Aeration is not a requirement for an oxidation pond.

Oxidation ponds are also called waste stabilization ponds or redox ponds or sewage lagoons. They have become a popular method of purifying sewage for small communities. It is usually an open, shallow pool of around 1 – 1.5m depth with an inlet and outlet.

Requisites for an oxidation pond include:

• Algae

• Saprophytic bacteria

• Sunlight

All of the above factors help in the treatment of sewage waste through aerobic and anaerobic processes. The effluent formed can be used for land irrigation or can be forwarded for further treatment.

questions.question: Which of the following is false regarding mosquitoes?
options: It is the definitive host in malaria
Mansonia is a vector for Malayan filariasis
Life span of mosquitoes is around 8 to 34 days
All mosquitoes can travel only for 100 metres
questions.answer: D. All mosquitoes can travel only for 100 metres
questions.explanation: Most mosquitoes can travel or fly for distances up to 11 kms.

questions.question: Which of the following species of mosquitoes breed in dirty water and water bodies containing aquatic vegetation respectively?
questions.explanation: Culex species of mosquitoes breed mostly in dirty and polluted water. Mansonia species of mosquitoes breed in water bodies containing aquatic vegetation.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about larva of mosquitoes?
options: Culex larva lies in water with head faced downwards
Anopheles larva lies parallel to the undersurface of water
questions.answer: A. Anopheles larva has siphon tube
questions.explanation:
Anopheles larva has no siphon tube as shown in the image below.

The image given below shows Culex larva having a siphon tube.

questions.question: Identify the species of mosquito shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
The given image is of an Aedes mosquito.

They can be identified with the stripes on the legs and body. They are also called tiger mosquitoes because of their stripes.

questions.question: A 25-year-old lady from a tribal area presented with fever, chills, vomiting, and abdominal pain for 4 days. The peripheral smear of the patient is given below. Which of the following is true about the mosquito which transmits this disease?
options: Keeps its body horizontal while feeding
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and peripheral smear showing ring form/ early trophozoites in erythrocytes are suggestive of Plasmodium falciparum malaria. It is transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes. They have spotted wings.

They breed in clean water. Their larva has no siphon tube and lies parallel to the undersurface of water. They tend to sit with their heads low and their rare ends raised high, especially when feeding.

questions.question: A patient presented with fever, headache, and retro-orbital pain for 3 days. He tested positive for the NS1 antigen. Which of the following mosquitoes transmits the disease he's suffering from?
questions.explanation: The given clinical scenario along with the positive NS1 antigen test is suggestive of dengue fever. It is transmitted by the Aedes mosquito, which is also called as tiger mosquito.

questions.question:
Which of the following diseases is not transmitted by Aedes mosquito?

1. Chikungunya

2. Yellow fever

3. Japanese encephalitis

4. Rift valley fever

5. West Nile fever
questions.explanation:
Japanese encephalitis and West Nile fever are transmitted by Culex mosquitoes.

Chikungunya, yellow fever, and rift valley fever are transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes.

questions.question: A banker who is scheduled to travel to Congo is advised to take the yellow fever vaccine. What is the flight range of the mosquito which transmits this disease?
questions.explanation: Yellow fever is transmitted by the Aedes mosquito. Its flight range is 100 metres.

questions.question: A patient with fever and mucosal bleeding is diagnosed with dengue fever. Which of the following is false about the mosquito which transmits this disease?
options: Development of larva from egg does not require water
It has a striped body pattern
questions.answer: B. Development of larva from egg does not require water
questions.explanation:
Dengue fever is transmitted by the Aedes mosquito. The conversion from the egg stage to the larval stage of this mosquito requires water.

Eggs of any mosquito species do not survive without water. But the eggs of Aedes mosquitoes lie dormant in dry conditions for up to about nine months. They can hatch if exposed to favourable conditions such as water and food.

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the OPD with complaints of fever and headache for 5 days. Serological examination shows the presence of IgM antibodies to the JE virus. Which of the following mosquitoes transmits this disease?
questions.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Japanese encephalitis. It is transmitted by Culex mosquitoes like Culex tritaeniorhynchus
